text:
On more than one occasion in his life, Aaron Reitz has sworn an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic. Most recently, it was on July 9, to serve as the lead federal prosecutor for the Southern District of Texas, one of the most significant U.S. attorney postings in the country.

By its own writing, this U.S. attorney's office, which encompasses Houston and Galveston down to the southern border, prosecutes more federal criminal cases than most other districts across the country.

"For forever, Texas has been underwater in terms of resources for the federal bench; all four districts, but especially Southern," Carl Tobias, a University of Richmond law professor, told Houston Public Media. "And that could be explained pretty clearly by the border, I think a lot of it."

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Reitz, a firebrand conservative who has drawn scrutiny for challenging the results of the 2020 presidential election and arguing that court orders can justifiably be disobeyed, was not tapped for the role by the usual route. Bloomberg Law reports he was not appointed by President Donald Trump to serve as the U.S. attorney, though he had worked for the Trump administration previously. Instead, the district's judges selected him to serve in the office, allowing Reitz to circumvent a Senate confirmation hearing.

That process, though permissible under federal law, is not the traditional route, by which a nominee is appointed by the executive branch of government and then confirmed by the Senate.

"I'm honored to serve as the chief federal law enforcement officer and lawyer for this mission-critical district," Reitz said in a news release when he was sworn in. "Our office will relentlessly combat violent crime, illegal immigration, drug and human trafficking, corruption, and fraud. We will faithfully uphold the rule of law and protect the public. Things are about to get very bad for criminals in the Southern District of Texas."

Two days before that, on July 7, a van carrying four immigrants without legal status in Houston was pursued by federal immigration agents. When U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents approached the van, the federal government alleged the driver, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, attempted to use his car as a weapon, a claim the other three men in the van dispute. An ICE officer fired his gun and shot Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old father of three who had lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years, according to his family.

"They're killing me," Salgado Araujo said, clutching his stomach, according to an attorney for one of the witnesses. He died thereafter. His killing has spurred the community into action, prompting multiple investigations at the local, state and federal levels. Protests have called for transparency from the federal government.

Now a month into the role, Reitz, whose office did not make him available for an interview, has helmed the federal government's legal representation related to the shooting. Following the FBI and U.S. Department of Homeland Security's investigation, they will present their findings to the U.S. attorney's office for the Southern District. It would then be up to Reitz and his affiliates to decide whether or not to press any federal charges against the agents involved.

Out of the arena — and back in

The first time Reitz swore an oath to defend the U.S. Constitution was just after he graduated from Texas A&M University, when he entered the U.S. military.

He had just married his wife, Meredith, whom he had met on the school bus to his first day of classes at Barbara Bush Middle School in San Antonio. The two began dating when they attended Ronald Reagan High School, and they both went to Texas A&M. Eventually, though, Meredith decided to transfer to the University of Texas at Austin — as Aaron has said, Meredith, who wanted to be a veterinarian, had taken the rectal temperatures of too many cows. They broke up in the process but soon rekindled and were married in October 2009.

Less than a year later, the Reitzes moved to Quantico, Virginia, before he was deployed to Afghanistan with the U.S. Marine Corps in early 2011. After returning to the United States, Reitz applied to the UT Law School.

His de-facto resume, which he touted during his first run for office in 2020, touts his conservative record: he was a fellow at the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative thinktank; he was chosen by his peers as the Lino Graglia Conservative Student of the Year at UT; he was a fellow at the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative nonprofit; he was president of UT's chapter of the Federalist Society; and served as editor-in-chief of the Texas Review of Law and Politics. After graduating, Reitz went into private practice at Bracewell LLP, a Houston-based law firm.

"Wonderful law firm, but really felt that I had been taken out of the arena," Reitz told The Texan in a 2019 interview.

At that time around 2017, Don Willett, a justice on the Texas Supreme Court, was appointed by Trump to the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. That left a vacancy on the state's highest civil court. After Willett was confirmed to the bench, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott appointed his general counsel, Jimmy Blacklock, to the Texas Supreme Court.

As luck had it, Reitz knew Blacklock. In Austin, he would recount, conservative circles ran small. He reached out to Blacklock and asked to serve as chief clerk to the new justice. Blacklock accepted.

In Reitz's own telling, he took a 70% pay cut to join Blacklock's team. But it was the jump into public policy that Reitz wanted to take advantage of. In the spring of 2019, Reitz decided to run for Texas House of Representatives in a district representing southwest Austin, which had flipped for Democrat Vikki Goodwin in 2018. He resigned from Blacklock's office in May 2019.

In the interview with The Texan, Reitz said that, while he would be voting for Trump’s reelection in November 2020, his district's voting trend was "proto-typical suburbia, that was a little bit squeamish about Trump. Not his policies, but you know, you had a lot of families that were saying, ‘Gosh, I'm for Trump, but I'm not super in favor of his Tweets... the persona, I don't want my young boy to grow up to be like Donald Trump."

On primary election day, March 3, 2020, days before much of the country shut down for the COVID-19 pandemic, Reitz placed fourth in the Republican primary for the Texas House seat. By that December, Reitz was working on the team with the Texas Attorney General's Office seeking to suspend certifying the results of the 2020 election won by Democrat Joe Biden.

The day before Reitz was set to begin working in the office of Texas AG Ken Paxton, Reitz told The Texas Tribune, several OAG officials reported Paxton to the FBI over concerns of abuses of office, the same allegations that would result in Paxton's impeachment in the Texas House of Representatives three years later.

But he opted to stick by Paxton through the scandal as the AG, who now is running for U.S. Senate, was acquitted by the Texas Senate. Through his time at the OAG, Reitz said he worked on border security matters, religious issues, and led the election integrity divisions in 2020 and 2022. That included working on Texas v. Pennsylvania, a lawsuit brought by Paxton's office to suspend the certification of election results in key states that were for Biden in the 2020 election.

In April 2021, Reitz led a lawsuit against the Biden administration that accused the federal government of lapsing in border security, allowing COVID-19 to spread via migrants traveling to the U.S. By October 2022, after the case had worked through the courts, both the OAG and the Biden administration agreed to dismiss the case.

Reitz led a similar effort a year later, in April 2022, which was also dismissed later that year. In the initial complaint, Reitz called the standard process of an immigration hearing to argue for or against removal "slow" and said it requires either paying for a migrant without legal status in detention or running the risk of their fleeing.

Years later, Reitz would compare his relationship with Paxton to a football game: Paxton was the head coach, and Reitz was the offensive coordinator. In total, he would tell Austin's ABC affiliate, KVUE, he led 46 lawsuits against the Biden administration, a significant portion of which were dedicated to immigration policy.

Eventually, Reitz left Paxton's office to work as a chief of staff to U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas. He resigned from the OAG on May 12, 2023, two weeks before Paxton would be impeached.

"We'll keep fighting this war together," Reitz said in his resignation letter to Paxton. "But now it's my time to fight it on a different front."

Just and unjust laws

Every Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Reitz said in an Instagram post in 2022, he rereads King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," an open letter the civil rights leader wrote in April 1963 while imprisoned for leading demonstrations in Alabama. In it, King writes that, just as people have a duty to follow just laws, they have a duty to break unjust laws as well.

It was that theory — that someone could justifiably break laws that they found morally wrong — that had rankled the U.S. Senate judiciary committee.

On a Wednesday morning in February 2025, the committee convened with the goal of establishing the backbone of the Department of Justice. Three nominees sat before them, making up three of the most crucial law enforcement roles in the federal government.

There was D. John Sauer, nominated to be Solicitor General, on the left and Harmeet Dhillon, Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights nominee, on the right. In between them sat Reitz, then 37 years old, in a blue pinstripe suit, awaiting his hearing to eventually become the Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Policy at the Department of Justice.

Sauer and Dhillon remain in their roles today. Reitz would hold his role for 72 days before resigning to run for an elected office.

When Trump stated on Truth Social he would appoint Reitz to the office, he called the Texan "a true MAGA attorney, a warrior for our Constitution, and will do an outstanding job at DOJ."

"He is currently my chief of staff and has the virtually impossible job of keeping me out of trouble," Cruz, a member of the committee, said with a laugh. "In that regard, he has failed spectacularly."

Reitz, in turn, called Cruz a mentor.

Democrats on the committee, though, had some concerns, mostly surrounding Reitz's digital footprint on X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter. One post Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois took issue with was from March 30, 2020, when U.S. Judge Lee Yeakel blocked Texas from closing abortion clinics during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Looking for some Andrew Jackson-level leadership on this one," Reitz wrote at the time. "‘Judge Yeakel has made this decision. Now let him enforce it.'"

"So you're saying that a legal court order from a federal court should not be followed under some circumstances," Durbin said. "What would those circumstances be?"

"What I'm saying is that there are some instances in which a public official is lawfully bound by the holding of a particular court, in which case that official would in fact be lawfully required to be bound by it," Reitz said. "I can't speak, though, ranking member Durbin, for all instances in which that dynamic may or may not be in play given a certain lawsuit."

Durbin called his response "an incredible statement by someone who wants to be a part of the Department of Justice." It was also prescient: during Reitz's time in the Trump administration, it began defying court orders on immigration policy.

Aside from his political theory on ignoring court orders, it was Reitz's social media presence that garnered the most attention from his confirmation hearing. He had deleted the vast majority of posts from his X account, which he had created in 2014.

"I have oftentimes observed a practice of regularly deleting old tweets," Reitz said in his written testimony. "I recall, though am not certain, clearing out my X account shortly before joining the Senate as a Chief of Staff in 2023, since most of my social media activity was related to my prior service in Texas and not related to my role as a Senate staffer."

"Friendly reminder that ‘birthright citizenship' is not a thing," Reitz had tweeted in 2021, according to a screenshot shared during the hearing.

Another tweet from February 2021 called the U.S. Supreme Court's Bostock decision, which codified protections from workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, "the worst SCOTUS decision since Obergefell,” which permitted same-sex marriage.

In September 2020, Reitz shared a photo of late Sen. Joe McCarthy, who spread fears of communism during the Red Scare of the 1950s, with the caption, "Bring back the good ol' days."

The posts, ultimately, were not enough to halt his confirmation. A month later, on March 26, 2025, Reitz became one of the senior most law enforcement officials in the nation, and he once again swore an oath to defend the U.S. Constitution.

By June 11, however, Reitz was resigning. As he put it in his resignation letter to Trump, "you charged me with developing and implementing the battle plans to advance your Law and Order Agenda and to restore integrity to our Justice System. ... Duty now calls me to continue that fight on a new front."

The next day, Reitz announced a bid to become the next attorney general of Texas, succeeding Paxton.

Battle tested

A month out from this year’s Republican primaries in Texas — when GOP voters would select their pick to run for Texas attorney general, among other seats — Reitz was thinking about the oaths he had sworn in the past to protect the U.S. Constitution from all enemies, foreign and domestic. Those domestic enemies, he postulated, include the modern day Democratic Party.

"What I have come to believe from long-fought personal experience is that there are — the leadership class of the Democratic Party today can rightfully be construed as enemies of the Constitution," Reitz told KVUE. "This isn't me being hyperbolic. This isn't me exaggerating with political rhetoric. We have seen what the left is capable of doing. We have seen what the Democratic Party is willing to push when they have the power. And I believe that what they want for this state and our nation is antithetical to our closest values, to American values, to western civilization, and to the United States Constitution."

That included, Reitz would write, the head of the Texas House of Representatives' Democratic Caucus, state Rep. Gene Wu of Houston. Responding to a post that depicted Wu stating that several marginalized groups, including Latino, Black, Asian and other communities, "share the same oppressor," Reitz said he wanted Wu's citizenship revoked.

"As AG, I want to see [Wu] de-naturalized," Reitz wrote on social media on Feb. 9. "On what basis? He likely concealed his anti-American sentiment throughout his citizenship app process — the details of which are conspicuously absent from public record."

Wu, whose office did not return a request for an interview, was born in China before moving to Texas with his family at a young age. He became a U.S. citizen around the age of 14, through his parents.

Reitz' former bosses, Cruz and Paxton, both criticized Wu for his "bigotry" and "racist" comments. Reitz was also not the only candidate in the race for Texas attorney general to raise concerns over Wu's comments. U.S. Rep. Chip Roy said Wu should resign from the state legislature. State Sen. Mayes Middleton of Galveston, who would go on to secure the Republican nomination, wrote that Wu was "showing us why only those born in America should be eligible to run for office."

It was Reitz, however, who drew the most attention for his comments. He had been the hand-picked successor to the attorney general's office — Paxton, who was leaving the role after three terms to run for U.S. Senate, endorsed him. As part of his campaign, Reitz labeled himself as the only candidate who was "battle tested" in a law enforcement office.

In the six years since Reitz last ran for public office, his platform had shifted further to the right. By his own submissions on Ballotpedia, his three key messages of his 2020 campaign for the state legislature were to "preserve Texas's vibrant economic climate through low taxes and light regulations," "Make our schools and communities safer," and, "Give our children a first-class education." By his 2026 campaign, his three key messages were "advancing an America First Law & Order agenda," "Securing our southern border," and, "root[ing] out corruption and stop[ping] far-left local governments from undermining Texas values."

Just as in his 2020 campaign, however, Reitz finished in fourth place. As Middleton and Roy headed to a runoff, Reitz threw his endorsement to Middleton. Since then, Reitz had stayed relatively quiet, campaigning for Paxton and Middleton and sharing the occasional social media post from Trump administration officials.

Then, on July 9, Reitz made his next career move known — he was sworn in as the new U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas.

His appointment prompted congratulations from Cruz, Paxton and Abbott, the Texas governor, who wrote on social media, “You'll do great. Huge win for Texas.”

Added Paxton: "I know Aaron will be an outstanding U.S. Attorney and will serve the Southern District of Texas with integrity and a strong commitment to the rule of law that will undoubtedly advance the cause of justice in our state."

‘Let the justice system work'

On July 15, a week after Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was shot and killed by an ICE agent, the FBI executed a search warrant on the van involved in the shooting, which Salgado Araujo was driving. In the search warrant, signed by FBI Special Agent David McNeilly and approved by federal magistrate judge Richard Bennett, a new allegation came forward: law enforcement officers had seen "plastic bags with what appeared to be a white crystal-like substance packaged in small plastic bags." The substance, McNeilly wrote, was "consistent with methamphetamine."

The search warrant was unsealed and made public soon after. Aside from the allegation itself, some officials questioned the decision to share the indictment publicly so soon into the investigation.

"I've been doing this 20 years. I've never seen a federal search warrant, at least before a grand jury presentation, let alone the probable cause statement behind it," Sean Teare, the Harris County District Attorney, said on Houston Matters on July 17. "And there was no evidentiary value to be gained from it anyway. It's puzzling. It's concerning."

It was the first time drugs had been mentioned at all in the investigation of the shooting, which was being investigated by the FBI, Harris County DA and the Texas Rangers, concurrently and independently. It was also an allegation that Salgado Araujo's family did not believe.

"After consulting with my client and his family, our understanding is that this was granulated salt, which is paired with lemon and water as a homemade electrolyte mix used by outdoor workers in extreme Texas heat, not methamphetamine or any other illicit substance," said Ruby Powers, an attorney for Salgado Araujo's brother, Victor, who was also in the van the day of the shooting.

Reitz confirmed to The Texas Tribune, in an Aug. 13 report, that the substance tested by the FBI was not meth.

It's not immediately clear what led up to the search warrant being unsealed, or who decided to unseal it. As federal attorneys who would oversee the prosecution of the shooting, if there were to be any, U.S. attorneys likely played a role in the decision, according to Jay Coons, a criminal justice professor at Sam Houston State University.

"There is a lot of controversy rising up out of this shooting, and there is not too much being said by federal authorities," Coons said in an interview with Houston Public Media. "In my experience, what I would believe is this is why the affidavit was unsealed as quickly as it was and made public: because this kind of takes away from the narrative that the deceased individual was this great guy. ... Well, this information would argue against that. And it also gives a reason why he would be attempting to escape."

Regardless of the decision to unseal the search warrant, Reitz made his preliminary stance on the shooting known by the end of the week. In a video statement shared by the U.S. attorney's office, Reitz stated that evidence indicated federal agents were searching for two Guatemalan men "known to be driving a white van" who were subject to deportation. While looking for that van, they allegedly found "a similar van" being driven by Salgado Araujo on July 7 and attempted to pull the van over, but the "aliens then fled, conducting a rapid U-turn and hopping a median to get away. The agents chose not to pursue."

Shortly before 7 a.m. that morning, the federal agents saw the van again, Reitz said.

"And again," Reitz said, "the illegal aliens attempted to flee, but this time the agents successfully surrounded the vehicle. At some point, two of the four officers got out of their vehicles and instructed the non-compliant aliens to put the van in park. Preliminary information indicates the driver shifted the van into reverse, then forward again, while an officer was partially inside the van or immediately next to it. During this confrontation between federal agents and a group of illegal aliens attempting to flee, one of the officers fired a single shot."

Reitz also raised the allegation of "possible narcotics trafficking and drug offenses," given the bags of powderlike substance in the van.

"I want to reiterate: This assessment is based on preliminary information given to my office," Reitz said. "We draw no decisive conclusions and believe federal law enforcement will conduct a thorough investigation."

As part of the investigation, the substance was tested for narcotics. Though the official results of the test have not been made public, U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, D-Houston, who has worked alongside the family and championed the independent investigation, said last month on social media that testing showed the substance was in fact an electrolyte powder.

Coons, who worked in the Harris County Sheriff's Office for more than three decades, said the decision to file a search warrant over the substances was proper police work. By contrast, he said, the decision to unseal the search warrant without knowing what the substances were could be perceived as hasty.

"If we release that document and not allege but insinuate that there was narcotics in there," Coons hypothesized, "what do we say when a test result comes back and it was whatever it was? That's going to do more harm than good. ... So, my thoughts there would have been, great idea to release it, but let's hold off until we know what we have."

Reitz's office has also pushed to keep at least one of the key witnesses to the shooting, Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, in federal custody, even after a federal judge ordered his release. On July 29, Reitz submitted a motion to reverse the decision permitting Pliego's release, which was denied days later. The U.S. attorney's office is appealing the decision to the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which had not made a ruling on Pliego's release as of Monday.

"We are doing everything we can to seek the truth and do the right thing," Reitz said in the July 16 video statement. "In the meantime, I encourage the public to give the FBI and DHS the opportunity to investigate. Let the justice system work. And pray for safer communities in which law, order, and justice prevail."

title: Trump's Border Wall is Working, but There's Still a Gaping Hole on Tribal Land | FAIRUS.org
description:
They do not, however, close the gap on Tohono O’odham land.
Tribal leaders have repeatedly refused consent for a continuous physical wall, sued to block construction, and posted “no trespassing” signs aimed at contractors.
Respect for tribal sovereignty should not require abandoning national sovereignty over the international boundary.
However, gaps like the Tohono O’odham Reservation remain problematic.
Respect for tribal sovereignty should not require abandoning national sovereignty over the international boundary.
text:
Americans hear endless talk about the southern border—walls, surges, gotaways—but few know about one of the border’s biggest vulnerabilities: the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation.

Stretching across roughly 2.8 million acres of Sonoran Desert in southern Arizona, this sovereign tribal land shares about 62 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border. That stretch is no minor footnote. It has long served as a preferred corridor for illegal aliens and Mexican cartels precisely because its legal status as sovereign tribal territory limits the full power of federal enforcement.

The Trump administration is moving aggressively to construct double-layer barriers, roads, lighting, and related infrastructure across large sections of the southern border. Those physical deterrents work where they exist. They do not, however, close the gap on Tohono O’odham land. Tribal leaders have repeatedly refused consent for a continuous physical wall, sued to block construction, and posted “no trespassing” signs aimed at contractors. The result is a weak point for exploitation that is common knowledge to cartels and smugglers.

Federal agents operate on the reservation under agreements for checkpoints, forward operating bases, surveillance towers, and vehicle barriers. Vehicle barriers are designed to stop cars, however, not people on foot. Integrated towers and sensors help interdict some traffic, but they do not create the physical obstacle that has proven effective elsewhere. Tribal refusal of a permanent barrier leaves open desert terrain that cartels treat as a highway.

Respect for tribal sovereignty should not require abandoning national sovereignty over the international boundary.

When enforcement tightened in other sectors in the 1990s and 2000s, traffic shifted onto the reservation. By the mid-2000s, tribal police and federal agents were dealing with daily crossings measured in the hundreds to over a thousand. Drug seizures ran into tens of thousands of pounds of marijuana annually, alongside cocaine and later methamphetamine and fentanyl. Cartels established scouts on mountain tops inside the reservation, using binoculars and radios to guide loads around patrols.

In one major 2011 operation, authorities dismantled a Sinaloa Cartel cell that had funneled multi-ton marijuana shipments and illegal aliens through remote areas near the San Miguel Gate—a tribal crossing point—while moving cash and weapons south. Nearly half the defendants in that case were tribal members.

Poverty on the reservation has incentivized tribal members to become participants in the trade. Federal investigators have repeatedly documented cases in which Tohono O’odham residents acted as scouts, drivers, or stash-house operators for cartel organizations. Court records show dozens of tribal members prosecuted for marijuana and human smuggling. Cartels have staged loads on the Mexican side near Tohono O’odham communities, then moved them north across the lightly controlled line.

Cartels also use migrant surges as diversions so backpackers carrying methamphetamine, heroin, or fentanyl can slip through elsewhere. Migrant remains recovered on the reservation number in the hundreds over two decades, acceptable collateral damage to the cartels in the lucrative business of ferrying drugs and human cargo across the border.

The federal government cannot simply seize the land or ignore tribal consent the way it can on ordinary federal or private property. The 1907 Roosevelt Reservation—a narrow 60-foot strip along the border—has been the subject of recent litigation, but the broader reservation remains contested ground. A federal judge recently declined to block wall construction in the strip, but the tribe’s opposition and legal challenges continue to slow and limit the project.

Meanwhile, the double wall rising in other Arizona and southwestern sectors will simply displace pressure onto this softer target. Every mile without a physical barrier is a comparative advantage for cartels.

The Trump administration’s efforts to tighten border security have been a game changer in dramatically reducing the number of illegal border crossings from the invasion-like levels under Joe Biden. However, gaps like the Tohono O’odham Reservation remain problematic. Respect for tribal sovereignty should not require abandoning national sovereignty over the international boundary. Until that gap is closed—by a wall, by enhanced federal authority, or by genuine full coordination—the Tohono O’odham Reservation will remain what it has long been: a little-known but critical hole in America’s border.

text:
EAST ELMHURST, Queens (WABC) -- Volunteers, local officials and immigration advocates launched "Know Your Rights Week" in parts of Queens, aiming to educate residents about their rights if approached by immigration enforcement officers.

Going door to door in East Elmhurst, volunteer Odilia Gonzalez spoke with neighbors about how to respond to encounters with immigration enforcement.

The effort is personal for Gonzalez, whose brother, an undocumented immigrant from Mexico, spent months in a detention center after being stopped on his way to work.

"At the time I felt sad, frustrated, I never thought that could happen," Gonzalez said.

The canvassing followed a rally organized by local leaders and advocates to kick off the initiative in District 35, which includes East Elmhurst, Corona, LeFrak City and Rego Park.

Assemblymember Lorinda C. Hooks said her office has recently received numerous calls about people being detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

"People who are here who work for a living, who pay taxes, never touched by the justice system, raising children, school runs, libraries, grocery store runs, working people treated like criminals," Hooks said.

Organizers said residents should be aware of their rights and prepare in advance for possible encounters with immigration authorities. Guidance shared during the campaign includes remaining silent and creating a communication plan with family members.

"When you know what your rights are, you are upholding your rights and ensuring that your rights will not be violated," said Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition.

In addition to advocating for limits on immigration enforcement activity in Queens, some officials are calling for Temporary Protected Status for Haitians to be restored following its termination by the Trump administration on Aug. 5.

Assemblymember Clyde Vanel, whose parents were born in Haiti, voiced support for restoring the designation.

"It's ironic that this is America's 250th birthday, a country of immigrants, everybody. Unless you're a Native American, everybody here is an immigrant. Everyone," Vanel said.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding reports of increased ICE activity in Queens.

The agency has consistently maintained that arrests are intended to protect public safety.

title: NV joins suit as Trump's anti-immigrant agenda targets truck drivers - Nevada Current
description:
“The Trump administration cannot strong-arm states into turning over millions of drivers’ private information without justification or adequate safeguards,” said Ford in a statement Thursday.
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) regulates all trucking companies, Nevada Trucking Association CEO Paul Enos told the Nevada Current in an interview.
According to the Nevada Trucking Association, only 9 of 994 previously issued non-domiciled CDLs in Nevada remained eligible under the new federal standards.
The Trump administration in justifying the crackdown has pointed to the 17 fatal trucking accidents in 2025 that involved non-domiciled CDL drivers.
To help offset the loss of non-domiciled drivers, the Trump administration has launched a “Freedom Haulers” initiative aimed at getting veterans into the trucking industry.
text:
Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford has joined a multistate lawsuit against the federal government over commercial driver license data—a move that is receiving pushback from the Nevada Trucking Association, which supports new federal rules that restrict noncitizen commercial drivers.

Ford, a Democrat, announced last week he joined a coalition of 22 states suing the Trump administration for demanding states turn over databases that contain sensitive personal identifying information — including the immigration status — of 17 million CDL holders.

The Trump administration has threatened to withhold $10 million in funding to the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators if states do not comply. The AAMVA is the private nonprofit that operates the Commercial Driver’s License Information System (CDLIS) used by states, and $10 million in withheld funds could result in the shuttering of the system, according to Ford’s office.

“The Trump administration cannot strong-arm states into turning over millions of drivers’ private information without justification or adequate safeguards,” said Ford in a statement Thursday. “My office is taking action to protect Nevadans’ privacy and stop this unlawful federal overreach.”

The lawsuit notes the Trump administration has similarly sought personal identifying information from state-maintained voter rolls and databases for food stamps and Medicaid. Those demands, which have routinely been blocked by courts, are driven by conspiracy theories over non-citizens.

The CDLIS “is not and never was intended for immigration enforcement,” argues this newest lawsuit.

Niskanen Center, a Washington think tank, has described the entire effort as “a de facto immigration raid.”

But supporters of the Trump administration’s approach believe the federal government should have access to the information and argue it is a safety issue.

The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) regulates all trucking companies, Nevada Trucking Association CEO Paul Enos told the Nevada Current in an interview. “I think that’s info they need to have. … We want to make sure anyone operating here is qualified and legal to drive.”

The trucking association on Friday released a statement saying it strongly opposes the state’s participation in the lawsuit, saying it “undermines non-domiciled CDL safety reforms.”

After being thwarted by courts in an attempt to act through executive order, the FMCSA earlier this year issued a new rule tightening visa standards and adding onerous steps for non-domiciled CDL drivers. The rule is expected to result in 200,000 drivers nationwide losing their credentials. Many of them hold valid work authorization as asylum seekers or recipients of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA). They will lose their CDL once their current licenses expire, if they have not already.

According to the Nevada Trucking Association, only 9 of 994 previously issued non-domiciled CDLs in Nevada remained eligible under the new federal standards.

However, all of those drivers will lose their CDL once their current license expires because Nevada opted to stop issuing or renewing non-domiciled CDLs altogether. Other states, including Oregon, have also done so.

Nevada DMV Director Tonya Laney in a February press release described the decision as the agency “reinforcing credential integrity, protecting federal highway funding and aligning with national commercial licensing requirements.”

The Nevada DMV did not respond by publication time to the Current’s request to elaborate on that decision and provide any available data on when exactly the nearly 1,000 non-domiciled CDLs will expire.

The Trump administration in justifying the crackdown has pointed to the 17 fatal trucking accidents in 2025 that involved non-domiciled CDL drivers. Those incidents make up less than 1% of all trucking accidents, critics have rebutted.

Labor groups have argued in previous court cases that banning non-domiciled CDLs will devastate workforces and lead to worse safety outcomes on roadways.

To help offset the loss of non-domiciled drivers, the Trump administration has launched a “Freedom Haulers” initiative aimed at getting veterans into the trucking industry.

Prior to the rule change, national and state trucking industry leaders warned of job shortages. The Nevada Governor’s Office of Economic Development (GOED has invested in CDL driver programs in the state as recently as February, citing strong employer demand.

Enos of the Nevada Trucking Association said the focus on driver shortages shifted post-covid pandemic as federal dollars funded what he calls “CDL mills” — trucking schools that graduated unqualified drivers. He said unsavory companies have popped up and hired the unqualified drivers for lower wages, undercutting the market and skirting safety protections like hours of service limits.

“Because of the state of the economy and the huge number of trucking companies that came into the market post-covid, the truck driver shortage isn’t the problem,” he added.

The diesel technician shortage is more acute, Enos added.

title: Will ICE take control of the privately run detention center in Tacoma? - KNKX
description:
It remains unclear whether those negotiations include the Northwest ICE Processing Center, which has been run by GEO Group since 2005.
ICE bought a facility similar to the Tacoma ICE center in California owned by Core Civic for nearly $500 million earlier this month.
The ICE request also requires that the detention center near Seattle have at least 1,500 beds.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told Time magazine that local government intervention is getting in the way of keeping these privately run immigrant detention facilities financially operational.
Those suits include six claims on behalf of people who were held in ICE detention in Washington state.
text:
The private owners of the immigrant detention center in Tacoma said they'll soon be in talks with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials to sell some of their detention facilities across the country to the feds.

It remains unclear whether those negotiations include the Northwest ICE Processing Center, which has been run by GEO Group since 2005. The company's recent 10-year contract to manage the center expired in 2025. GEO Group's founder told investors they aim to wrap up pricing negotiations of any sales as soon as late September.

"There's a mutual interest by us and ICE that this process hopefully be completed by the end of this quarter," said George Zoley, chairman, CEO, and founder of GEO Group, during an investor call.

Back in July ICE issued a "Request for Information" looking to purchase turn-key detention facilities in several states, including in Washington near Seattle. The three other sites where ICE is looking to buy a facility line up with the centers GEO Group owns and operates near those locations.

ICE bought a facility similar to the Tacoma ICE center in California owned by Core Civic for nearly $500 million earlier this month.

"The potential sale of multiple facilities to ICE could represent a significant liquidity and shareholder value-enhancing event for our company," Zoley said.

U.S. Rep. Emily Randall (D-Washington), whose district includes the Tacoma facility, said this is part of a greater plan by President Donald Trump and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to make CEOs like Zoley richer. Zoley, and GEO Group, donated heavily to Trump's reelection campaign.

"Nothing about this cruel immigration agenda makes us safer or makes our lives more affordable," Randall said. "My neighbors… want a future where our immigrant neighbors aren't terrorized in our streets, where they can safely raise their kids, and afford gas, groceries, and healthcare."

ICE declined to say whether they intend to buy the Tacoma facility and GEO Group has not said they are looking to sell it.

But records show the Tacoma immigrant lockup fits the type of facility ICE is looking to buy. One of the stipulations is that the turn-key facility should be within 30 miles of ICE's Seattle office in Tukwila, which the Tacoma facility is. The ICE request also requires that the detention center near Seattle have at least 1,500 beds. The Tacoma center has 1,575 beds.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told Time magazine that local government intervention is getting in the way of keeping these privately run immigrant detention facilities financially operational. Zoley has said federal ownership would be a way to avoid oversight from state governments.

Critics and immigrant advocates call that a strategy to sidestep attempts by local and state governments to shore up already weak federal accountability and transparency practices. A report from the University of Washington Center for Human Rights calls the current accountability process managed by the feds "Compliance Theater."

"As we watch the federal government use the billions of dollars they received from Congress to buy these facilities, we're seeing both a decrease in accountability and oversight," said Nayna Gupta, policy director at the American Immigration Council. "It allows them to sidestep efforts that states have been leading to push back, and it can mean increased enforcement in the areas where they've purchased facilities if they're expanding them to include space for immigration detention."

Gupta said Congress needs to pass a bill that makes getting legal status in the U.S. clearer and more accessible to avoid the human and constitutional rights violations created by the president's mass detention and deportation efforts.

While GEO Group maintains that it would continue running day-to-day operations under potential federal ownership, documents detailing ICE's purchase of a Seattle-area facility say "federal supremacy" rules would shield them from local or state government oversight.

"Applicable or more stringent state or local laws or regulations shall not apply to the performance under this contract when they would directly or indirectly regulate, dictate, or control the contractor's performance under these standards," one of the documents states.

The Washington Department of Health is one of the state agencies pressing for accountability and oversight. Health officials have been blocked repeatedly from inspecting the GEO Group-run Tacoma ICE center, despite their wins in federal court after suing to inspect it.

Health officials said state law allows them to conduct inspections, regardless of whether the feds buy the facility.

"The Tacoma facility does not sit on a federal enclave, so state laws still apply," said the health department's Kara Kostanich. "Even if GEO sold the property to ICE, it would maintain its contract as the operator of the facility, so it would still be subject to the duties of [state laws]."

Father Bryan Pham, a senior lecturer at Gonzaga Law School and an advocate investor with GEO Group, agreed with Kostanich's assessment.

"We teach our students this," said Pham, who invests in GEO Group as the USA West Jesuit Province liaison for Responsible Investment. "When it comes to health issues, that falls under the state mandate."

Pham said he, like many others, is concerned about human rights violations at the Tacoma facility and post deportation — and has struggled to bring in a third party to inspect conditions at the facility.

The concerns are twofold. One involves GEO Group allegedly aiding and abetting the federal government in violating federal court orders, due process rights, and sending deportees to a prison outside of U.S. jurisdiction where they could face torture. The other concern is the reportedly poor and small portioning of food, sanitation, coercive behavior by ICE officials, and poor dental and medical care in the Tacoma facility. Much of the latter has been the subject of multiple hunger strikes at the facility.

After a recent rejection for an investor motion, Pham said he's now beginning talks with GEO Group to address those concerns.

In the earnings call to investors, GEO Chairman Zoley detailed the Trump administration's future blueprint to implement mass detention and deportation across the U.S.

"They wanna be in fewer, larger facilities with a normal detention capacity of about 100,000, not including maybe a lot of these little jails, which are just feeder locations to the main facilities that they wanna have," Zoley said.

ICE issued another Request for Proposals to build new secure housing units on pre-existing ICE properties like in Texas and Arizona last month, Gupta said.

"That is an example of ICE taking what's really supposed to be a center where people get stamped for paperwork and move on to other facilities or to other kinds of monitoring, and turning those processing centers into actual carceral facilities, which really underscores their desperation to expand beds and space as quickly as possible," she said.

Several cases show that federal immigration enforcement officials have been pushing the boundaries of their short-term processing facilities in Washington state.

Last year a family was held in a windowless federal immigration processing facility in Blaine for four weeks. U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen (D-Washington) has raised questions about ICE's Ferndale office over its long-term detention practices. Both facilities typically are only meant to hold people for a short amount of time.

The family held in Blaine is now being represented by the Washington ACLU in a lawsuit.

"Federal law enforcement are committing civil rights violations at a scale without precedent in our nation's recent history, and with the support of an administration that encourages violence and disregard for the law," the ACLU wrote in a statement announcing dozens of lawsuits that span 17 states. Those suits include six claims on behalf of people who were held in ICE detention in Washington state.

description:
The Department of Homeland Security has consistently denied that it uses racial profiling when determining who to stop, but now we have receipts: bodycam footage that shows otherwise.

Last year, the Supreme Court allowed ICE terror to continue.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security has consistently denied that it uses racial profiling when determining who to stop, but now we have receipts: bodycam footage that shows otherwise.

The American Civil Liberties Union and other groups obtained DHS bodycam footage as part of a lawsuit alleging that the agency is using racial profiling in its enforcement stops. The footage shows repeated instances of ICE and Border Patrol agents using racial slurs to describe people when discussing potential stops.

While DHS claims that stops are not racially motivated and that the agency identifies its targets ahead of time, ICE’s actions say otherwise. We’ve read the stories of citizens detained by ICE and released days later. We’ve collectively mourned Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who were murdered by ICE in broad daylight. They weren’t targets–just two men on their way to work.

Immigration stops aren’t about public safety or enforcing immigration law. They are about terror. And right now, our Latino communities are bearing the brunt of this terror.

Last year, the Supreme Court allowed ICE terror to continue. Now, DHS agents’ own bodycam footage shows them targeting people based on their perceived race.

We can’t trust a captured, corrupt Supreme Court or the Trump administration to uphold the constitution and protect immigrants. Congress has the power to end this reign of terror and these racially motivated attacks on our communities. It’s their duty to step in—and it’s the duty of the people to demand they do.

title: Political Prosecution of Movement-Aligned Elected Officials | Nonprofit Quarterly
authors: Jeree Thomas, Muthoni Wambu Kraal, Lisa Holder, Gregory Haile, Jason Collins, Cason Murphy, Chelsea Fuller, Takara Pierce, Tiffany Hearsey
description:
If philanthropy is serious about protecting democracy, it must invest in protecting the state and local elected officials, in particular, from communities of color who are holding the line.
The Leaders We Have Many Americans over the past few years have yearned for elected leaders who would rise to the moment and fight authoritarian consolidation.
They were advocates before they were elected officials, and they continue to serve as bridges between movements and government.
What we have not done is properly invest in the support systems movement-aligned elected officials need when they become targets.
This is where lessons from attacks against protesters, activists, and movements can be supportive of movement-aligned women of color elected officials.
text:
“That abuse of power demands resistance…I knew there would be consequences for standing up for what is right but there was never a question about which side of history I would stand on.”

Tennessee State Senator Charlane Oliver

When philanthropy considers defending democracy, they often envision national elected leaders, lawyers, organizers, journalists, and bolstering civic institutions. Less often do they consider the state legislators, county commissioners, school board members, and local elected officials standing between their communities and increasingly aggressive attacks on civil rights, voting rights, reproductive justice, immigrants, trans people, and religious minorities. Yet many of the leaders holding the line serve in those roles, and they are often the first to pay a price for speaking out.

We have built movements around the assumption that certain people—especially Black women—will continue absorbing extraordinary risk on behalf of everyone else. Too often, we have come to expect those sacrifices from the very people we rely on most. That assumption is unsustainable.

When these women are doxed, threatened, censured, stripped of committee assignments, lose income, face office raids or political investigations, or are otherwise punished for their dissent, they are often left to figure it out themselves.

If philanthropy is serious about protecting democracy, it must invest in protecting the state and local elected officials, in particular, from communities of color who are holding the line.

The Leaders We Have

Many Americans over the past few years have yearned for elected leaders who would rise to the moment and fight authoritarian consolidation. We have those leaders. Many of them come directly from movement spaces. They were advocates before they were elected officials, and they continue to serve as bridges between movements and government. They are using the authority available to them to block, slow down, or repeal harmful policies. They stand alongside organizers in the streets and then return to legislative chambers to protect their communities.

“We have built movements around the assumption that certain people—especially Black women—will continue absorbing extraordinary risk on behalf of everyone else. That assumption is unsustainable.”

Take State Senator Charlane Oliver from Nashville, co-founder of The Equity Alliance. In May, Oliver protested from the Senate floor during the Tennessee General Assembly’s special session redrawing the state’s congressional maps to eliminate the state’s only majority-Black district and silence Black voters. Following her protest, she posted, “When the rules of the chamber are used to protect the powerful and silence the marginalized, standing on that desk is the least I can do.” As a result, the working mother was reassigned to a different committee, had her per diem restricted, and her out-of-state travel stipend stripped.

In Virginia, State Senator Louise Lucas, the first woman and first African American to serve as Senate president pro tempore, saw her office raided soon after leading her state’s redistricting efforts. Organizations scrambled to secure legal, communications, and crisis-response support.

In Georgia, Fulton County Commissioner Mo Ivory spoke out after the FBI seized hundreds of boxes of 2020 election materials from the Fulton County Elections Hub. Afterward, she received a wave of hostile messages across social media, email, and other channels. Her office had also recently experienced a break-in, adding to the climate of intimidation and vulnerability surrounding local officials who are expected to defend democracy while absorbing personal risk.

“Speaking out was not a choice between comfort and conflict,” Commissioner Ivory told us. “It was a choice between being quiet and being honest. Afterward, the hostility came quickly. And when you are already dealing with real safety concerns around your office, that kind of targeting is not abstract. It follows you home. But the answer cannot be silence. If we want leaders to defend democracy, especially women of color at the local level, then we have to stop treating their safety as an afterthought.”

When you think about people making sacrifices to do public service, there is nothing more depleting than watching outspoken legislators become invisible during times of unsafety, from no longer attending as many public events to hesitating around legislation they know will bring aggressive opposition.

The people we most want in public office are often the ones who never saw themselves there. They are the women who have to be asked seven times before they finally say yes. Teachers. Nurses. Parents. Movement organizers. People who are not coming from already overrepresented professions, political dynasties, or generational power structures. They are not insulated from the consequences when retaliation comes. When one of these leaders burns out or decides the cost is too high, communities lose voices they spent years cultivating and encouraging to lead.

We know how to mobilize around elections, recruit candidates, and celebrate victories. What we have not done is properly invest in the support systems movement-aligned elected officials need when they become targets.

This is where lessons from attacks against protesters, activists, and movements can be supportive of movement-aligned women of color elected officials. Generations of criminalization, surveillance, and political prosecutions of movement organizations have taught us that there is critical support infrastructure that philanthropy must resource to strengthen democracy.

The Infrastructure We Need

The In Defense of Movements Project (IDOM), a movement-advised and aligned resource and support mobilization project focused on supporting base-building movement organizations at risk of or currently experiencing political prosecution, calls this holistic safety and security. This holistic safety and security infrastructure includes physical and emotional security, digital security and data autonomy, financial and regulatory compliance, civil, immigration, and criminal legal defense support, and narrative and reputational support.

“If we want leaders to defend democracy, especially women of color at the local level, then we have to stop treating their safety as an afterthought.”

Part of IDOM’s mission is to engage, educate, and encourage philanthropy to build and strengthen this infrastructure, particularly since the onset of the RICO prosecutions against Stop Cop City activists in 2023. There are a number of powerful philanthropic examples of resource mobilization in the defense of movement formations, including the Movement Protection Fund, the Financial Futures Fund, Moxie Fund, Urgent Action Fund, Emergent Fund, RISE Together Fund, Third Wave’s Mobilize Power Fund, and Piper Fund, just to name a few.

As more and more base-building organizations contend for political power at the ballot box, we must also recognize the critical threats facing movement-aligned candidates for elected office—particularly women of color—as part of the larger call to defend social movements from state repression and political violence.

That’s why last year, Women’s Democracy Lab (WDL) joined forces with IDOM, recognizing that local and state elected officials are often from or deeply tied to local movement infrastructure.

WDL builds the support, rapid response, training, and community that should already exist around these leaders, including when they face political prosecutions, targeted investigations, and other efforts to silence them. Today, this includes a network of 300-plus elected officials across over 30 states, built over years of co-created programming centered on women, with a focus on women of color and Indigenous women.

Philanthropy has invested billions of dollars in defending democracy. Yet much of that investment remains concentrated at the federal level, even as many of the most consequential fights over democracy and civil rights are being waged in statehouses, county commissions, school boards, and city halls across the country. The leaders holding the line in those spaces need more than encouragement. They need infrastructure, security preparedness, coordinated rapid response, and communities of peers who have been through it before. And they need funders willing to invest before the next attack becomes tomorrow’s emergency.

We have a small window to build that infrastructure. Efforts like WDL show what is possible when leaders have access to trusted networks, rapid response, training, and community. The question is whether philanthropy will invest in growing that infrastructure at the scale this moment requires.

name: Human Rights
title: When will she be safe? The continuum of violence in refugee and migrant women's lives
description:
For many refugee and migrant women, violence does not end when they cross an international border.
Violence against refugee women is better understood as a continuum rather than a series of isolated events.
Understanding violence as a continuum helps explain why so many migrant and refugee women continue to experience insecurity long after arriving in places officially described as safe.
Many refugee and migrant women living in South Africa escaped countries devastated by war, political instability or economic collapse.
If violence follows refugee and migrant women across borders, then our understanding of protection must also change.
text:
South Africans observe August as Women’s Month to celebrate the contributions of women to society and the country’s liberation struggle, while highlighting issues that most affect them, such as gender-based violence (GBV), intimate partner violence and women’s health. But as we recognise and honour past, current and future women pioneers, let us also remember that not all women are celebrating in South Africa.

Not all women feel safe, seen, valued or protected. For many, this month is another reminder of the violence, discrimination, inequality and exclusion women continue to endure every day.

Seventy years ago, thousands of women marched to the Union Buildings in Pretoria to protest against pass laws that reduced dignity and freedom to a piece of paper. This Women's Month, refugee and migrant women stand outside clinics, schools and government offices asking a remarkably similar question: when will a document stop determining whether we deserve protection?

The recent xenophobic mobilisation has exposed how overlapping vulnerabilities shape the everyday lives of women. For migrant and refugee women, the burden is often doubled or even tripled. Many fled their home countries because armed conflict, persecution or political instability made staying impossible.

Increasingly, in South Africa, the barriers they face are not soldiers but citizens who demand IDs before allowing them access to healthcare, education, employment and other essential services.

The violence the women experience is not confined to physical attacks. It is the child turned away from school because officials question their documentation. It is the woman denied healthcare because she cannot produce the “correct” papers. It is the market trader whose livelihood disappears when anti-foreigner protests target migrant-owned businesses. It is the mother who chooses not to report GBV because she fears deportation more than the abuse.

In an article in the Journal of Migration and Health (2025), Alexis Harerimana, Julian Pillay and Gugu Mchunu identified pervasive medical xenophobia and exclusion of refugees and migrants in African healthcare systems.

This is the second violence. The first violence drove them from home. The second waits where they hope for safety.

For many refugee and migrant women, violence does not end when they cross an international border. It changes form.

Women’s Month offers an opportunity for us to recommit ourselves to ending GBV. Yet it should also prompt us to ask a difficult question: when is a refugee woman safe?

According to the latest UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Global Trends report, Forced Displacement in 2025, published in June 2026, more than 41.6 million people worldwide were refugees at the end of 2025. Across Africa, conflicts and economic insecurity continue to force families from their homes. Increasingly, many of the families are led by women responsible not only for finding safety but also for rebuilding family life after unimaginable loss.

Humanitarian responses often assume that safety begins once refugees reach another country. My research with African refugee and migrant communities suggests something different. Violence against refugee women is better understood as a continuum rather than a series of isolated events.

Armed conflict may force women to flee but crossing a border rarely marks the end of violence. Instead, violence is reconfigured through immigration systems, xenophobia, economic exclusion, institutional discrimination and, for some women, continuing abuse in the family. Understanding violence as a continuum helps explain why so many migrant and refugee women continue to experience insecurity long after arriving in places officially described as safe.

South Africa illustrates this continuum particularly clearly during protests against undocumented migrants and refugees.

Many refugee and migrant women living in South Africa escaped countries devastated by war, political instability or economic collapse. They sought protection, only to encounter new forms of insecurity. These include xenophobia, discrimination, barriers to employment, insecure immigration status, limited access to healthcare and profound social isolation. Violence, in other words, becomes personal and structural.

South Africa faces one of the world's most serious crises of violence against women. The landmark First South African National Gender-Based Violence Study (2022), conducted by the Human Sciences Research Council and released in 2024, found that 35.5% of women aged 18 and older in South Africa have experienced physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime.

Recognising the additional vulnerabilities experienced by refugee and migrant women does not diminish the reality. Rather, it acknowledges that some women experience violence through multiple, intersecting systems of exclusion. Gender, nationality, immigration status, race and poverty combine to create forms of vulnerability that responses often struggle to recognise.

For some families, the consequences are devastating. Women return to countries they originally fled, not because conflict has ended or economic insecurity has improved but because they no longer feel safe where they sought refuge. Others remain, living with the daily uncertainty that safety depends not on their rights but on whether they can produce the right documents at the right moment.

This is not simply a South African story.

My research with African refugee communities in Australia revealed remarkably similar patterns. Although the political contexts differ, women consistently described losing the extended family networks that once provided care, experiencing discrimination in employment and public institutions and learning that belonging remained conditional. Violence had changed its form but not its effects.

If violence follows refugee and migrant women across borders, then our understanding of protection must also change. Safety cannot be measured simply by whether a woman has crossed an international border. It must include the ability to access healthcare without fear, report abuse without risking deportation, enrol children in school, secure decent work and participate fully in community life regardless of immigration status.

Achieving this requires action at several levels. Governments, including the South African government, must ensure that immigration status never becomes a barrier to protection or justice. Community organisations and other institutions have a vital role in challenging xenophobia before it becomes normalised. International organisations and wealthier states must also recognise that deterrence policies and exclusionary migration practices reinforce, rather than reduce, the continuum of violence experienced by displaced women.

Until refugee and migrant women no longer move from one form of violence to another, we cannot honestly say they have found safety. We have simply relocated the violence.

Therefore, as we honour women in South Africa throughout August, let us ensure that our celebration is accompanied by a renewed commitment to creating a world where every woman here and elsewhere can live with dignity, safety, equality and hope.

name: Human Rights
title: No one should be sent back to Taliban rule | Human Rights Watch
description:
Governments are fully aware of this but are still moving toward migration deals and engagement with the Taliban leadership that could send Afghans back into the Taliban nightmare.
Anyone deemed dissenting from Taliban rule, regardless of their gender, lives under the constant threat of arbitrary detention and torture.
On June 22, European Union officials hosted a Taliban delegation in Brussels — for the first time since the 2021 Taliban takeover — to discuss migration and return policies.
But it’s the height of hypocrisy to condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and cooperate in sending people back to them in the next.
Other countries should not normalize engagement with the Taliban without clear and measurable human rights benchmarks.
text:
Nearly five years after the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan in August 2021, one issue should be beyond dispute: Afghanistan is not safe for anyone forcibly returned there. Governments are fully aware of this but are still moving toward migration deals and engagement with the Taliban leadership that could send Afghans back into the Taliban nightmare.

Forcing people back to Afghanistan exposes them to a genuine risk of persecution and dire economic circumstances, while bolstering the global standing of the Taliban authorities who are responsible for crimes against humanity.

Afghanistan today is one of the world’s worst human rights crises — and for women and girls, it is a uniquely devastating one. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls are banned from education beyond sixth grade. Women have been pushed out of public life and face severe restrictions in employment. Anyone deemed dissenting from Taliban rule, regardless of their gender, lives under the constant threat of arbitrary detention and torture.

What is most concerning is not only the brutality inside Afghanistan, but the growing willingness of governments to act as though these realities no longer carry consequences.

On June 22, European Union officials hosted a Taliban delegation in Brussels — for the first time since the 2021 Taliban takeover — to discuss migration and return policies. Germany has already resumed deportations and allows Taliban officials to provide consular services in Berlin and Bonn. Officials in the United Kingdom have signaled that they may be prepared to negotiate with the Taliban over returns, as they watch similar debates unfold elsewhere in Europe.

Reports have surfaced that the U.S. has pressured people evacuated from Afghanistan and stranded in camps in Qatar to choose between forced returns or uncertain relocation elsewhere. The U.S. has already ended the temporary protected status of Afghans inside the country and halted the processing of other categories of protection for them.

The message: Return voluntarily, or we will deport you.

United Nations high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, and the U.N. special rapporteur on Afghanistan, Richard Bennett, have warned against deportations, stressing that returns would violate human rights law and breach the principle of nonrefoulement. The U.N. Refugee Agency said there are substantial obstacles to a “safe and dignified return” to the country.

That principle is simple and foundational: No one should be sent to a place where they face persecution, torture or other serious harm.

The near absence of robust and transparent human rights and humanitarian monitoring inside Afghanistan will also mean that returnees do not or cannot report the truth of their situation. At Human Rights Watch, we have documented cases in which forced returnees have been arbitrarily detained and tortured by the Taliban, as well as the abuses faced by women and girls every day.

A former security officer who had escaped to Pakistan and was then deported back to Afghanistan told me last year that upon his return, the Taliban detained and tortured him for two months.

He said that the Taliban “would cover their faces and beat me every night. Then, they would take me out of my cell, put me in a car and tell me that they were taking me to my ‘death place.’ For two months, every night, I expected to be killed.” He also said that the Taliban had detained and disappeared many of his colleagues. He’s currently living in hiding in Afghanistan.

Afghanistan is not a safe country for returns. Governments cannot pretend that their deportation policy is separate from human rights policy. In fact, most Western governments continue to harshly criticize the Taliban’s human rights record in international forums.

Commendably, the EU led on the establishment by the U.N. Human Rights Council of an investigative mechanism tasked with collecting and preserving evidence of serious abuses in the country. Germany, Netherlands, Australia and Canada are pursuing an initiative to hold the Taliban accountable for their violations of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

But it’s the height of hypocrisy to condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and cooperate in sending people back to them in the next. Many of the governments now looking for ways to send Afghans back were deeply involved in Afghanistan for two decades. They cannot wash their hands of the debt of responsibility they owe to Afghans who worked with them or in projects they supported.

Migration deals will take the pressure off the Taliban for their ongoing abuses. This kind of “technical” engagement will send a dangerous message to every abusive government that no range of rights abuses and oppression will stop other countries from making deals with you, even at the expense of those most affected.

Other countries should not normalize engagement with the Taliban without clear and measurable human rights benchmarks. And they should not deport Afghans to a country where persecution is systematic and well documented. The EU, U.K.. U.S. and others considering this path should take stock of this harsh reality and act accordingly: no one should be sent to live in an Afghanistan ruled by the Taliban.
