title: Challenging Systemic Home Office Errors to Protect Our Home - CrowdJustice
description:
Short summary My six-year-old son Neo and I face losing our home in the UK following serious Home Office caseworking errors.
I relied on that information and submitted my Global Talent visa application believing I remained lawfully in the UK.
The Home Office Errors We Are Challenging The Home Office then made a critical legal error.
It mistook my Global Talent endorsement application for a paid visa application and, on that basis, said it would "not consider" my outstanding fee waiver.
Instead, my official UKVI online account continued to show my immigration status as active and lawful.
text:
Short summary

My six-year-old son Neo and I face losing our home in the UK following serious Home Office caseworking errors.

The Home Office wrongly treated an application for professional endorsement as though it were a visa application and, on that basis, stopped considering my outstanding fee waiver, which was the first step towards our Family Route application. At the same time, my official UKVI digital status continued to show that I could remain in the UK while a decision was pending.

I relied on that information and submitted my Global Talent visa application believing I remained lawfully in the UK. It was only months later, when the Home Office contacted me about the application, that I first learned it considered me to have become an overstayer months earlier. Despite the evidence I then provided explaining what had happened, the Home Office refused my application on that basis.

I am now challenging that decision with specialist immigration and public law lawyers. This case is about protecting our home, but also about whether people should be able to rely on official government communications and whether public bodies are held accountable when their errors have life-changing consequences.

A Stand for Our Home, Our Values, and Home Office Accountability

This campaign is first and foremost about protecting our home, but it also raises a serious wider issue. As the Home Office increasingly relies on digital eVisas, interconnected systems and individual caseworker decisions, administrative errors, unclear notices and inaccurate official records can have profound consequences. We are not the first people to experience problems of this kind.

My six-year-old son Neo and I are now taking legal action to challenge the Home Office's decision, hold it accountable for the errors in our case, and defend the principle that people must be able to rely on official government communications and processes.

Our Story and What Is at Stake

The UK is our home.

I am a dual German and US citizen and Neo's single parent and sole carer. We live in London, which is home to us both.

England was home to me long before I returned here with Neo. I spent the second half of my childhood here, including going to school here as a teenager. My father had close ties to England, spoke English with me at home, and brought me here many times even before I moved.

Neo has lived here since he was two and is thriving at school. With no immediate family on my side elsewhere in the world, the people I have considered family since my childhood here are now the closest family Neo and I have, and we see them regularly. Raising Neo here has deepened my own roots even further. Our home, family, close friends, his school and our community are here. This is the country where I want to raise him and where I hope to grow old.

Although England has long felt like home, I am not a British citizen and growing up here did not give me an automatic right to live here as an adult. I returned to the UK legally on a Skilled Worker visa three and a half years ago.

What Happened

Before my Skilled Worker visa expired, I applied for a fee waiver as the first step towards making a Family Route application on human rights grounds. While that application was pending, my lawful immigration status continued.

Family Route applications can take a long time. As a single parent whose ability to work remained restricted, I looked for another legitimate immigration route that could allow me to return to work sooner and support my son.

I applied to Arts Council England for endorsement under the Global Talent route. This was an assessment of my professional work and achievements, not an application for a visa. Because there was no guarantee I would be endorsed, I continued pursuing the Family Route in parallel and never withdrew my fee waiver application.

The Home Office Errors We Are Challenging

The Home Office then made a critical legal error.

It mistook my Global Talent endorsement application for a paid visa application and, on that basis, said it would "not consider" my outstanding fee waiver.

But an endorsement application is not a visa application.

Our legal case is that saying the fee waiver would not be considered for this legally irrelevant reason did not amount to a lawful decision granting or refusing it. On that basis, the fee waiver remained pending and my lawful immigration status continued.

The Home Office's notification also failed to tell me that it considered my lawful status to be coming to an end. Instead, my official UKVI online account continued to show my immigration status as active and lawful.

I relied on that official information.

My right to work was limited to my former employer, so I had already stopped working in February 2025. I continued not to work because I wanted to comply fully with my immigration conditions, exhausting my savings and eventually accumulating more than £24,000 in personal debt to cover rent and our living expenses.

Arts Council England subsequently endorsed me for Global Talent. With my UKVI digital status still showing that I could remain in the UK while awaiting a decision, I submitted the Global Talent visa applications for Neo and me.

It was only months after I submitted our visa applications that the Home Office contacted me and, for the first time, told me it considered my lawful status to have ended months earlier.

I immediately responded with comprehensive evidence, including screenshots of my UKVI digital status and the Home Office's own correspondence.

When my Global Talent application was subsequently refused, the decision failed adequately to engage with material evidence and relevant considerations I had submitted, including the nature of the endorsement application, the Home Office's earlier notification, the information displayed through my UKVI account and my reliance upon those official communications.

That failure forms another part of the caseworking errors we are challenging.

These arguments have now been put formally to the Home Office through the Pre Action Protocol process. If the Home Office maintains its decision, we are preparing to pursue Judicial Review.

What We Stand to Lose and What This Has Already Cost Us

If I simply accept the decision and leave the UK, the consequences do not end when we board a plane.

On the Home Office's current finding that I overstayed for more than 30 days, leaving voluntarily at my own expense could result in a mandatory 12-month refusal period applying to many future applications to return to the UK.

Even after that period, accepting an adverse overstaying history could create continuing uncertainty for future immigration applications. It could therefore affect whether Neo and I are able to return to live in the country we consider home during key years of his childhood.

I also stand to lose thousands of pounds in government immigration fees already paid, before the costs of this legal challenge are taken into account, and could face substantial application fees again.

But the greatest losses cannot be measured financially.

We face losing our home, our close friends and wider community, and the people who have become our family. Neo would lose his school, friendships, familiar routines and trusted relationships.

Professionally, I am an experience designer and creative director working across brand, cultural and educational experiences. I would lose the professional community and career I have rebuilt here.

Alongside my career, I spent two years building Spark&Bond, an educational startup that I see as my life's work. It creates story-led participatory learning experiences for primary school children and their families and has been successfully piloted in a London primary school.

Spark&Bond has now been on hold for over a year because I cannot responsibly seek investment without certainty about my immigration position. If we are forced to leave the UK, I cannot simply take the company elsewhere. I would lose much of the groundwork, partnerships and knowledge I spent years building here, including my educator and child psychology partner, and would have to establish whether another country was even right for it before rebuilding its ecosystem from the beginning. Rebuilding it elsewhere could set the work back by years or make it impossible for me to continue it at all.

At 46, raising Neo alone, with no immediate family elsewhere in the world and already carrying the financial consequences of this process, starting again somewhere else would not simply mean finding another job and another flat. It would mean rebuilding our entire support system, community, professional relationships and financial stability from the beginning.

A Parenting Imperative: Why I Have to Fight

Beyond the legal arguments, financial costs and everything we stand to lose, there is a fundamental parenting reason driving this challenge.

Neo is six. If we were forced to leave our home, his school, his friends and the people he considers family, I would have to explain why.

I have chosen to raise my son with honesty, in ways appropriate to his age. I cannot tell him that this happened because I failed to follow the rules when I submitted the fee waiver application in time, relied on the Home Office's own communications and digital status, and took legal advice to challenge what went wrong.

Nor do I want the lesson he takes from this to be that when an institution makes a serious mistake that profoundly affects your life, there is nothing you can do about it.

There is a third option: to challenge what has happened and stand up for us.

I can show my son that when something important is wrong, you stand up for yourself, use the processes available to you and ask institutions to be accountable for their decisions.

Whatever the eventual outcome, I will be able to look him in the eye and tell him that when something happened that I knew was wrong, I stood up for us.

Why This Matters Beyond Our Family

This legal challenge is first and foremost about protecting Neo and our home, but it raises a much larger principle.

People across the UK are navigating an increasingly complex and fully digital immigration system. When someone's legal status can depend upon Home Office correspondence, digital records and interactions between different parts of that system, people must be able to trust the information the Government gives them.

And when something goes wrong, access to justice should not depend upon whether someone has enough money to hire specialist lawyers.

I could not afford legal representation. I have had to borrow money to instruct a specialist immigration and public law solicitor and begin challenging what happened.

By pursuing this case, I want not only to protect our home but to defend a simple principle: public bodies must be accountable for their mistakes, and individuals should be entitled to rely upon official government communications.

Why We Need Your Support

I have already borrowed money to take the first legal steps.

With my solicitor, I submitted an Administrative Review and have now served a formal Pre Action Protocol letter challenging the Home Office's actions. If the Home Office maintains its position, we are preparing to issue Judicial Review proceedings.

The case will require specialist solicitor work and, if Judicial Review becomes necessary, a barrister specialising in public law litigation. Specialist counsel will draft the Judicial Review grounds and provide an additional expert assessment of the case.

Every contribution to this CrowdJustice campaign goes directly to our instructed legal team's client account to cover solicitor fees, barrister fees, court fees and formal representation.

Initial Target (£10,600): Covers the specialist solicitor and barrister work required to pursue the challenge through the Judicial Review permission stage, including the Administrative Review and Pre Action Protocol work, reviewing the Home Office's response, preparing the Judicial Review grounds and court filing fees.

Stretch Target (£28,600): If permission is granted, the additional £18,000 covers preparation for a substantive Judicial Review hearing, including further solicitor and barrister work, evidence, skeleton arguments and advocate representation.

If you can contribute, however much, you will be helping us challenge a decision that could determine whether Neo and I can protect the home and life we have built in the UK.

If you cannot donate, sharing our story with your network or media contacts can also make an enormous difference.

Thank you for standing with us for fairness, integrity and accountability.

The Constitutional Court has recently filled a grave legislative gap which, for over twenty-six years, hindered a category of foreign nationals from exercising fundamental rights guaranteed by the Italian Constitution.
The judge noted that the legislator had in fact provided for compulsory and free enrolment in the National Health Service only for a number of specific categories of foreign nationals, excluding those who are recipients of a civil disability pension.
In addition, the safeguarding of these people’s rights finds “constitutional basis in the guarantee of human dignity and the fundamental right to health[...]”.

text:
The Constitutional Court has recently filled a grave legislative gap which, for over twenty-six years, hindered a category of foreign nationals from exercising fundamental rights guaranteed by the Italian Constitution. Indeed, in Order No.97 of June 5, 2026, the Court provided a constitutionally oriented interpretation of the contested Article 34 paragraphs 1 and 3, of Legislative Decree No.286 of 1998 (the so-called Consolidated Act on Immigration – TUI). The ruling guarantees compulsory and free enrolment in the National Health Service (SSN) even to foreign nationals who, already holding a residence permit for work or family reasons, are subsequently granted a residence permit for elective residence following the award of a civil disability pension.

The case arose from an appeal lodged with the labour division of the Court of Milan by two non-EU citizens against the Lombardy Region, in which they complained that the requirement to pay €2,000 for voluntary enrolment in the National Health Service (SSN) was discriminatory. The judge noted that the legislator had in fact provided for compulsory and free enrolment in the National Health Service only for a number of specific categories of foreign nationals, excluding those who are recipients of a civil disability pension. This legislative omission would violate Article 3 of the Constitution on the grounds of unreasonable discriminatory treatment, both in relation to other foreign nationals who are equally indigent and in relation to Italian citizens with disabilities. For the same reason, this omission would violate Articles 32 and 117(1) of the Constitution, and would be contrary to Article 13 of the European Social Charter and Articles 4 and 25 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The Court of Milan therefore requested that the provision be declared unconstitutional.

In its ruling, whilst declaring the questions of constitutional legitimacy to be unfounded, the Court specified that if the only possible interpretation of Article 34, paragraphs 1 and 3, were the one presented by the referring judge, there would be no doubts as to the violations of Articles 3, 32, 117.1 of the Constitution. This relies on consolidated constitutional case-law, which places persons with severely incapacitating disabilities at the crossroads of “a complex of values that drew upon the fundamental inspiring motives of the constitutional framework”. In addition, the safeguarding of these people’s rights finds “constitutional basis in the guarantee of human dignity and the fundamental right to health[...]”.

However, in line with a systematic interpretation of the legal system , the Court clarified that the omission should not be read as a deliberate exclusion by the legislator. In fact, the elective residence permit and its conversion mechanism did not exist at the time of the adoption of the contested provision.

Order No. 97/2026 finally provides constitutional certainty regarding the right of foreign nationals with disabilities who hold an elective residence permit to register with the National Health Service free of charge. The Court’s interpretative ruling thus puts an end to nearly three decades of obstacles to the exercise of foreign nationals’ constitutional rights.

text:
The City of West Hollywood strongly condemns the detention of West Hollywood resident Alex Pereira-Alves by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The City calls on ICE to halt any removal of Mr. Pereira-Alves while his legal claims receive full and fair consideration.

Mr. Pereira-Alves, who is originally from Brazil, was detained last week and is currently being held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center. According to media reports, federal immigration authorities have sought to remove him to Guyana, a country he has never visited and to which he has no ties. A federal judge has temporarily blocked his removal. The prospect of removing Mr. Pereira-Alves to a country with which he has no connection is deeply troubling, particularly given the documented discrimination and violence faced by LGBTQ+ people in Guyana.

The City of West Hollywood stands firmly for due process, human rights, and the dignity and safety of every member of our community. The City has reached out to U.S. Representative Laura Friedman, who represents California’s 30th Congressional District, and U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff to request their intervention on behalf of Mr. Pereira-Alves.

West Hollywood has long served as a safe haven for LGBTQ+ people, immigrants, and other marginalized communities. Our immigrant communities are not threats; they are our neighbors, co-workers, friends, and loved ones, and they are integral to the social, cultural, and economic fabric of our city and our region.

The City of West Hollywood will not remain silent when a member of our community faces detention and potential removal while significant questions about due process, fairness, and personal safety remain unresolved. We urge federal authorities to respect due process and fundamental rights.

The City contracts with service providers to assist community members impacted by immigration enforcement actions, including immigration legal assistance, rental assistance, and other support. The City is working through Mr. Pereira-Alves’ network of friends to help connect him with available resources.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration said Monday it is temporarily pausing construction of a contentious border construction project in Texas' Big Bend National Park while the head of the agency tasked with building the wall visits to do an “on-the-ground evaluation.”

The project through the national park in southern Texas has faced fierce bipartisan opposition by critics who say it is marring the area's pristine environment. They argue the region’s rugged and remote terrain already serves as a deterrent to migrants and smugglers. Border crossings in the area have historically been lower than other regions and have dropped even further over the past two years.

“CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation,” Rodney Scott, who heads Customs and Border Protection, said on X. Scott said over the next couple of days, he was going to “listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders” to address what he said were “real” national security threats while protecting the park.

Customs and Border Protection did not respond to questions about how long the construction was paused or give any details on whom Scott would be meeting with in Texas.

A rare concession from Trump administration

While it isn’t clear whether the brief suspension portended a more permanent halt to the construction in the area, it reflected the intensity of the bipartisan opposition and was a rare concession from the administration on a signature promise of the president’s that it has raced to complete.

Congress gave the Trump administration $46 billion last summer to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, and the administration has been charging ahead and waiving numerous regulations in an effort to swiftly build the wall.

Scott has said he expects the first layer of the wall to be built by the end of next year.

But the administration has run into fierce opposition in Texas, especially when it comes to construction in and near Big Bend National Park and a state park to the west.

Customs and Border Protection earlier this year backed off plans to build a 30-foot-tall bollard wall through the parks but was still moving forward with other border protection measures such as a new road, lights, barriers designed to stop cars from crossing the border and technology such as buried fiber optic cables.

That has sparked opposition from Democratic and Republican sheriffs in the region, former national park officials, local residents who rely on the parks for their livelihood and some Texas elected officials. Critics have said it will scar the rugged landscape that attracts tourists who raft down the Rio Grande River and take advantage of some of the clearest night skies in the U.S. to gaze at stars.

The sheriff of Brewster County, which includes Big Bend National Park, said Monday that he'll be meeting with Scott during his trip and that he was glad the commissioner was going to have the opportunity to see the terrain with his own eyes and hear firsthand from people in the region.

Ronny Dodson is concerned about possible damage to archeological sites and Native American burial grounds caused by construction for the new road that's supposed to be built through the park. He hopes Scott will see how closely the new road mirrors an already existing road, and Dodson said he wants more information about the technology the agency plans to use to secure the border.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said he spoke with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin over the weekend and suggested that the construction pause was a result of their talk. Abbott said the secretary committed to the governor that there would be no wall or barriers built in the park, but the governor made no mention of the road building that has concerned local residents.

Bulldozers seen recently in park clearing land

Last week, bulldozers were seen clearing land at the park, sparking even more concern and raising questions from one of the state's Republican senators.

At the time the bulldozers were seen, the Department of Homeland Security said on X that they were related to “survey and design work.”

Sen. John Cornyn, who lost the Republican primary to the state's attorney general, wrote to Mullin over construction concerns.

“My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States. The dangerous terrain includes steep mountains, deep canyons, and expansive deserts which they believe act a natural barrier that limits large-scale movements,” Cornyn wrote.

As the wall-building efforts have shifted into high gear this year along the roughly 2,000-mile border, opposition has spiked as well.

The administration has faced criticism from Native American groups saying wall contractors are desecrating religious sites, a small Texas town worried the wall will damage its levee system, and a Catholic archdiocese that says wall construction in the El Paso area mars an important religious site.

Activists praise the pause but say it's only a first step

Activists who have been rallying opposition to the administration's plans said they were encouraged by the pause but they would be watching closely to see if CBP makes any significant changes or simply goes back to its previous plans.

Bob Krumenaker was the superintendent of Big Bend National Park from 2018 to 2023 and now chairs the organization “Keep Big Bend Wild,” which aims to preserve the park's wild nature. He said he was “wary but optimistic” after news of the pause.

“They are paying attention to all of the objections that have been raised across the political spectrum,” he said.

But Krumenaker said it's unlikely that CBP is going to entirely abandon all its plans in the region. Krumenaker said he and others would be watching to see whether the equipment like the bulldozers is removed from the park, the agency outlines a clear plan going forward and it repairs any damage already done.

“Let’s hope they significantly modify their plans in response to what they hear, and make it transparent,” he said.

Another group, which sued Homeland Security over its decision to broadly waive regulations to speed up construction projects in the Big Bend region, called the announcement “welcome news” but warned that construction could resume “at any moment.”

“This temporary pause proves how much non-partisan public pressure is mounting in West Texas and across America to stop the irreversible destruction unfolding in this crown jewel national park,” said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity.

“We’re not resting until these contracts are canceled, these workers are sent packing, the waivers are rescinded and every wall plan for the greater Big Bend region is scrapped for good.”

title: HRW urges Thailand to halt deportation of 26 Karen villagers to Myanmar | The Daily Star
description:
Authorities said they were targeting people without proof of Thai citizenship.
Two villagers were later released after officials verified their residence registration records, while the remaining 26 were transferred to Bangkok’s Suan Phlu Immigration Detention Center for prosecution on immigration charges and deportation to Myanmar.
“Deporting ethnic Karen villagers to Myanmar would put them at risk of grave danger,” HRW Asia Director Elaine Pearson said.
The rights group said ethnic Karen communities have lived in the area for generations, predating the establishment of Kaeng Krachan National Park.
HRW urged Thai authorities to ensure the Karen’s access to their ancestral lands and end the “abusive treatment of the community”.
text:
Thai authorities should halt the imminent deportation of 26 ethnic Karen villagers to Myanmar and release them from immigration detention, Human Rights Watch (HRW) said

A press release issued yesterday said the villagers were among 28 people arrested on August 10 during a raid by district and forestry officials, along with Thai military personnel, at Ban Pa Deng village in Phetchaburi province’s Kaeng Krachan National Park.

Authorities said they were targeting people without proof of Thai citizenship. Two villagers were later released after officials verified their residence registration records, while the remaining 26 were transferred to Bangkok’s Suan Phlu Immigration Detention Center for prosecution on immigration charges and deportation to Myanmar.

“Deporting ethnic Karen villagers to Myanmar would put them at risk of grave danger,” HRW Asia Director Elaine Pearson said.

HRW said the deportations could violate Thailand’s obligations under the United Nations Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face a genuine risk of persecution, torture or other serious harm.

The rights group said ethnic Karen communities have lived in the area for generations, predating the establishment of Kaeng Krachan National Park.

HRW urged Thai authorities to ensure the Karen’s access to their ancestral lands and end the “abusive treatment of the community”.

Shara helps clients navigate trade remedies, tariffs, and customs regulations in support of their U.S. and global market strategies.

Shara is the Chair of Covington’s International Trade Practice Group, and co-leads the Customs practice.

Drawing on her 20 years of service in the U.S. government, she develops legal and public policy strategies to assist clients engaging with the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Congress, and the courts. In high-stakes antidumping and countervailing duty investigations, Shara helps global manufacturers, distributors, and retailers protect their access to the U.S. market. She assists technology, life sciences and manufacturing companies enforce and defend their intellectual property rights in cross-border Section 337 investigations. Chambers praises her for bringing “behind-the-curtain knowledge to the private sector” in proceedings before the ITC by leveraging her experience as a decision maker.

Shara also regularly advises clients in a wide range of industries on Customs compliance and tariff mitigation, including:

Providing legal opinions or seeking Customs rulings on classification, valuation, country of origin, and product marking/labelling.

Conducting internal compliance reviews, drafting compliance policies, and providing training.

Responding to CBP audits and inquiries and filing voluntary disclosures.

Developing strategies to reduce tariffs and take advantage of trusted trader programs.

Prior to joining the firm, Shara was a Commissioner and Chairman of the ITC, where she was a decision-maker in hundreds of Section 337, antidumping, countervailing duty, and safeguard investigations.

She previously served as Senior International Trade Counsel for Senator Max Baucus (D-MT) at the U.S. Senate Committee on Finance, where she was responsible for legislative and policy issues including Trade Promotion Authority; negotiations involving the World Trade Organization and free trade agreements; and trade remedy and customs laws. She was also an attorney-advisor in the Office of the General Counsel at the ITC, where she was lead counsel in litigation before the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit and the Court of International Trade.

Tom Plotkin advises companies on a broad range of ESG and sustainability issues with a focus on social responsibility, including business and human rights, equity and civil rights, and external engagement and brand reputation.

As a member of Covington’s Business and Human Rights practice, Tom advises clients on all aspects of the corporate responsibility to respect human rights, including issues related to supply chain due diligence and responsible sourcing, downstream product use and human rights impacts, and strategies for integrating human rights oversight into broader compliance programs.

Tom is also a member of Covington’s Institutional Culture and Social Responsibility practice, where he assists companies in evaluating and managing the legal, business, and reputational risks associated with social impacts of business practices. Tom’s work in this area focuses on civil rights and diversity, equity, and inclusion.

As a member of Covington’s Sustainability practice, Tom draws on his social responsibility portfolio to assist companies in bridging internal practices and external engagement strategies. Tom assists with public ESG reporting, responding to shareholder ESG proposals, and external stakeholder engagement.

Tom is also a member of Covington’s Employment practice, where he advises on a range of domestic and international employment law issues.

Mary Mikhaeel advises clients on developing sophisticated human rights compliance programs, based on human rights-focused hard law and international best practices. She works with clients to develop cutting edge solutions to forced labor supply chain risks, and also advises clients on a wide range of Customs matters.

As a member of Covington’s Business and Human Rights Practice Group, Mary supports companies in furthering their commitment to respecting human rights, as articulated in the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs). She has experience in assisting companies with building compliance programs, conducting human rights risk assessments and investigations, and developing human rights due diligence procedures.

Mary has extensive experience counseling clients across a wide range of industries on how to mitigate forced labor risks in the context of U.S. anti-forced labor laws, including the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) and Withhold Release Orders (WROs).

Mary is also a member of Covington’s customs practice and advises clients on a wide range of issues related to customs compliance and tariff mitigation strategies. She has experience advising clients on seeking ruling requests with Customs, assisting clients in submitting prior disclosures, and conducting internal compliance reviews.

Prior to law school, Mary was part of a research team that developed the Corporations and Human Rights Database, the first database created to monitor public allegations of business’ possible human rights violations. She also worked at the University of Minnesota’s Human Rights program on a variety of business and human rights matters, including issues related to a forced displacement case before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and interned for a human rights non-government organization that holds consultative status with the United Nations.

Alex Chinoy assists clients with the resolution of inbound U.S. trade disputes, appearing before a range of U.S. courts and agencies. He is an accomplished trade litigator who has represented clients at both the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) and the U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC) in antidumping (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) investigations. He has also been involved in more than 30 Section 337 unfair import investigations before the ITC. He has appeared in a range of other trade enforcement and regulatory matters, including litigation at the Court of International Trade (CIT) and the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC), involving actions against U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the DOC, and the ITC.

Outside the courtroom, Alex assists clients with a range of CBP compliance and enforcement matters, including inter partes IP enforcement proceedings, 19 CFR 177 ruling requests, investigative inquiries including RASAs and audits, prior disclosures, penalty notice responses, development of corrective action plans, and tariff evaluation and mitigation counseling.

In addition to his litigation and customs work, Alex has been repeatedly recognized by Chambers for his work at the ITC, with sources noting he is “impressive beyond his years of practice.” Alex is a past President of the ITC Trial Lawyers Association, the leading bar association for Section 337 practitioners. He has hands-on experience with every phase of Section 337 investigations. He has participated in a dozen hearings at the ITC ranging from trials on violation to enforcement hearings and temporary relief proceedings. His experience spans every phase of 337 litigation, from pre-complaint counseling through appeal of final ITC determinations to the CAFC, with a particular focus on disputes and counseling involving CBP enforcement of ITC exclusion orders.

Dan Feldman co-chairs the firm’s ESG and Business & Human Rights practices.

Drawing on his prior positions in government service spanning multiple Administrations, former Ambassador Dan Feldman’s practice focuses on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) counseling, business and human rights (BHR), global public policy, as well as broader international regulatory compliance. He is a member of the firm’s Global Problem Solving initiative.

As Chief of Staff and Counselor to Secretary John Kerry when he was appointed the first Special Presidential Envoy for Climate (SPEC) by President Biden, Dan helped drive the U.S. government’s international climate agenda, coordinating high level interagency policy-making, engaging with corporate stakeholders, and contributing to key bilateral and multilateral climate discussions, including the 2021 Leaders’ Summit on Climate and the landmark UN Conference of Parties (COP26) in Glasgow.

Previously, Dan served as deputy and then U.S. Special Representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan at the U.S. Department of State in the Obama Administration, as Director of Multilateral and Humanitarian Affairs at the National Security Council in the Clinton Administration, and as Counsel and Communications Adviser to the U.S. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. He also has served as a senior foreign policy and national security advisor to a number of Democratic presidential and Congressional campaigns.

Dan has extensive experience counseling multinational corporations on mitigating risk and maximizing opportunities in the development and implementation of their ESG and sustainability strategies, with a particular background in advising on BHR matters. He was one of the first attorneys in the U.S. to develop a practice in corporate social responsibility, and has been cited by Chambers for his BHR expertise. He assists clients in strategizing about their engagements with a range of key stakeholders, including Members of Congress, executive branch officials, foreign government officials and Embassy representatives, multilateral institutions, trade and industry associations, non-governmental organizations, opinion leaders, and journalists.

Don Ridings co-chairs Covington’s Anti-Corruption + Corporate Compliance practice, and the firm’s Business and Human Rights practice.

As co chair of the firm’s global Anti-Corruption + Corporate Compliance Practice Group, Don leads a team of compliance and investigation lawyers based in the U.S., Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. He is a broad gauge compliance lawyer and for more than 10 years has also been recognized as a leading Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) practitioner by Chambers Global and Chambers USA.

Don has advised clients in nearly every major industry on compliance issues arising under the FCPA and other compliance regimes. He has served as outside compliance counsel to dozens of Fortune 500 companies. Don advises clients on compliance risks in investment transactions, designs and helps implement compliance programs, and counsels clients on a broad range of anti-corruption and other compliance risks. For companies with mature compliance programs, he leads independent compliance program assessments that allow companies to benchmark their corporate compliance programs against peer companies and regulator expectations.

Don has led dozens of internal investigations arising from conduct in Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Middle East, and North America. He represents clients before the U.S. Department of Justice and Securities and Exchange Commission, where he has secured several non-public declinations.

As co-chair of the firm’s Business and Human Rights practice, Don advises clients on the evolving legal regimes related to the corporate responsibility to respect human rights. He counsels clients on issues relating to supply chain due diligence and responsible sourcing, human rights due diligence in investment transactions, integrating human rights elements into corporate compliance programs, NCP and other non-judicial dispute resolution processes, and responding to demands from NGOs, investors, regulators, and other stakeholders.

Paul Mertenskötter advises companies, investors, and governments on regulatory sustainability, international trade, and public policy matters.

Paul has particular experience advising multinational companies on EU sustainability laws, including the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), the Taxonomy Regulation, the Forced Labor Regulation, and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). His practice also spans a wide range of climate change issues, including carbon offsets, accounting rules, and related international sustainability reporting frameworks such as the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB). Paul further advises clients on their strategic engagement with the rules of the World Trade Organization (WTO), free trade agreements, the Paris Agreement, and general public international law.

Prior to joining the firm, Paul was a Visiting Scholar at the WTO in Geneva, clerked at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, and was a Fellow at the Institute for International Law and Justice at NYU Law School.

title: United States: The historical roots of Trump's anti-Haitian racism - Green Left
authors: Malik Miah, Barry Sheppard, Malik Miah Barry Sheppard
description:

Trump’s racism Haitians and their children are seen by the government as “the worst of the worst”.
The remaining 30% were made up of permanent residents (“green card” holders), TPS holders, parolees, visa holders or undocumented immigrants.
In 1909, the National City Bank of New York secured a controlling interest in Haiti’s National Bank.
In 1910 a US investor acquired Haiti’s national railroad, with rights to establish banana plantations on both sides of the tracks.
text:
United States President Donald Trump’s government overturned the temporary protected status (TPS) of 350,000 Haitians living in the country this month, following a June 25 Supreme Court decision to greenlight the administration's actions.

According to the American Civil Liberties Union, the Supreme Court case, Mullin v. Dahlia Doe challenged the Trump administration’s decision to terminate TPS for thousands of Syrian immigrants living and working legally in the US while it is unsafe for them to return home. The case was consolidated with Trump v. Miot, the case concerning Haitian TPS holders.

“TPS has historically allowed people from specific countries to remain in the US and to work here if it is not safe for them to return home due to war, disasters, or other emergencies,” the ACLU said.

Following the court’s decision, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved quickly to end Haitians’ TPS, despite State Department advice saying it is unsafe for anyone to travel to Haiti.

Work permits for all Haitians were terminated on August 6, which will lead to mass layoffs and TPS holders losing their homes.

Thousands of these legal residents are now “illegal” and subject to deportation.

Haitians waiting for hearings on their residency status are being forced to wear ankle monitors — reminiscent of the iron shackles forced on enslaved people.

Trump’s racism

Haitians and their children are seen by the government as “the worst of the worst”.

Trump’s hatred for Black people — whether from Africa or their descendants in other countries — has spilled over into racism against other non-whites, as seen by the forced detention and deportation of Latinx residents and citizens by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents.

Trump’s goal is clear: “Make America White Again”.

Many Haitians have been living in the US under protected status since the devastating earthquake that struck Haiti in January 2010. TPS was extended and re-designated several times due to the ongoing humanitarian, political and security crises in Haiti.

Soon after taking office, Trump’s administration rescinded former president Joe Biden’s TPS extension, saying it believed TPS was being used far beyond its intended purpose.

The DHS said it was “returning TPS to its original status: temporary”.

The administration contended that repeated extensions allowed increasing numbers of Haitians to qualify for the program over time and described the system as having been “exploited and abused”.

The DHS also said the move was part of Trump's broader effort to reverse policies it viewed as “encouraging illegal immigration”.

Critics of the decision, including human rights, civil libertarian and immigrant rights advocates, argue that TPS protections should remain in place, as Haitians continue to face severe political instability, gang violence and humanitarian crises, making it unsafe for them to return.

Significant community

People of Haitian descent living in the US number 1.1–1.5 million, depending on the definition and dataset used.

The 2021–22 census estimated there were about 1.14 million people of full or partial Haitian ancestry in the US.

Of the 852,000 Haitian-born immigrants living in the US in 2024, about 70% (585,000) were naturalised citizens.

The remaining 30% were made up of permanent residents (“green card” holders), TPS holders, parolees, visa holders or undocumented immigrants.

DHS reported that 235,350 Haitians received green cards between 2010 and 2022.

Parts of Central and South Florida, including Miami-Dade County, North Miami, Little Haiti, Fort Lauderdale and surrounding areas have some of the largest Haitian communities in the country.

In New York, Brooklyn’s neighbourhoods of Flatbush and East Flatbush have long-established Haitian populations.

Haitians have also settled in Boston, Brockton, Randolph, and nearby communities in Massachusetts, and there are significant Haitian populations in parts of Connecticut and New Jersey.

There is also a growing Haitian community in Atlanta, Georgia.

Haitians in Ohio, home of Vice President JD Vance, were falsely accused by Vance and Trump of killing and eating cats and dogs. The Republican governor repudiated those attacks, saying Haitians are hard-working members of the community.

Trump’s anti-Haitian racism is not unique. Historically, hostility towards Haitians and Black people has long been a policy of US imperialism. Direct intervention by the US into Haiti dates back to the 1800s, following Haiti’s struggle for independence from French colonial rule, when the Haitian people rose up and overthrew slavery and French colonial rule in a revolutionary struggle that lasted from 1791 to 1804.

Haiti's struggle for liberation

Led by the revolutionary, Toussaint Louverture (1743–1803), enslaved people in the French colony began a major uprising in August, 1791. Haiti declared its independence from France on January 1, 1804, under the leadership of Jean Jacques Dessalines, Louverture’s lieutenant.

This ended French rule and created the world’s first independent Black republic.

It was the only revolution by slaves to have ever succeeded.

Defeated, France declared that the Haitians owed it an indemnity for the “property” (slaves) French slave holders had lost. Imperialist pressure finally forced Haiti to pay up in 1947.

For more than a century after independence, Haiti faced hostility from France and the US.

By 1862, the US government wanted control over Haitian finances, labour, ports and resources to benefit US capitalism’s banking and business interests.

By 1905, the US replaced France as Haiti’s main trading partner. In 1909, the National City Bank of New York secured a controlling interest in Haiti’s National Bank. In 1910 a US investor acquired Haiti’s national railroad, with rights to establish banana plantations on both sides of the tracks.

Peasants who held this land for generations were evicted. This prompted fierce resistance. For four years peasant armies fought back.

In 1915 President Woodrow Wilson sent the US Marines into Haiti. This act demonstrated the emergence of the US as an imperialist power on a par with European imperialists and based on the rule of powerful financial-industrial monopolies.

The marines seized the customs house, imposed martial law and media censorship, and outlawed dissent. They disbanded the Haitian legislature and eliminated the ban on foreign land ownership in the Haitian constitution.

During the occupation, the marines seized US$500,000 in gold from Haiti’s National Bank and transferred it to the National City Bank of New York.

US atrocities

After World War I, a resurgent Black leadership in the US opposed the US occupation of Haiti.

In 1920, James Johnson, Field Secretary of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), visited Haiti and reported for The Nation about the brutality and atrocities carried out by US marines against the people of Haiti, including rapes, murders and massacres of resisting Haitian peasant guerrillas, as well as the reimposition of forced labour to build a major highway.

The Haitian hero under the US occupation was Charlemagne Péralte (1885–1919). Like Augusto César Sandino in Nicaragua and Emiliano Zapata and Pancho Villa in Mexico, Péralte led a nationalist peasant army resisting foreign domination.

Péralte had been dismissed from the army when he refused to surrender his weapons and flag to US marines who took over his district.

For this, he was court martialled and sentenced to five years hard labour in 1917 and his brother Saul was sentenced to death and executed by order of the marines.

In September 1918 Péralte escaped and began recruiting a guerrilla movement. Resistance spread over much of the country, and the US responded with brutal repression. The marines’ campaign against the guerrillas became a war of extermination. The US couched its campaign with racist terms about Black Haitians.

Prisoners were routinely executed. Villages suspected of harbouring guerrillas were burned; suspected sympathisers were shot. Villages and livestock were bombed from the air. Ground troops followed the bombings, killing survivors.

The occupation lasted until 1934. One of its chief legacies was the creation of a new army, the Haitian Gendarmes, under US command, to keep Haitians “in line”.

When the occupation ended, the US turned over power to the Haitian Gendarmes. Several dictatorships followed, most notably that of Francois Duvalier, known as “Papa Doc”. Duvalier’s regime killed 30–60,000 Haitians.

Duvalier ruled from 1957–71, and his son, Jean-Claude, or “Bébé Doc”, continued the dynastic regime until 1986, when the military intervened and he was ousted.

Elections were held and Jean-Bertrand Aristide was elected president in 1990. On September 30, 1991, a military coup overthrew him. Mass protests erupted, and the turmoil caused the US to intervene, and allowed Aristide to return to power from 1994–96.

Aristide led a new organisation, Lavalas, based among the nation’s workers, peasants and the poor. He disbanded the military and organised free and fair elections.

He was elected again in 2001. An opposition, representing Haiti’s bourgeoisie, and marked by political intrigues, forced him into exile, with the US again occupying Haiti to enforce his exile in 2004.

Turmoil again rocked the country, which has intensified due to political destabilisation, corruption, rising street violence, natural disasters and the impacts of decades of foreign military and political intervention and resource theft.

text:
(Bangkok) – Thai authorities should halt the imminent deportation of 26 ethnic Karen villagers from Phetchaburi province to Myanmar and release them from immigration detention, Human Rights Watch said today.

On August 10, 2026, district and forestry officials along with the Thai military raided the Karen community in Ban Pa Deng village in Phetchaburi province’s Kaeng Krachan National Park, targeting those without proof of Thai citizenship. The authorities arrested twenty-eight villagers, including eight children and two pregnant women, and placed them in the custody of the Phetchaburi provincial immigration office. Two villagers were later released after local officials verified their residence registration records. The immigration office then transferred the remaining 26 villagers to the Suan Phlu Immigration Detention Center in Bangkok to prosecute them on immigration charges and deport them to Myanmar.

“Deporting ethnic Karen villagers to Myanmar would put them at risk of grave danger,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai authorities should work with the community to ensure access to their ancestral lands for their livelihood.”

Since the February 2021 coup, Myanmar’s military junta has carried out a nationwide campaign of mass killings, torture, arbitrary arrests, and unlawful attacks that amount to crimes against humanity and war crimes. More than two million people have been internally displaced and over 100,000 refugees have fled to neighboring countries.

In the face of recent escalating fighting in Myanmar, Thai authorities have summarily determined that undocumented Karen in the Kaeng Krachan National Park, including local villagers, are “illegal immigrants,” community leaders told Human Rights Watch. Such classification means they are vulnerable to arrest and deportation to Myanmar. Residents of Ban Pa Deng village said that at least 10 villagers remain unaccounted for after Thai authorities deported them to Myanmar about two months ago.

Deporting the 26 Karen villagers to Myanmar could violate Thailand’s obligations as a party to the United Nations Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment as well as the customary international law principle prohibiting refoulement, the forcible return of anyone to a place where they would face a genuine risk of persecution, torture or other ill-treatment, or a threat to their life. In addition, Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act prohibits deportation when there is a substantial risk of torture or ill-treatment.

Ethnic Karen people have lived in both Thailand and Myanmar for generations, including in the jungle in Phetchaburi and Prachuap Khiri Khan provinces, long before the establishment of the Kaeng Krachan National Park. Hundreds of thousands of Karen in Thailand have colored identification cards, meaning they are a recognized hilltribe group in Thailand, but others who arrived in Thailand more recently have no legal status. Karen frequently travel between their communities across the Thailand-Myanmar border, Human Rights Watch said.

In 2021, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee placed the Kaeng Krachan Forest Complex on the World Heritage List, leading the Thai authorities to prohibit human settlement, including of Karen people, in the Kaeng Krachan National Park. This decision was made despite concerns raised by UN human rights experts, the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand, and Indigenous groups about the ancestral land rights of ethnic Karen.

The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People, a nonbinding international instrument, provides in article 26(2) that “Indigenous peoples have the right to own, use, develop and control the lands, territories and resources that they possess by reason of traditional ownership or other traditional occupation or use.” The UN human rights experts raised the lack of “good faith consultations with the [Karen] community allowing them to participate in the UNESCO nomination process.”

Over the past three decades, Thai authorities have pressured Karen villagers to leave their homes in the Kaeng Krachan National Park, at times violently, including by raiding their villages, burning their farms and properties, and forcibly relocating them. The relocation sites set up by Thai authorities for the Karen are inadequate and unsuitable for their traditional farming, Human Rights Watch said. In August 2022, Kaeng Krahan National Park officials were indicted in relation to the enforced disappearance of the Karen leader and human rights defender Ban Pa Deng Porlajee “Billy” Rakchongcharoen in April 2014. In September 2023, they were acquitted of murder based on lack of evidence.

“Ahead of the UN Human Rights Council’s review of Thailand’s human rights record in November, the Thai government should immediately end its abusive treatment of ethnic Karen in the Kaeng Krachan National Park,” Pearson said. “Concerned governments and UN agencies should press the Thai government to ensure that the fundamental rights of Karen are respected and protected.”

text:
A bill authorizing the California Department of Public Health to inspect residential detention facilities was halted in an Assembly hearing Thursday.

Senate Bill 995, known as the Masuma Khan Justice Act, would create a uniform statewide system to regulate heating, ventilation, air, water and electrical systems in detention centers. It would also mandate adherence to occupational safety and health regulations in an effort to address reported deficiencies in access to mental health and medical care.

The measure is named after Masuma Khan, a 65-year-old resident of Altadena, California. During an April hearing in the Senate Standing Committee on Health, bill author state Sen. Sasha Pérez, D-Alhambra, said Khan was held for over a month in a cold facility without access to warm clothing, edible food, clean drinking water or the medications she needed.

“SB 995 is grounded in a simple principle,” Pérez said. “If detention facilities operate in California, they must meet California’s standards for safety, dignity and human rights.”

Khan has lived in the U.S. since 1997 with her daughter and husband, both American citizens. Though she has no criminal record, Khan was detained at California City Detention Center after a routine immigration check-in in downtown Los Angeles. During a month in detention, Khan was denied access to necessary medications for hypothyroidism, high blood pressure and glaucoma, according to testimony by her daughter, Riya Khan.

“When I visited her one day, she was having shortness of breath, she couldn’t walk, her legs were so swollen and painful that they were bruising up and she was shaking,” Khan said in an interview with The Sacramento Bee. “That scared me because I was afraid my mom was going to die in that place when she’s done nothing wrong.”

Riya Khan said those held in the facility were served moldy, insect-infested bread, drank dirty water and lived in below-freezing conditions. The LED floodlights outside the center are left on all night, she said, and guards slam doors at all hours, keeping detainees awake.

“This is unacceptable and disgusting,” Riya Khan said. “We have people dying at a record rate … There is a complete and utter disregard for human lives at this point. And this can be prevented by having certain rules and regulations in place.”

After seeing the conditions in which her mother was held, Khan said she “reached out to anyone and everyone” — news organizations, social media creators and legislators like Pérez. According to Pérez, she pledged to author the bill last fall after hearing what Masuma Khan went through.

“Masuma looked at me at one point and said, ‘If these facilities are located in California and you’re a California state senator, why would you not be able to … do something about this?’” Pérez said in an interview with The Bee. “I felt like the point she made in that moment was very accurate. Why should we not be able to do anything? Why haven’t we done more?”

Pushback over redundancy

While the bill received unanimous support in Senate votes and during committee hearings in both chambers, some said its provisions may have been duplicative of existing law.

“We have concerns with some of the provisions in the bill that we believe would create … duplicative oversight for health facilities that are already licensed and regulated under some of the most stringent regulations in the nation,” said Leah Barros on behalf of the California Hospital Association.

Barros said there were worries that permitting state-run health inspections on federally overseen detention facilities may invite legal challenges. Additionally, the bill would group private detention facilities with licensed behavioral health facilities already governed by strict state operating guidelines.

“While SB 995 addresses a serious issue, its significant costs and lengthy implementation timeline raised concerns about whether the proposal, as written, would translate into timely, meaningful protections for the people it was intended to help,” Wicks said in a written statement to The Bee.

Loading…

Some were opposed to the inclusion of county juvenile facilities in the definition of “involuntary residential facility” in the bill. At an Assembly Health Committee hearing in June, Chief Probation Officers of California Legislative Director Danielle Sanchez said these facilities are already subjected to judicious inspection and would not benefit from additional oversight.

“Because there’s an existing framework, adding duplication and layering a new one … actually does more harm than good in carrying out the state framework that has been established,” Sanchez said in testimony.

Pérez maintained that the state has the authority to implement the legislation outlined in the bill. She referenced a bill passed in 2024 that would allow county-level health inspections of detention facilities. Though the bill’s language is similar to SB 995, it is limited by county-specific politics, according to Pérez.

“[The 2024] bill was very powerful and innovative,” Pérez said. “But I don’t think we considered what would happen if a privately run immigration detention facility needed to be investigated and the county itself, the board of supervisors, did not want to initiate the investigation. And that’s what’s happened.”

According to Pérez, California City Detention Center is located in a conservative area whose county officials refused to initiate an investigation into the facility’s conditions. This made it difficult, she said, to hold elected officials accountable for Masuma Khan’s treatment while there.

“This is part of the reason why I believe, and will continue to argue, that the state needs to take over that oversight and accountability framework,” Pérez said. “This is a statewide issue, it is a national issue, and we can no longer just rely on these county agencies.”

The bill was halted by the Assembly Appropriations Committee along with dozens of other measures.

“I’m so heartbroken,” Pérez said. “We are moving past a moment where this is a partisan issue, and I think people are beginning to realize that these are human rights abuses that we need to take action around. I really hope there will be reconsideration here … I cannot think of a more urgent issue than this one.”

name: Litigation
title: Advance Parole Is No Longer a Safe Harbor From the Unlawful Presence Bars
description:
Practitioners evaluated a client's unlawful presence history by distinguishing between an advance parole authorized trip from other trips for purposes of § 212(a)(9)(B).
It also pointed to other provisions of the INA where Congress expressly addressed the consequences of departures under advance parole.
The Delcarmen-Lara decision requires a new analysis of how much unlawful presence a client has accrued before departing on advance parole.
What Practitioners Should Do Now Immigration practitioners should consider taking the following steps: Identify clients with outstanding advance parole documents.
And the lengthy processing time for Form I-131 advance parole applications — currently 23 months — has made applying for advance parole less desirable.
text:
The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) overturned one of the more important interpretations of immigration law affecting adjustment of status applicants who have accrued unlawful presence. In Matter of Milagro Delcarmen-Lara, 29 I&N Dec. 830 (BIA 2026), decided Aug. 13, 2026, the BIA held that a trip outside the United States pursuant to a grant of advance parole is a “departure” for purposes of INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). That statutory ground of inadmissibility governs the ten-year bar for unlawful presence that is triggered by a departure.

The Board expressly overruled Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly, 25 I&N Dec. 771 (BIA 2012), which for more than 14 years has provided protection to people who had accrued unlawful presence and traveled abroad on advance parole. The BIA has now held unequivocally that a departure from the United States pursuant to a grant of advance parole is a “departure” for purposes of § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). While noncitizens may still travel on advance parole and, upon their return, be considered “inspected and admitted or paroled” for adjustment of status eligibility under INA § 245(a), their departure may trigger the unlawful presence bars. In addition, they may be refused entry to the United States by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) if they are found inadmissible under INA § 212(a)(9)(B).

What Arrabally and Yerrabelly Used to Provide

INA § 212(a)(9)(B) states that noncitizens become inadmissible after they accrue a certain amount of unlawful presence and then depart the United States. Before this recent BIA decision, the Arrabally and Yerrabelly decision provided an important exception. The BIA held that someone who temporarily left the United States pursuant to advance parole did not make the statutory “departure” that triggered the unlawful presence bar.

The BIA viewed an advance parole departure as fundamentally different from other departures because the government had authorized the person to leave temporarily and contemplated that they would return to continue pursuing adjustment of status. That interpretation became an important part of adjustment practice. Practitioners evaluated a client's unlawful presence history by distinguishing between an advance parole authorized trip from other trips for purposes of § 212(a)(9)(B). They had encouraged, for example, Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders who had entered without inspection to leave under advance parole and create eligibility for adjustment of status should they become classified as an immediate relative (spouse, parent or child under 21 of a U.S. citizen).

The New Rule

Delcarmen-Lara holds that the word “departure” means what it ordinarily means: leaving the United States. The BIA relied heavily on the statutory text. Neither “depart” nor “departure” is defined in the INA, and the BIA found no language in § 212(a)(9)(B) creating an exception for departures pursuant to advance parole. It also pointed to other provisions of the INA where Congress expressly addressed the consequences of departures under advance parole. The BIA reasoned that Congress's decision to include such language elsewhere, but not in § 212(a)(9)(B), supported the conclusion that no advance parole exception should be implied here.

The BIA also pointed out that the Department of Homeland Security and the former Immigration and Naturalization Service had historically treated advance parole departures as potentially triggering the unlawful-presence bar before Arrabally. It noted that advance parole documents issued at that time had warned applicants that departure could result in inadmissibility.

Leaving the United States on advance parole is now a “departure” for purposes of triggering the INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II) ten-year unlawful presence bar.

Who Is Most Affected?

The Delcarmen-Lara decision requires a new analysis of how much unlawful presence a client has accrued before departing on advance parole. This demands a thorough understanding of the definition of unlawful presence as well as the exceptions. The decision specifically cites to § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II), which addresses the ten-year bar. But the same statutory definition of “departure” is relevant to the three-year bar in § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(I). Thus, a person who accrued more than 180 days but less than one year of unlawful presence will trigger the three-year bar after departing on advance parole; a person who accrued one year or more will trigger the ten-year bar.

The BIA decision does not eliminate waiver possibilities under INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(v). Adjustment of status applicants can still file Form I-601, Application to Waive Grounds of Inadmissibility, to waive the three- or ten-year bars based on a showing of extreme hardship to a lawful permanent resident or U.S. citizen spouse or parent. Remember that the three or ten years can run while the person is residing in the United States after the reentry, pursuant to the BIA’s decision in Matter of Duarte-Gonzalez, 28 I&N Dec. 688 (BIA 2023).

This decision will likely mean that advance parole is no longer a viable option for those seeking to use it for adjustment of status eligibility. In addition, traveling under advance parole puts the noncitizen at risk of being refused entry to the United States altogether if they are subject to an inadmissibility ground. Rather than departing, triggering the ten-year bar, returning (hopefully), and then filing an I-601 waiver together with the adjustment application, they may opt instead to consular process. In those situations, they would file Form I-601A, Application for Provisional Unlawful Presence Waiver. After that is approved, they would depart for their immigrant visa interview. While the departure would trigger the ten-year unlawful presence bar, it would be waived at the immigrant visa application stage. Note that under the current administration, consular processing is an increasingly difficult option for those subject to either the travel ban for nationals from 39 countries or the immigrant visa suspension currently impacting 75 countries.

DACA recipients will be among the most affected, since those who had accrued unlawful presence before obtaining DACA had been able to use advance parole to travel abroad without triggering § 212(a)(9)(B). But it will also affect adjustment of status applicants, U-visa and T-visa holders, and others who are eligible for advance parole.

Note that USCIS policy since July 1, 2022, has been that TPS beneficiaries have traveled pursuant to “authorized travel” and not technically advance parole. However, it is likely that USCIS will take the position that the reasoning of Delcarmen-Lara applies equally to TPS beneficiaries traveling and “departing” pursuant to authorized travel.

Battered spouses and children require individualized analysis because INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(iii) contains a special provision concerning certain Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) self-petitioners. The unlawful presence bar does not apply if “there was a substantial connection between the battery or extreme cruelty…and the alien’s unlawful presence in the United States.”

Departure on Advance Parole Executes Removal Order

It has long been USCIS’s interpretation that those who travel on DACA advance parole execute any underlying removal order, although USCIS has taken the opposite approach for TPS-based advance parole and authorized travel. That interpretation appears to be unchanged by the Delcarmen-Lara decision. Therefore, the Delcarmen-Lara case should not have even come before the BIA because the underlying motion to reopen is likely to have been unnecessary.

The Delcarmen-Lara case arose out of the BIA’s consideration of a motion to reopen removal proceedings for a DACA beneficiary who had traveled under advance parole and sought to reopen her removal proceedings so she could apply to adjust status. The BIA denied reopening, and then separately made its findings on the statutory meaning of the term “departure” under § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). But by departing pursuant to a grant of advance parole, the respondent in Delcarmen-Lara likely executed the removal order, leaving her free to pursue adjustment of status before USCIS with a Form I-212 waiver without reopening her proceedings.

Indeed, Ms. Delcarmen Lara may still be able to pursue adjustment of status before USCIS since she apparently is no longer in immigration proceedings. Practitioners should screen for this issue of execution of a removal order after leaving on advance parole when evaluating their clients’ eligibility for adjustment, as this may obviate the need to file a motion to reopen before the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

Prospective Application

The BIA determined that the new interpretation of departure under advance parole will be applied prospectively. It emphasized that Arrabally had been longstanding precedent, that the new rule represents a significant change, and that the government's interest in applying the new interpretation did not outweigh the reliance interests created by the former rule. This means that the decision does not apply to clients who traveled and returned on advance parole before Aug. 13, 2026.

The decision does not elaborate on what “prospective” means in every possible setting. For example, does it cover people who left on advance parole before Aug. 13, 2026, but returned on or after that date? Arguably yes, because they relied on the prior interpretation of the statute at the time they left. Practitioners may need to demonstrate their client’s reliance on Arrabally in those particular fact situations and argue that Delcarmen Lara does not apply to them.

What About Federal Appellate Court Decisions?

The Eleventh Circuit had previously applied Arrabally in Ortiz-Bouchet v. U.S. Attorney General, 714 F.3d 1353 (11th Cir. 2013). In that case, the appellate court followed the BIA decision and held that a departure under advance parole did not qualify as a departure under § 212(a)(9)(B). The BIA acknowledged this holding and stated that it did not read Ortiz-Bouchet as preventing it from revisiting its interpretation of “departure.” But practitioners practicing within that circuit can argue that Ortiz-Bouchet remains binding until the circuit itself rules otherwise.

More broadly, after the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises, 603 U.S. ___, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), federal courts are no longer required to defer to an agency's interpretation or reinterpretation of a statutory term if the court determines it is ambiguous. Litigation over the new interpretation of “departure” and the precedential effect of Delcarmen-Lara seems highly likely.

What Practitioners Should Do Now

Immigration practitioners should consider taking the following steps:

Identify clients with outstanding advance parole documents. Advise them of the effects of departing now with that travel document if they have accrued more than 180 days of unlawful presence. Advise them of the effect of departing if they have an outstanding order of deportation or removal. Advise them that it is possible that they will be refused entry by CBP if they are determined to be inadmissible.

Hold off applying for advance parole for clients who are eligible but would be affected by the BIA decision. • Revise office forms, travel-consent language, and engagement letters. Advance parole counseling should expressly address § 212(a)(9)(B) and the Delcarmen-Lara decision.

Explain the consular processing path to permanent residency for clients who will no longer qualify for adjustment of status due to their having entered without inspection and their inability to depart under advance parole.

Develop more experience in filing I-601A provisional waivers for clients who will now have to consular process and trigger the unlawful presence bars upon their departure.

Watch for implementing guidance in a USCIS Policy Manual update or a follow-on BIA decision refining how "prospective" application will be measured.

Conclusion

The result in Delcarmen-Lara should not be surprising to practitioners who have watched the BIA issue dozens of precedential decisions over the past year and a half that nearly all favor the Trump administration’s extreme policies. The immediate impact of Delcarmen-Lara may be somewhat muted, as many noncitizens who traveled on advance parole did so prior to the effective date of the decision and thus can benefit from the more favorable Arrabally interpretation. And the lengthy processing time for Form I-131 advance parole applications — currently 23 months — has made applying for advance parole less desirable. But the long-term impact could be significant, making it far more difficult for noncitizens to obtain adjustment of status.
