text:
On more than one occasion in his life, Aaron Reitz has sworn an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic. Most recently, it was on July 9, to serve as the lead federal prosecutor for the Southern District of Texas, one of the most significant U.S. attorney postings in the country.

By its own writing, this U.S. attorney's office, which encompasses Houston and Galveston down to the southern border, prosecutes more federal criminal cases than most other districts across the country.

"For forever, Texas has been underwater in terms of resources for the federal bench; all four districts, but especially Southern," Carl Tobias, a University of Richmond law professor, told Houston Public Media. "And that could be explained pretty clearly by the border, I think a lot of it."

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Reitz, a firebrand conservative who has drawn scrutiny for challenging the results of the 2020 presidential election and arguing that court orders can justifiably be disobeyed, was not tapped for the role by the usual route. Bloomberg Law reports he was not appointed by President Donald Trump to serve as the U.S. attorney, though he had worked for the Trump administration previously. Instead, the district's judges selected him to serve in the office, allowing Reitz to circumvent a Senate confirmation hearing.

That process, though permissible under federal law, is not the traditional route, by which a nominee is appointed by the executive branch of government and then confirmed by the Senate.

"I'm honored to serve as the chief federal law enforcement officer and lawyer for this mission-critical district," Reitz said in a news release when he was sworn in. "Our office will relentlessly combat violent crime, illegal immigration, drug and human trafficking, corruption, and fraud. We will faithfully uphold the rule of law and protect the public. Things are about to get very bad for criminals in the Southern District of Texas."

Two days before that, on July 7, a van carrying four immigrants without legal status in Houston was pursued by federal immigration agents. When U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents approached the van, the federal government alleged the driver, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, attempted to use his car as a weapon, a claim the other three men in the van dispute. An ICE officer fired his gun and shot Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old father of three who had lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years, according to his family.

"They're killing me," Salgado Araujo said, clutching his stomach, according to an attorney for one of the witnesses. He died thereafter. His killing has spurred the community into action, prompting multiple investigations at the local, state and federal levels. Protests have called for transparency from the federal government.

Now a month into the role, Reitz, whose office did not make him available for an interview, has helmed the federal government's legal representation related to the shooting. Following the FBI and U.S. Department of Homeland Security's investigation, they will present their findings to the U.S. attorney's office for the Southern District. It would then be up to Reitz and his affiliates to decide whether or not to press any federal charges against the agents involved.

Out of the arena — and back in

The first time Reitz swore an oath to defend the U.S. Constitution was just after he graduated from Texas A&M University, when he entered the U.S. military.

He had just married his wife, Meredith, whom he had met on the school bus to his first day of classes at Barbara Bush Middle School in San Antonio. The two began dating when they attended Ronald Reagan High School, and they both went to Texas A&M. Eventually, though, Meredith decided to transfer to the University of Texas at Austin — as Aaron has said, Meredith, who wanted to be a veterinarian, had taken the rectal temperatures of too many cows. They broke up in the process but soon rekindled and were married in October 2009.

Less than a year later, the Reitzes moved to Quantico, Virginia, before he was deployed to Afghanistan with the U.S. Marine Corps in early 2011. After returning to the United States, Reitz applied to the UT Law School.

His de-facto resume, which he touted during his first run for office in 2020, touts his conservative record: he was a fellow at the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative thinktank; he was chosen by his peers as the Lino Graglia Conservative Student of the Year at UT; he was a fellow at the Alliance Defending Freedom, a conservative nonprofit; he was president of UT's chapter of the Federalist Society; and served as editor-in-chief of the Texas Review of Law and Politics. After graduating, Reitz went into private practice at Bracewell LLP, a Houston-based law firm.

"Wonderful law firm, but really felt that I had been taken out of the arena," Reitz told The Texan in a 2019 interview.

At that time around 2017, Don Willett, a justice on the Texas Supreme Court, was appointed by Trump to the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. That left a vacancy on the state's highest civil court. After Willett was confirmed to the bench, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott appointed his general counsel, Jimmy Blacklock, to the Texas Supreme Court.

As luck had it, Reitz knew Blacklock. In Austin, he would recount, conservative circles ran small. He reached out to Blacklock and asked to serve as chief clerk to the new justice. Blacklock accepted.

In Reitz's own telling, he took a 70% pay cut to join Blacklock's team. But it was the jump into public policy that Reitz wanted to take advantage of. In the spring of 2019, Reitz decided to run for Texas House of Representatives in a district representing southwest Austin, which had flipped for Democrat Vikki Goodwin in 2018. He resigned from Blacklock's office in May 2019.

In the interview with The Texan, Reitz said that, while he would be voting for Trump’s reelection in November 2020, his district's voting trend was "proto-typical suburbia, that was a little bit squeamish about Trump. Not his policies, but you know, you had a lot of families that were saying, ‘Gosh, I'm for Trump, but I'm not super in favor of his Tweets... the persona, I don't want my young boy to grow up to be like Donald Trump."

On primary election day, March 3, 2020, days before much of the country shut down for the COVID-19 pandemic, Reitz placed fourth in the Republican primary for the Texas House seat. By that December, Reitz was working on the team with the Texas Attorney General's Office seeking to suspend certifying the results of the 2020 election won by Democrat Joe Biden.

The day before Reitz was set to begin working in the office of Texas AG Ken Paxton, Reitz told The Texas Tribune, several OAG officials reported Paxton to the FBI over concerns of abuses of office, the same allegations that would result in Paxton's impeachment in the Texas House of Representatives three years later.

But he opted to stick by Paxton through the scandal as the AG, who now is running for U.S. Senate, was acquitted by the Texas Senate. Through his time at the OAG, Reitz said he worked on border security matters, religious issues, and led the election integrity divisions in 2020 and 2022. That included working on Texas v. Pennsylvania, a lawsuit brought by Paxton's office to suspend the certification of election results in key states that were for Biden in the 2020 election.

In April 2021, Reitz led a lawsuit against the Biden administration that accused the federal government of lapsing in border security, allowing COVID-19 to spread via migrants traveling to the U.S. By October 2022, after the case had worked through the courts, both the OAG and the Biden administration agreed to dismiss the case.

Reitz led a similar effort a year later, in April 2022, which was also dismissed later that year. In the initial complaint, Reitz called the standard process of an immigration hearing to argue for or against removal "slow" and said it requires either paying for a migrant without legal status in detention or running the risk of their fleeing.

Years later, Reitz would compare his relationship with Paxton to a football game: Paxton was the head coach, and Reitz was the offensive coordinator. In total, he would tell Austin's ABC affiliate, KVUE, he led 46 lawsuits against the Biden administration, a significant portion of which were dedicated to immigration policy.

Eventually, Reitz left Paxton's office to work as a chief of staff to U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas. He resigned from the OAG on May 12, 2023, two weeks before Paxton would be impeached.

"We'll keep fighting this war together," Reitz said in his resignation letter to Paxton. "But now it's my time to fight it on a different front."

Just and unjust laws

Every Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Reitz said in an Instagram post in 2022, he rereads King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," an open letter the civil rights leader wrote in April 1963 while imprisoned for leading demonstrations in Alabama. In it, King writes that, just as people have a duty to follow just laws, they have a duty to break unjust laws as well.

It was that theory — that someone could justifiably break laws that they found morally wrong — that had rankled the U.S. Senate judiciary committee.

On a Wednesday morning in February 2025, the committee convened with the goal of establishing the backbone of the Department of Justice. Three nominees sat before them, making up three of the most crucial law enforcement roles in the federal government.

There was D. John Sauer, nominated to be Solicitor General, on the left and Harmeet Dhillon, Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights nominee, on the right. In between them sat Reitz, then 37 years old, in a blue pinstripe suit, awaiting his hearing to eventually become the Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Policy at the Department of Justice.

Sauer and Dhillon remain in their roles today. Reitz would hold his role for 72 days before resigning to run for an elected office.

When Trump stated on Truth Social he would appoint Reitz to the office, he called the Texan "a true MAGA attorney, a warrior for our Constitution, and will do an outstanding job at DOJ."

"He is currently my chief of staff and has the virtually impossible job of keeping me out of trouble," Cruz, a member of the committee, said with a laugh. "In that regard, he has failed spectacularly."

Reitz, in turn, called Cruz a mentor.

Democrats on the committee, though, had some concerns, mostly surrounding Reitz's digital footprint on X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter. One post Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois took issue with was from March 30, 2020, when U.S. Judge Lee Yeakel blocked Texas from closing abortion clinics during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Looking for some Andrew Jackson-level leadership on this one," Reitz wrote at the time. "‘Judge Yeakel has made this decision. Now let him enforce it.'"

"So you're saying that a legal court order from a federal court should not be followed under some circumstances," Durbin said. "What would those circumstances be?"

"What I'm saying is that there are some instances in which a public official is lawfully bound by the holding of a particular court, in which case that official would in fact be lawfully required to be bound by it," Reitz said. "I can't speak, though, ranking member Durbin, for all instances in which that dynamic may or may not be in play given a certain lawsuit."

Durbin called his response "an incredible statement by someone who wants to be a part of the Department of Justice." It was also prescient: during Reitz's time in the Trump administration, it began defying court orders on immigration policy.

Aside from his political theory on ignoring court orders, it was Reitz's social media presence that garnered the most attention from his confirmation hearing. He had deleted the vast majority of posts from his X account, which he had created in 2014.

"I have oftentimes observed a practice of regularly deleting old tweets," Reitz said in his written testimony. "I recall, though am not certain, clearing out my X account shortly before joining the Senate as a Chief of Staff in 2023, since most of my social media activity was related to my prior service in Texas and not related to my role as a Senate staffer."

"Friendly reminder that ‘birthright citizenship' is not a thing," Reitz had tweeted in 2021, according to a screenshot shared during the hearing.

Another tweet from February 2021 called the U.S. Supreme Court's Bostock decision, which codified protections from workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, "the worst SCOTUS decision since Obergefell,” which permitted same-sex marriage.

In September 2020, Reitz shared a photo of late Sen. Joe McCarthy, who spread fears of communism during the Red Scare of the 1950s, with the caption, "Bring back the good ol' days."

The posts, ultimately, were not enough to halt his confirmation. A month later, on March 26, 2025, Reitz became one of the senior most law enforcement officials in the nation, and he once again swore an oath to defend the U.S. Constitution.

By June 11, however, Reitz was resigning. As he put it in his resignation letter to Trump, "you charged me with developing and implementing the battle plans to advance your Law and Order Agenda and to restore integrity to our Justice System. ... Duty now calls me to continue that fight on a new front."

The next day, Reitz announced a bid to become the next attorney general of Texas, succeeding Paxton.

Battle tested

A month out from this year’s Republican primaries in Texas — when GOP voters would select their pick to run for Texas attorney general, among other seats — Reitz was thinking about the oaths he had sworn in the past to protect the U.S. Constitution from all enemies, foreign and domestic. Those domestic enemies, he postulated, include the modern day Democratic Party.

"What I have come to believe from long-fought personal experience is that there are — the leadership class of the Democratic Party today can rightfully be construed as enemies of the Constitution," Reitz told KVUE. "This isn't me being hyperbolic. This isn't me exaggerating with political rhetoric. We have seen what the left is capable of doing. We have seen what the Democratic Party is willing to push when they have the power. And I believe that what they want for this state and our nation is antithetical to our closest values, to American values, to western civilization, and to the United States Constitution."

That included, Reitz would write, the head of the Texas House of Representatives' Democratic Caucus, state Rep. Gene Wu of Houston. Responding to a post that depicted Wu stating that several marginalized groups, including Latino, Black, Asian and other communities, "share the same oppressor," Reitz said he wanted Wu's citizenship revoked.

"As AG, I want to see [Wu] de-naturalized," Reitz wrote on social media on Feb. 9. "On what basis? He likely concealed his anti-American sentiment throughout his citizenship app process — the details of which are conspicuously absent from public record."

Wu, whose office did not return a request for an interview, was born in China before moving to Texas with his family at a young age. He became a U.S. citizen around the age of 14, through his parents.

Reitz' former bosses, Cruz and Paxton, both criticized Wu for his "bigotry" and "racist" comments. Reitz was also not the only candidate in the race for Texas attorney general to raise concerns over Wu's comments. U.S. Rep. Chip Roy said Wu should resign from the state legislature. State Sen. Mayes Middleton of Galveston, who would go on to secure the Republican nomination, wrote that Wu was "showing us why only those born in America should be eligible to run for office."

It was Reitz, however, who drew the most attention for his comments. He had been the hand-picked successor to the attorney general's office — Paxton, who was leaving the role after three terms to run for U.S. Senate, endorsed him. As part of his campaign, Reitz labeled himself as the only candidate who was "battle tested" in a law enforcement office.

In the six years since Reitz last ran for public office, his platform had shifted further to the right. By his own submissions on Ballotpedia, his three key messages of his 2020 campaign for the state legislature were to "preserve Texas's vibrant economic climate through low taxes and light regulations," "Make our schools and communities safer," and, "Give our children a first-class education." By his 2026 campaign, his three key messages were "advancing an America First Law & Order agenda," "Securing our southern border," and, "root[ing] out corruption and stop[ping] far-left local governments from undermining Texas values."

Just as in his 2020 campaign, however, Reitz finished in fourth place. As Middleton and Roy headed to a runoff, Reitz threw his endorsement to Middleton. Since then, Reitz had stayed relatively quiet, campaigning for Paxton and Middleton and sharing the occasional social media post from Trump administration officials.

Then, on July 9, Reitz made his next career move known — he was sworn in as the new U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas.

His appointment prompted congratulations from Cruz, Paxton and Abbott, the Texas governor, who wrote on social media, “You'll do great. Huge win for Texas.”

Added Paxton: "I know Aaron will be an outstanding U.S. Attorney and will serve the Southern District of Texas with integrity and a strong commitment to the rule of law that will undoubtedly advance the cause of justice in our state."

‘Let the justice system work'

On July 15, a week after Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was shot and killed by an ICE agent, the FBI executed a search warrant on the van involved in the shooting, which Salgado Araujo was driving. In the search warrant, signed by FBI Special Agent David McNeilly and approved by federal magistrate judge Richard Bennett, a new allegation came forward: law enforcement officers had seen "plastic bags with what appeared to be a white crystal-like substance packaged in small plastic bags." The substance, McNeilly wrote, was "consistent with methamphetamine."

The search warrant was unsealed and made public soon after. Aside from the allegation itself, some officials questioned the decision to share the indictment publicly so soon into the investigation.

"I've been doing this 20 years. I've never seen a federal search warrant, at least before a grand jury presentation, let alone the probable cause statement behind it," Sean Teare, the Harris County District Attorney, said on Houston Matters on July 17. "And there was no evidentiary value to be gained from it anyway. It's puzzling. It's concerning."

It was the first time drugs had been mentioned at all in the investigation of the shooting, which was being investigated by the FBI, Harris County DA and the Texas Rangers, concurrently and independently. It was also an allegation that Salgado Araujo's family did not believe.

"After consulting with my client and his family, our understanding is that this was granulated salt, which is paired with lemon and water as a homemade electrolyte mix used by outdoor workers in extreme Texas heat, not methamphetamine or any other illicit substance," said Ruby Powers, an attorney for Salgado Araujo's brother, Victor, who was also in the van the day of the shooting.

Reitz confirmed to The Texas Tribune, in an Aug. 13 report, that the substance tested by the FBI was not meth.

It's not immediately clear what led up to the search warrant being unsealed, or who decided to unseal it. As federal attorneys who would oversee the prosecution of the shooting, if there were to be any, U.S. attorneys likely played a role in the decision, according to Jay Coons, a criminal justice professor at Sam Houston State University.

"There is a lot of controversy rising up out of this shooting, and there is not too much being said by federal authorities," Coons said in an interview with Houston Public Media. "In my experience, what I would believe is this is why the affidavit was unsealed as quickly as it was and made public: because this kind of takes away from the narrative that the deceased individual was this great guy. ... Well, this information would argue against that. And it also gives a reason why he would be attempting to escape."

Regardless of the decision to unseal the search warrant, Reitz made his preliminary stance on the shooting known by the end of the week. In a video statement shared by the U.S. attorney's office, Reitz stated that evidence indicated federal agents were searching for two Guatemalan men "known to be driving a white van" who were subject to deportation. While looking for that van, they allegedly found "a similar van" being driven by Salgado Araujo on July 7 and attempted to pull the van over, but the "aliens then fled, conducting a rapid U-turn and hopping a median to get away. The agents chose not to pursue."

Shortly before 7 a.m. that morning, the federal agents saw the van again, Reitz said.

"And again," Reitz said, "the illegal aliens attempted to flee, but this time the agents successfully surrounded the vehicle. At some point, two of the four officers got out of their vehicles and instructed the non-compliant aliens to put the van in park. Preliminary information indicates the driver shifted the van into reverse, then forward again, while an officer was partially inside the van or immediately next to it. During this confrontation between federal agents and a group of illegal aliens attempting to flee, one of the officers fired a single shot."

Reitz also raised the allegation of "possible narcotics trafficking and drug offenses," given the bags of powderlike substance in the van.

"I want to reiterate: This assessment is based on preliminary information given to my office," Reitz said. "We draw no decisive conclusions and believe federal law enforcement will conduct a thorough investigation."

As part of the investigation, the substance was tested for narcotics. Though the official results of the test have not been made public, U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, D-Houston, who has worked alongside the family and championed the independent investigation, said last month on social media that testing showed the substance was in fact an electrolyte powder.

Coons, who worked in the Harris County Sheriff's Office for more than three decades, said the decision to file a search warrant over the substances was proper police work. By contrast, he said, the decision to unseal the search warrant without knowing what the substances were could be perceived as hasty.

"If we release that document and not allege but insinuate that there was narcotics in there," Coons hypothesized, "what do we say when a test result comes back and it was whatever it was? That's going to do more harm than good. ... So, my thoughts there would have been, great idea to release it, but let's hold off until we know what we have."

Reitz's office has also pushed to keep at least one of the key witnesses to the shooting, Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, in federal custody, even after a federal judge ordered his release. On July 29, Reitz submitted a motion to reverse the decision permitting Pliego's release, which was denied days later. The U.S. attorney's office is appealing the decision to the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which had not made a ruling on Pliego's release as of Monday.

"We are doing everything we can to seek the truth and do the right thing," Reitz said in the July 16 video statement. "In the meantime, I encourage the public to give the FBI and DHS the opportunity to investigate. Let the justice system work. And pray for safer communities in which law, order, and justice prevail."

text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WKRN) — A mother seeking asylum was detained in South Nashville and transported to a Louisiana detention center after an unfounded report of potential child abuse.

The detention of Sulma Johanna Munoz-Castro took place on Thursday outside a home near South Lyle Lane and Imperial Drive, according to authorities.

After receiving a report of potential child abuse, the Metro Nashville Police Department said it sent officers to check on the health and safety of Munoz-Castro’s children.

“The child appeared to be in good health and showed no indications of abuse,” said Don Aaron, MNPD public affairs director.

Aaron said the second child was reportedly with a babysitter, and a standard referral was submitted with the Department of Children’s Services for a routine follow-up.

Following the welfare check, immigration agents detained Munoz-Castro and transported her to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center.

In a statement to News 2, an ICE spokesperson said Munoz-Castro is facing removal proceedings.

The statement also alleged that Munoz-Castro, a Honduran national, unlawfully entered the United States in December 2021. An ICE spokesperson said that the mother missed two scheduled appointments with federal agents.

The agency recommended downloading the CBP Home App to manage voluntary departure from the United States, saying that those who choose to self-deport can receive $2,600 and a free flight.

description:

text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine —

A field hearing was held Monday at Biddeford High School regarding the shooting death of Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero.

Guerrero, 25, was shot and killed in his car in Biddeford last month by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer.

Democratic members of Congress hosted the hearing, including Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine; Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass.; and Rep. Troy Carter, D-La.

"Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero should be alive today," Pingree said.

Witnesses who spoke at the hearing included Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain; Sue Roche, executive director of the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project; Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition; and the Guerrero family's attorney, Ben Gideon.

"He came to Biddeford to build a life," LaFountain said of Guerrero. "He worked multiple jobs and was raising his daughter here. He was one of us."

Guerrero's father, Omar Duran, delivered a statement during the field hearing and the hosts granted the family's request to not answer any questions. Guerrero's mother, Dora Guerrero, also attended the hearing and sat next to her husband, but did not speak.

"The death of Johan Sebastian, under those conditions, at the hands of ICE, filled our community with fear and uncertainty. That is why I ask only of God and of the justice system that my son’s case be brought to light, along with the cases of the many others who have had to go through something like this," Duran said.

Watch Duran's full statement in the video player at the top of this page.

Gov. Janet Mills also spoke during the field hearing.

"This has to end. It has to end," Mills said. "And if ICE cannot be reined in and fundamentally reformed, then it is time to abolish it!"

Pingree said the hearing was held in Maine because Republicans would not hold one in Washington. According to the congresswoman, members of ICE and Republican members of Congress were invited to the hearing in Biddeford.

According to Pingree, Guerrero's roommate was the target of the immigration enforcement operation that led to his death. Pingree said neither Guerrero nor his roommate had an order for removal from the United States.

In a news conference held after the hearing, Gideon and the congressional lawmakers said there is no sign that the federal government is investigating the shooting.

"We have not been contacted by a single federal agency," Gideon said.

In a statement, Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey said his office continues to actively investigate the deadly shooting. Frey said that, under Maine law, the Attorney General's Office has exclusive responsibility both for any criminal investigation of a homicide and for the use of deadly force by law enforcement acting in any official capacity.

"The Office of the Maine Attorney General is keenly aware of the public interest in this case and is committed to a thorough, impartial investigation that ensures meaningful transparency and public confidence," Frey said in his statement. "While completeness and transparency are objectives of equal importance, protecting the integrity of the investigation takes priority while evidence is still being gathered. This office is regularly assessing whether substantive updates may be made available without interfering with this important work. At the appropriate time, more information will be made publicly available. In the meantime, we appreciate patience as we proceed."

Frey said that once the investigation is complete and he has determined whether available evidence supports any action under Maine law, the entire file will be provided to the Maine Deadly Force Review Panel for review and recommendations in an effort to minimize and prevent the use of deadly force to the greatest extent possible.

However, Frey noted that neither his office nor the Deadly Force Review Panel may exercise jurisdiction over the practices of the Department of Homeland Security, and that it will be the responsibility of either the federal administration or Congress to address any questions raised by such review.

The Biddeford field hearing was a formal congressional hearing, so all of the comments that were made are on the record. The members of Congress who hosted the hearing said they plan to take what they learned back to Washington and demand answers from the Trump administration.

name: Policy
title: Amid Trump administration silence, national Democrats hold 'shadow' hearing on fatal ICE shooting
authors: Emma Davis, Eesha Pendharkar, Shalina Chatlani
description:
ICE agents shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 in Biddeford.
“If not now, in four months.” President Donald Trump launched a mass deportation effort when he started his second administration in 2025.
With a lack of subpoena power, Democrats do not have the ability to compel officials from the administration to testify.
Instead, they’ve used this type of field hearing, also called a shadow hearing, to hear from willing witnesses.
“It will be the responsibility of either the federal administration or Congress to address any questions raised by such review,” the statement read.
text:
Local leaders told Democratic members of Congress that the fatal U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shooting in Biddeford last month has left a lasting impact, with federal silence and inaction leaving the community to carry the burden.

The members of the minority party convened the hearing to collect information with the hope of spurring accountability, however the limits of Democratic oversight were underscored through demands for action that would require the cooperation of Republicans.

ICE agents shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 in Biddeford. Thirty five days later, no video footage of the shooting has emerged.

While the state Attorney General’s Office confirmed it is continuing to investigate, whether there is a federal investigation is unknown, according to the members of Congress who convened Monday’s hearing and the legal counsel for the victim’s family.

“When you look at the course of history, sometimes there are events, we call them inflection points,” said Ben Gideon, legal representation for the Guerrero family. “This could serve as an inflection point going forward, and I very much hope that it does.”

Gideon and other witnesses testified on Monday about the events leading up to the fatal shooting and the fallout before the convening panel, composed of U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree of Maine, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, and two members of the Homeland Security Committee, ranking member Bennie Thompson of Mississippi and Troy Carter of Louisiana.

“We will use what we’ve heard to investigate these operations and to demand answers and to hold this administration accountable,” Carter said, before referring to the upcoming midterm elections. “If not now, in four months.”

President Donald Trump launched a mass deportation effort when he started his second administration in 2025. Since then, with the help of congressional Republicans, he has passed a record $240 billion in immigration enforcement funding, so far.

With a lack of subpoena power, Democrats do not have the ability to compel officials from the administration to testify. Instead, they’ve used this type of field hearing, also called a shadow hearing, to hear from willing witnesses. However, as Thompson put it on Monday, those hearings have so far been met with “crickets” from the GOP.

“I know this hearing cannot bring Johan Sebastián back,” Pingree said in her opening remarks, “but Congress has an obligation to make sure that his death is not dismissed as an unfortunate consequence of immigration enforcement, and that his life is remembered for the humanity and dignity and love that he embroidered.”

Unanswered questions

After the hearing, Attorney General Aaron Frey confirmed his office is continuing to actively investigate the shooting. Once it is complete and he has determined whether the evidence collected supports any action under Maine law, the entire file will be provided to the Maine Deadly Force Review Panel for review and recommendations to prevent this use of deadly force in the future, a statement from his office read.

However, neither the office nor the panel may exercise jurisdiction over the practices of the Department of Homeland Security. “It will be the responsibility of either the federal administration or Congress to address any questions raised by such review,” the statement read.

Every Democratic member of Congress requested information about the shooting in a letter to Homeland Security on July 15. They have not received a response, Thompson confirmed on Monday.

Gideon told reporters that no federal agency has reached out to the family or wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, who heard the shots and soon after saw her husband’s body, which would be typical when such an investigation occurs.

“As far as we can tell the federal government has chosen to turn a blind eye completely,” Gideon said.

The state Attorney General’s Office has interviewed Rojas Alvarez. The car Guerrero was shot in has been turned over to that office as well, Gideon said.

LaFountain said the city has not heard anything from federal agencies regarding the fatal shooting.

“The authority was federal,” he said. “The burden has been local.”

That burden included securing the aftermath of the shooting scene while also standing up mental health and crisis support, he said.

“Our police, fire, public works, schools, and community organizations have been stretched ever since,” he said. “We secured the aftermath of a scene we were not permitted to investigate.”

Several of the roughly 250 people who attended the hearing, which included many state legislators and local officials, shared frustration with Maine Morning Star about the lack of communication between the federal government and state and local authorities. That included Kate Bauer Burke, a former lawyer from Kennebunkport, who said it was “appalling,” and another Kennebunkport resident Audrey Lakin, who said she attended the hearing in the hope of getting more first-hand information.

Gideon condemned the federal government for blaming the victims in shootings.

At first, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told independent U.S. Sen. Angus King Guerrero “weaponized” his vehicle before being shot by an ICE agent, an explanation the agency has frequently used. But ICE later said he attempted to flee and “fearing for public safety” an agent shot him. But, ICE said Guerrero was not the target of the operation.

The federal government has not said who the intended target of the operation was, but ICE has said its agents were responding to the address of a person with a final order of removal.

During the hearing, Pingree pointed to reporting in the Washington Post that Guerrero had been driving a car owned by his roommate when he was shot. Neither Guerrero nor his roommate had final orders of removal, Pingree said.

Sue Roche, executive director of Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, said the organization has reviewed immigration documents provided by his family and confirmed that he had a pending asylum application and was authorized to work in this country.

The federal government has also not confirmed the name of the shooter. Throughout the hearing, the members of Congress frequently cited media reports about the background of the alleged shooter, which included accusations of domestic violence, as evidence of a lack of vetting by the federal agency.

Lasting impact

Traveling from Colombia for the hearing, Guerrero’s father, Omar Durán Plata, shared more about his son, while his mother, Dora Guerrero, sat beside, tears in her eyes.

His son was responsible, honest and loving, he said, known for his big smile, kind heart, and for always being willing to help others.

“We feel a deep pain in our souls when his little daughter, our three-year-old granddaughter, asks for her daddy and why he doesn’t come home from work,” Durán Plata said.

Since the start of Trump’s second term, particularly in the wake of a large-scale operation in January, many immigrants and people of color in Maine have become fearful to leave their homes, go to work and drop their children off at school.

“The arrest may take minutes, but the disruption takes months,” said Mufalo Chitam, Executive Director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.

She added, “ICE never left our state. As we speak, ICE is still picking [up] people.”

People in Cumberland County have been detained outside court and at the airport in recent weeks, following a national trend of federal immigration authorities employing new tactics to boost arrest numbers.

Demands

On behalf of Guerrero’s family, Gideon called on the Homeland Security Committee to immediately begin subpoenaing witnesses and documents to investigate the circumstances that led to the fatal shooting.

However, Democrats are unable to do so on their own with Republicans in the majority. If Democrats flip the balance of power in November, Thompson told reporters he’d have “absolutely no problem with issuing subpoenas.”

Specifically, Gideon called for the committee to determine what policies allowed the agent who shot and killed him to have been deemed fit for hire, identify those responsible for hiring this agent and demand that they be held accountable. Gideon also urged the committee to determine what is behind the pattern of agents unlawfully shooting into motor vehicles and demand that the practice stop immediately.

Further, Gideon said he intends to file a lawsuit against the U.S. government over the conduct of the officer’s shooting into a vehicle.

Presente! Maine Executive Director Crystal Cron called on Congress to pass a pending bill from U.S. Reps. Delia Ramirez (D-IL) and Yvette Clarke (D-NY), called the “Melt ICE Act,” which would end funding for the Department of Homeland Security to detain and monitor immigrants, and redirect that funding toward wrap-around services, including housing and healthcare, for communities affected by immigration enforcement.

Public officials also reiterated their calls to fundamentally reform ICE, or if that is not possible, abolish it.

“If Congress cannot hold ICE accountable, who can?” LaFountain asked the panel. Last month, he issued a formal proclamation calling for a transparent investigation and reform of the nation’s immigration system.

“Our state has taken action. Our city has tried to take action,” LaFountain said. “This is a federal problem that we need a federal solution for.”

Sudan TPS: Automatic EAD Extension Through October 19, 2026

USCIS announced that Sudan’s TPS designation and related benefits are scheduled to terminate on October 19, 2026.

To avoid employment authorization disruptions, USCIS is issuing notices to eligible Sudan TPS beneficiaries who:

Have pending TPS-based EAD renewal applications;

Continue to qualify for TPS;

Have not yet received a renewed EAD in category A12 or C19.

For these individuals, certain expired TPS-based EADs are automatically extended through October 19, 2026.

Eligible Sudan EAD Expiration Dates

Affected workers may use an EAD showing one of the following expiration dates together with the USCIS extension notice:

November 2, 2017

November 2, 2018

April 2, 2019

January 2, 2020

January 4, 2021

October 4, 2021

December 31, 2022

June 30, 2024

April 19, 2025

Form I-9 and E-Verify Guidance

Employers should:

Enter October 19, 2026 in the expiration date fields of Form I-9.

Record the extension in the Additional Information field.

Use October 19, 2026 as the expiration date in E-Verify.

Somalia TPS Officially Terminated

In a significant development, USCIS confirmed that TPS for Somalia terminated effective August 14, 2026.

The announcement follows prior DHS determinations that Somalia no longer meets TPS statutory requirements and references recent litigation developments following the Supreme Court’s decision in Mullin v. Doe.

Impact on Somalia TPS EADs

USCIS has stated that:

TPS Somalia EADs issued under categories A12 and C19 are no longer valid.

Employers must immediately review affected employees’ work authorization documentation.

Continued employment is only permitted if the employee can present alternative proof of valid work authorization.

Employer Reverification Required

Employers must:

Reverify affected employees using Form I-9 procedures.

Obtain valid evidence of continuing employment authorization.

Discontinue employment where no valid work authorization can be demonstrated.

This guidance supersedes USCIS’ August 12, 2026 Somalia TPS notice.

text:
Progressive House lawmakers and far-left Democratic candidates are traveling to Uruguay this week to challenge President Trump’s ‘Donroe Doctrine’ in Latin America.

The lawmakers are participating in the PanAmerican Congress in Montevideo, Uruguay, The Hill has learned, set to take place Aug 21-23.

“We need to build a durable and lasting coalition of progressives that can take on the right-wing forces and answer them with the necessary call of the people,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), one of the lawmakers leading the delegation, said in a statement.

“This is a critically important opportunity to build solidarity in the fight against interventionism and democratic backsliding, and to learn how the United States can be a partner in those efforts.”

The summit was founded in 2024 to bring together progressive leaders from across North, Central, South America and the Caribbean to combat the rise of far-right governments across the Hemisphere. These conservative governments have found common cause with Trump’s hardline policies against drug traffickers and illegal immigration but are criticized for suspending democratic practices and violating human rights.

Jayapal sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on August 14, shared exclusively with The Hill, that criticizes the “Trump corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine — the 19th century policy which sought to assert U.S. dominance in the region.

The administration frames their new strategy as working with Latin American countries to combat crime, curb illegal immigration and box out threats from China. Critics say it dispenses with human rights, citing Trump’s military offensive against suspected drug-runners in the Caribbean, and weaponizes tariffs to pressure governments. They also criticize it for interfering in sovereign elections, and fault Trump for imposing a blockade against Cuba to force regime change, which they say is worsening hardships for Cubans.

“Taken together, the interventions conducted under the banner of the ‘Donroe’ Doctrine appear to follow a partisan playbook: the endorsement of favored candidates, the placement of political allies, the weaponization of tariffs and sanctions, and, where those fail, the application of direct military force,” Jayapal, joined by 10 other colleagues, wrote in the letter.

“These are tactics that destabilize our hemisphere and endanger our neighbors.”

The signatories included Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.), who is joining Jayapal in attending the PanAmerican Congress.

Other attendees include a group of progressive and Democratic socialist candidates who have gained attention for ousting traditional and centrist Democrats.

The group includes three members of the Democratic Socialists of America: Claire Valdez, who is running for the House in New York’s 7th district; Darializa Ávila Chevalier, who is running for New York’s 13th district; and Chris Rabb, who is running for Pennsylvania’s third district. Also attending is progressive Democratic candidate Dr. Adam Hamawy, who is running for New Jersey’s 12th district.

Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, is not traveling to the conference but issued support, describing the mission as building a coalition “pushing back against right-wing radicalization, tackling the climate crisis and addressing our joint economic crisis.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) will address the conference virtually. In a statement provided to The Hill, he said that the mission is to unite progressive voices across the hemisphere to combat “oligarchy, authoritarianism and greed.”

The PanAmerican Congress will bring together more than 150 lawmakers from across the hemisphere at a time when right-wing political parties have taken control of some of Latin America’s largest economies.

Former Colombian president Ernesto Samper, who is attending the PanAmerican conference, called Latin America’s shift to the right as leading toward “a form of neo-fascism, much more complex than what we had before.”

Trump endorsed the winning candidate in Colombia’s June election, the conservative outsider Abelardo de la Espriella, who narrowly defeated the progressive candidate, Iván Cepeda.

Samper called out Trump’s election interference, and his rallying of like-minded candidates, which he said are promoting “autocratic and authoritarian pretensions.”

“Therefore, this hegemonic aggression that the region is facing deserves a progressive and sensible response, which I hope will emerge from this forum,” Samper said.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration said Monday it is temporarily pausing construction of a contentious border construction project in Texas’ Big Bend National Park while the head of the agency tasked with building the wall visits to do an “on-the-ground evaluation.”

The project through the national park in southern Texas has faced fierce bipartisan opposition by critics who say it is marring the area’s pristine environment. They argue the region’s rugged and remote terrain already serves as a deterrent to migrants and smugglers. Border crossings in the area have historically been lower than other regions and have dropped even further over the past two years.

“CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation,” Rodney Scott, who heads Customs and Border Protection, said on X. Scott said over the next couple of days, he was going to “listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders” to address what he said were “real” national security threats while protecting the park.

While it isn’t clear whether the brief suspension portended a more permanent halt to the construction in the area, it reflected the intensity of the bipartisan opposition and was a rare concession from the administration on a signature promise of the president’s that it has raced to complete.

Congress gave the Trump administration $46 billion last summer to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, and the administration has been charging ahead and waiving numerous regulations in an effort to swiftly build the wall.

text:
The Lancaster County District Attorney’s Office on Monday said it has seen an increase in crimes committed by undocumented immigrants and praised its ongoing partnership with federal immigration authorities as a bolster to public safety.

Timed to mark the first year anniversary of the prosecutor’s office partnering with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the statement said working with ICE helped law enforcement manage the purported rise in crimes by persons in the country illegally.

“Over the past year, we do not believe the community has been harmed in any way by this agreement, and we do not intend to withdraw from it,” District Attorney Heather Adams said in a statement released Monday.

Last year, the district attorney’s office was one of seven local law enforcement agencies in Lancaster County to enter into partnership agreements with ICE that deputize local law enforcement to act as immigration agents.

One agency, the Quarryville Police, has since backed out of the agreement.

Over the same period, local progressive activist groups have repeatedly criticized the agreements, and called on local officials, including Adams, to end their ICE partnerships.

In a February news release responding to criticisms from activists, the district attorney’s office wrote it had performed limited operations with ICE, including custody transfers of criminal defendants prosecuted by the office and welfare checks of “a small handful” of children in the immigration system.

Monday’s statement said the county’s cooperation with ICE “has mitigated the need for a large-scale ICE presence and large-scale targeted enforcement actions.”

The office said it has shared information with ICE for decades when it is actively prosecuting a case against someone without legal immigration status. “The only difference now is that we have formalized this communication and partnership with the signing of the [ICE agreement] and more notably, the stark and noticeable increase in the number of crimes committed by illegal aliens,” the district attorney’s office wrote.

LNP | LancasterOnline asked for the office’s source of information regarding an uptick in crimes committed by immigrants without legal status, but the office did not immediately respond Monday. The district attorney’s office “began noticing a sharp increase in the number of crimes committed by illegal aliens in June 2024,” according to the news release.

Through its agreement, the district attorney’s office has requested $45,000 in reimbursements from ICE, according to the statement.

text:
Welcome to Court Crawl, Colorado Politics’ roundup of news from the third branch of government.

Colorado’s citizen-led judicial performance commissions released their voter narratives for the judges standing for retention in November, plus a disciplinary panel imposed consequences on a Montezuma County judge for his misconduct.

Judicial retention

• There are 123 state judges standing for retention this year, including one Supreme Court justice and six Court of Appeals judges who will appear on every voter’s ballot. All but three judges received recommendations of “meets performance standards” from their local performance commissions.

• In the 13th Judicial District, which covers northeastern Colorado, the local commission found that District Court Judge Dina M. Christiansen does not meet standards, but it also

violated the law and the rules of judicial discipline in its handling of her evaluation. So, the statewide performance commission took the unprecedented step of calling out the violation and recommending that Christiansen meet performance standards under the circumstances.

• The statewide commission also cautioned that lawyers and judges reported concerns about Court of Appeals Judge Elizabeth L. Harris’ ability to release opinions without delay. Colorado Politics’ analysis found that Harris seemingly takes longer on average than judges she sits alongside on appellate panels.

Judge disciplined

• A three-member disciplinary panel imposed an unpaid suspension, a public censure, and additional training on Montezuma County Court Judge Ian J. MacLaren for his admitted misconduct. By 2-1, the panel accepted the agreement between MacLaren and the judicial discipline commission to resolve the case without a trial.

• Former Pueblo County District Attorney Jeff Chostner dissented, noting he would have proceeded to trial on the allegations that MacLaren lied to the discipline commission, which weren’t addressed in the parties’ agreement.

Heard on appeal

• The state Supreme Court will hear a case that implicates the somewhat complicated calculation of a defendant’s parole-eligibility date, and a case about the Court of Appeals’ “hard line” approach to attorneys who blow past the deadline to appeal.

• The Court of Appeals clarified that the duration of a relationship and the characterizations by the participants aren’t the only factors for determining if it is “intimate” for domestic violence purposes.

• A trial judge should take a second look at whether Denver Water has immunity for a bicyclist’s injuries, the Court of Appeals decided.

• The Court of Appeals overturned an illegal $7,000 crime victim restitution order from nearly a decade ago.

• The Court of Appeals rejected former Douglas County Commissioner Lora Thomas’ request for attorney fees in responding to investigations into her conduct.

In federal news

• The U.S. Court of Appeals from the 10th Circuit seemed sympathetic to the idea that a trial judge “punished” Denver Water for relying on a seemingly valid federal permit to commence a massive dam expansion project in Boulder County.

• The 10th Circuit decided a rare federal criminal appeal from a juvenile defendant, finding that Congress’ prohibition on juvenile handgun possession was constitutional.

• A Routt County landowner can’t sue a state judge for his commentary about her property in an unrelated criminal case, the 10th Circuit decided.

• The 10th Circuit revived a man’s wage violation lawsuit against Papa John’s locations in Colorado.

• Tomorrow morning, the 10th Circuit will hold a rare all-judges oral argument in a case out of Colorado questioning whether the state can apply its own interest rate caps to other states’ banks that lend to Colorado consumers.

• A federal judge green-lit claims of excessive force and retaliation for trial against three Fort Collins police officers.

• People in immigration detention do not have to ask an immigration judge for a bond hearing before challenging the lawfulness of their confinement, a federal judge ruled.

• A judge is exploring sanctions against the federal government for re-arresting a man after an immigration judge just granted release on bond.

• Adams County may proceed with its cost-recovery lawsuit for water contamination against Denver.

• An incarcerated plaintiff may proceed to sue various prison officials for allegedly retaliating against him and turning off his electricity.

• A federal judge dismissed a conspiracy lawsuit against the state judiciary filed by Colorado’s former director of judicial discipline.

• An incarcerated woman may sue a prison official for allegedly retaliating against her as she sought to exercise her Native American religion.

• A judge rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to force Colorado to hand over voter information.

• Colorado’s two part-time magistrate judges on the Western Slope spoke about how their jobs look different from other federal judges’ and from each other’s.

• The Colorado Attorney General’s Office has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to permit a lawsuit out of Boulder County to proceed that seeks damages from fossil fuel companies over local climate change impacts.

Vacancies and appointments

• The governor appointed civil litigator, former municipal judge, and recent Democratic state House candidate M. Christina Floyd to the Lake County Court to succeed retiring Judge John G. Scott.

• The governor also appointed civil litigator and municipal judge Jeffrey M. Cure to succeed retiring Kit Carson County Court Judge Michael K. Grinnan.

• There are three finalists to succeed retiring District Court Judge Michael P. McHenry in the Fourth Judicial District (El Paso and Teller counties): David Michael Lipka, Magistrate Lara Yoder Nafziger, and Magistrate Kayla Michelle Wingard.

• There are two finalists to succeed retiring District Court Judge Arturo G. Hernandez in the 17th Judicial District (Adams and Broomfield counties): County Court Judge Marques A. Ivey and Magistrate Thomas M. Ward.

• There are three nominees to succeed retiring Larimer County Court Judge Kraig S. Ecton: Luke Douglas Birky, Leeah Brennan Lechuga, and Michael W. Deschenes.

• Applications are due by Aug. 17 to succeed District Court Judge Anthony Baca in the Sixth Judicial District (Archuleta, La Plata, and San Juan counties). He is departing before his first retention election.

• Applications are due by Aug. 17 to succeed Weld County District Court Judge Renee Doak, who is also not standing for her first retention election.

• Applications are due by Aug. 17 to succeed Jefferson County Court Judge Mark M. Randall, who is also not standing for retention.

• Applications are due by Aug. 17 to succeed retiring Denver District Court Judge A. Bruce Jones.

Miscellaneous proceedings

• Denver has filed suit against multiple cigarette manufacturers over cigarette litter.

• The National Rifle Association’s Colorado chapter is suing over a new state law mandating training as a condition of certain firearm purchases.

• Denver has moved to dismiss a federal lawsuit challenging its 1989 firearm ordinance.

• A Denver judge dismissed a lawsuit seeking records from Democratic lawmakers over a 2025 closed-door retreat in Vail.

• A judge overturned a defendant’s 2008 murder conviction in El Paso County because prosecutors withheld key evidence.

On break

• Because things will be a bit slower during the summer, Court Crawl will be published every other week during July and August.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) led their colleagues in urging the Trump Administration to extend and redesignate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Sudan as ongoing violence and a worsening humanitarian crisis continue to put citizens at grave risk.

TPS is a temporary, legal immigration status granted to foreign citizens in the U.S. who are endangered by conditions in their home country resulting from extraordinary events such as ongoing armed conflict, environmental disaster, or epidemic. TPS status is granted for set periods ranging from six to 18 months, requiring the Department of Homeland Security to extend a country’s status on a recurring basis. Each time a country is recertified, recipients must reapply and pass a thorough background check. Sudan’s current TPS designation is set to expire October 19, 2026. An extension and redesignation would protect current Sudanese TPS holders from returning to the country amid its ongoing conflict and would offer protected status to Sudanese nationals who arrived in the United States after August 16, 2023.

"After war erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), DHS extended and redesignated Sudan for TPS, citing ongoing armed conflict, widespread violence, severe humanitarian conditions, mass displacement, and serious human rights abuses. DHS again extended Sudan's TPS designation in 2025 after determining that these conditions continued to prevent the safe return of Sudanese nationals," the senators wrote.

“The armed conflict between the SAF and the RSF has intensified and expanded, causing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. Fighting has spread across much of the country, resulting in tens of thousands of deaths, the displacement of millions of people, widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, severe food insecurity, and credible reports of war crimes and other serious human rights violations. The U.S. government has determined that the RSF and SAF have committed war crimes and that the RSF is responsible for crimes against humanity and genocide. Secretary Rubio has further recognized the genocide in Sudan and joined G7 countries in warning against further atrocities in El Obeid in July 2026," the senators highlighted.

“Humanitarian access remains severely restricted, and large areas of Sudan continue to be unsafe for civilians, making the return of Sudanese nationals unsafe under current conditions. Sudan continues to face catastrophic humanitarian conditions – including the risk of famine in several areas – that have been compounded by climate shocks, widespread food insecurity, and the destruction of critical infrastructure. Since the outbreak of the war in April 2023, hospitals, schools, water systems, roads, and electrical infrastructure have been damaged or destroyed, severely limiting access to basic services and humanitarian assistance,” the senators concluded.

The senators also noted that the Trump administration has already acknowledged the dangers posed by the war and humanitarian crisis in Sudan. The State Department maintains a Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory for the entire country, citing risks including armed conflict, civil unrest, and terrorism. Furthermore, the U.S. Embassy in Khartoum has suspended operations since April 2023, leaving the U.S. government unable to provide routine or emergency consular services to U.S. citizens in Sudan.

In addition to Warner and Kaine, the letter was signed by Senators Michael Bennet (D-CO), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and Raphael Warnock (D-GA).

Since the conflict erupted, Warner and Kaine have been outspoken voices in the Senate on the need for increased diplomatic and humanitarian support for Sudan. In June 2025, the senators sponsored the Safe Environment from Countries Under Repression and Emergency (SECURE) Act, legislation to provide qualified TPS and Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) recipients a path to legal permanent residency. In January 2025, Warner and Kaine urged then-President Biden to extend or redesignate TPS for all 17 TPS-eligible countries, including Sudan. The senators have fought to strengthen the U.S. response to the Sudan crisis, introducing the Response to Conflict in Sudan Act to bolster and coordinate the U.S. response to the war in Sudan by codifying the Special Envoy for Sudan position at the U.S. Department of State.

Read the full letter here and below.

Dear Secretary Mullin and Secretary Rubio:

We write to urge you to issue an 18-month extension and redesignation of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Sudan. The ongoing violence and humanitarian crisis in Sudan continue to place its citizens at severe risk. An extension would protect current Sudanese TPS holders from returning to Sudan amid ongoing violence, and a redesignation would offer protected status to Sudanese nationals who arrived after August 16, 2023.

After war erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), DHS extended and redesignated Sudan for TPS, citing ongoing armed conflict, widespread violence, severe humanitarian conditions, mass displacement, and serious human rights abuses. DHS again extended Sudan's TPS designation in 2025 after determining that these conditions continued to prevent the safe return of Sudanese nationals.

The armed conflict between the SAF and the RSF has intensified and expanded, causing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. Fighting has spread across much of the country, resulting in tens of thousands of deaths, the displacement of millions of people, widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, severe food insecurity, and credible reports of war crimes and other serious human rights violations. The U.S. government has determined that the RSF and SAF have committed war crimes and that the RSF is responsible for crimes against humanity and genocide. Secretary Rubio has further recognized the genocide in Sudan and joined G7 countries in warning against further atrocities in El Obeid in July 2026.

Humanitarian access remains severely restricted, and large areas of Sudan continue to be unsafe for civilians, making the return of Sudanese nationals unsafe under current conditions. Sudan continues to face catastrophic humanitarian conditions – including the risk of famine in several areas – that have been compounded by climate shocks, widespread food insecurity, and the destruction of critical infrastructure. Since the outbreak of the war in April 2023, hospitals, schools, water systems, roads, and electrical infrastructure have been damaged or destroyed, severely limiting access to basic services and humanitarian assistance.

More than 30 million people – two-thirds of Sudan's population – are in need of humanitarian assistance, including 15 million children. More than 8 million people are internally displaced, making Sudan the world's largest internal displacement crisis. Millions more have fled to neighboring countries as refugees. Humanitarian organizations continue to warn that funding shortfalls, ongoing insecurity, and restrictions on aid delivery are preventing life-saving assistance from reaching millions of people in need. These overlapping crises – ongoing armed conflict, mass displacement, widespread hunger, disease outbreaks, climate-related disasters, and the collapse of essential services – have significantly worsened since Sudan's most recent TPS designation and continue to make the safe return of Sudanese nationals impossible.

The posture of the State Department demonstrates the dangers of the war in Sudan. The U.S. Department of State currently maintains a Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory for all of Sudan, warning U.S. citizens not to travel to the country due to ongoing armed conflict, civil unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, landmines, and serious health and security risks. The State Department also notes that the U.S. Embassy in Khartoum has suspended operations since April 2023 and that the U.S. government cannot provide routine or emergency consular services to U.S. citizens in Sudan. These conditions underscore the continued instability throughout the country and further demonstrate that Sudan remains unsafe for the return of Sudanese nationals.

At the beginning of this administration, approximately 1.2 million foreign nationals were protected under TPS, including 1,790 individuals from Sudan. These individuals make significant contributions to the U.S. economy and the communities they call home. They are taxpayers, consumers, entrepreneurs, and essential members of the workforce. According to the American Immigration Council, TPS holders collectively generated more than $10.3 billion in household income, held nearly $8 billion in spending power, and contributed over $2.2 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2021 alone. Beyond these measurable economic contributions, TPS holders strengthen local economies by purchasing homes, renting apartments, starting businesses, and filling critical labor shortages across a range of industries. Although Sudanese TPS beneficiaries represent only a portion of the overall TPS population, they likewise contribute to the U.S. workforce and economy while lawfully employed under TPS.

In light of these circumstances, we strongly urge you to extend and redesignate Sudan for TPS. The ongoing armed conflict, catastrophic humanitarian crisis, and widespread human rights abuses make the safe return of Sudanese nationals impossible at this time, meeting the legal standard for extension and redesignation of TPS under Sec. 244 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. TPS for Sudanese nationals in the United States remains both a humanitarian necessity and a prudent policy to ensure that individuals are not forced to return to conditions that continue to threaten their safety and well-being.

We thank you for your consideration of this request.

LOUISVILLE, Ky. —

A Louisville woman's final green card interview resulted in her being arrested and detained by ICE.

Armelle Bondonga was taken into ICE custody on Aug. 12 after she and her husband voluntarily appeared for an interview with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, her attorney Arianit Osmani said.

As for why she was detained? ICE said she "overstayed her welcome."

Osmani says Bondonga came to the United States from the Democratic Republic of the Congo as a child with her family in 2013.

She is married to a U.S. citizen, and the couple is raising their young child together, who was born the state, her attorney said.

According to community leader Sadiqa Reynolds, the child is 19 months old, and Bondonga was arrested in front of her family.

"What should have been a joyful milestone—their final green card interview—turned into an absolute nightmare," Reynolds wrote on social media.

Both Reynolds and Osmani said Bondonga has significant ties to the community, which she actively serves.

Osmani said her immigration history is complicated because, as a child, she was included as a derivative family member in asylum proceedings initiated by her father.

According to ICE, her visa expired in 2014 and "under the Obama administration began accruing more than a decade’s worth of unlawful presence in the United States."

An ICE spokesperson said she was given final order of removal by an immigration judge last November.

But Osmani points out the circumstances have changed since Bondonga is now married to a U.S. citizen and has willingly showed up to scheduled USCIS interviews, including the latest.

"What is particularly significant is that Armelle was not attempting to evade immigration authorities," Osmani said. "She voluntarily appeared with her husband for the scheduled USCIS interview to pursue her marriage-based immigration case through the lawful process. She complied with the government's requirements, appeared for the interview as instructed, and was taken into ICE custody following that appearance."

There are ongoing legal proceedings concerning that matter, which are being handled by separate immigration counsel.

Her lawyer said multiple immigration matters are now being pursued on her behalf and that her husband's Form I-130 petition, the application to sponsor her for a green card, remains pending with USCIS.

He added that there are also other ongoing legal matters surrounding her prior immigration proceedings.

Osmani says he is coordinating with other attorneys and will continue advocating for Bondonga to make sure she receives due process.

She is being housed at the Clark County jail in Jeffersonville, Indiana.

text:
Legal aid groups said they will continue to represent unaccompanied immigrant children in the Bay Area even after the Trump administration shifted federal funding away from seasoned service providers to a controversial anti-trafficking group.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services awarded a $158 million contract — which could grow to $244 million — to Our Rescue, a Utah-based anti-human-trafficking group whose founder was accused of sexual exploitation and whose current director led Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, during the first Trump administration. The group touts its expertise assisting law enforcement with sting operations, but advocates say it lacks experience representing children in immigration court.

Katrina Logan, executive director of Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto, said her team of lawyers and social workers is not walking away from the 33 children they represent, even though their contract with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services expired July 31.

Immigration cases can go on for years and can involve complex forms of humanitarian relief, especially for children, she said.

“Our attorneys have been doing this type of law for many years. They’ve developed the expertise,” Logan said. “They understand how to support clients. So it’s definitely tough to be losing this funding.”

Logan’s organization is the lead plaintiff in a federal lawsuit that blocked HHS last year when it tried to terminate funding for lawyers to represent more than 20,000 children — including more than 4,000 in California.

On Aug. 6, an Oakland federal judge ordered HHS to release $65 million in back-due payments to the network of legal service providers, including Logan’s group and several others in California. The agency had stopped cutting checks in December, after the groups refused to comply with a new requirement to turn over information about the children and their cases.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín rejected the information-sharing requirement — which was not part of the original contract — and said the government was violating her 2025 order to pay for legal services, as Congress intended.

In a declaration last week, the government said it was looking for additional contractors to provide legal representation for kids and trying to work out a transitional contract with Acacia to “support an orderly transition of cases to new legal service providers, including Our Rescue.”

It also said it had engaged the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants on a short-term $20 million contract to provide legal services for the 1,800 children who are in ORR shelters. The Virginia-based nonprofit has performed immigration legal services for Afghan arrivals and helped settle white South Africans granted refugee status in an expedited process last year.

“These interim measures are intended to ensure that eligible children appearing without counsel have immediate access to representation while successor contracts are being negotiated,” attorneys for the government wrote.

text:
The Alabama Department of Corrections signed an agreement in July with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to assist the federal agency to identify and process immigrants with pending or active criminal charges.

According to an ICE spreadsheet updated last week on law enforcement agencies that have signed onto a local immigration enforcement program known as the 287(g) program, ADOC and ICE signed a memorandum of understanding on July 22. The agreement was not immediately available on the website; the Alabama Reflector requested a copy of the contract from ICE and ADOC on Monday and sent messages seeking comment.

The Alabama Coalition for Immigrant Justice, which advocates for immigrants in the state, said in a statement Monday that that communities need more support and not fear, and called on Corrections to end its agreement with ICE, which it wants abolished.

“We condemn the continuous cooperation between these and other agencies who are assisting in this mass deportation agenda,” the statement said. “Alabama has a history of using law enforcement and other criminal justice agencies to take beloved Alabamians from their homes and their communities.”

The ICE website lists ADOC as part of a Jail Enforcement Model that permits “designated immigration officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.”

ADOC has struggled for years with violence and overcrowding in state prisons, and faces multiple lawsuits over safety and inadequate services in Alabama’s correctional facilities. The U.S. Department of Justice sued the state in 2020 after releasing three reports detailing physical and sexual assaults throughout men’s prisons in the state.

The 287(g) program allows Immigration and Customs Enforcement to deputize local and state agencies to enforce the nation’s immigration laws in different capacities. The ADOC is one of 67 agencies within the state to have such agreements with the federal government.

ADOC is the only state agency that has entered into any agreement with ICE as part of the 287(g) program, according to the spreadsheet. Other Alabama law enforcement agencies involved in the program include the Wetumpka and Demopolis police departments and the sheriff’s offices of Pickens and Blount counties.

The Mobile County Sheriff’s Office has joined the program, according to ICE, but is the only county or city-wide law enforcement agency among the state’s four largest cities — Huntsville, Birmingham, Montgomery and Mobile — to be in it.

Besides the Jail Enforcement Model, ICE uses two other models. The Task Force Model allows designated immigration officers to enforce the country’s immigration laws while they are on duty or as part of a task force. The third model is a Warrant Service Officer Model that allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants for those within their custody.

Some agencies have agreements in place with ICE to serve in multiple capacities. The Autauga County Sheriff’s Office has agreements for all three models, while the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office is part of the Task Force and Warrant Officer models.
