text:
Over the past three months, the immigration file in the United States has shifted from a traditional focus on border control and the pursuit of irregular migrants, to building a “more comprehensive enforcement system,” extending to legal residents, students, journalists, and asylum and temporary-protection seekers. The momentum peaked this past July, after the Supreme Court, on June 30, rejected Executive Order 14160 — the January 2025 order restricting the granting of birthright American citizenship to the children of non-Americans or non-permanent residents. Trump objected to the ruling and announced stricter measures against what he described as “birth tourism.” In contrast, confusion emerged within the administration over the suspension of most Immigration and Customs Enforcement checkpoints, following the deaths of two migrants during its operations that same month. Reports indicated that more than 590,000 people had been deported from January 2025 through July 2026.

In truth, the hardening is linked to the approaching midterm elections in November 2026 and declining support from some Republican and right-wing sectors for Trump. The trend exacerbates tension between the administration and the judiciary, complicates its relationship with the states, and makes immigration a key tool for mobilization and polarization — an influential issue in shaping voter trends and the outcomes of the upcoming elections.

Indicators of the Hardening

Recent measures between May and July 2026 reveal that the Trump administration’s hardening is no longer confined to border control. It has transformed into an integrated financial, security, and legal system, under which enforcement powers have expanded to tighten restrictions on migrants and foreigners, even those residing legally. The shift is reflected in the following:

1- Signing the Secure America Act: On June 10, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the “Secure America Act,” which adds 70 billion dollars to the budget of the Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), with the aim of funding border security and immigration activities through 2029. The law aims to achieve three main objectives: supporting the border by providing immediate and full funding for the Department of Homeland Security and border patrols; funding deportation campaigns by ensuring the flow of funds necessary to implement the administration’s plans for deportation operations and apprehending violators; and combating crime by curbing drug smuggling, suppressing human trafficking networks, and dismantling organized crime gangs.

2- Expanding migrant arrest operations: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection have expanded arrest operations targeting foreigners unprecedentedly over the past three months — from May to July 2026 — with arrests in June alone exceeding 43,000, the highest figure ever recorded since the start of President Trump’s second term. Estimates indicate that this increased rate is due to the White House pressuring Immigration and Customs Enforcement to raise the arrest rate to 3,000 per day.

3- Resisting decisions and rulings: The Department of Homeland Security issued a memo on July 14, 2026, stipulating the suspension of traffic checkpoint operations, following recent inspections that resulted in the deaths of two men — one Colombian, one Mexican — within a single week. The White House, however, rescinded the decision just 24 hours later. The reversal was accompanied by a comment from President Trump on the “Truth Social” platform, in which he said that “we must be strong, firm, and smart, and we cannot give up one of the most important and effective crime-fighting tools available to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, namely traffic checkpoints! If we do that, we are directly serving criminals.”

Similarly, President Trump appeared resistant to the Supreme Court’s decision to strike down his executive order aiming to abolish birthright citizenship. He expressed his displeasure, demanding that the Court reconsider the case immediately and adding that the justices would destroy the United States if they did not change their decision. The remarks prompted acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche to affirm that the administration would intensify its campaign against birth tourism by putting in place measures targeting foreign women intending to give birth in the United States.

4- Legal obstruction of foreigners and migrants: Since last May, numerous indicators have emerged reflecting the American administration’s legal orientation toward tightening restrictions on foreigners and migrants, embodied in the following measures:

– Legal tightening: The courts specialized in immigration cases have aligned with the American administration’s approach, becoming facilitators of deportation decisions rather than a forum for hearing and investigation. Court hearings have been sped up and time limits reduced to a minimum, meaning dozens of cases are scheduled for a single judge in a single day, while Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s own attorneys have also imposed restrictions on migrants’ lawyers.

– Revoking protected status for certain nationalities: The Supreme Court issued a ruling on June 25 allowing the revocation of “temporary protected status” for a number of migrant groups from Syria and Haiti, enabling the Trump administration to deport them, as happened with Venezuelan migrants earlier this year.

– Further imposition of fines: The Department of Homeland Security issued a decision on July 23 imposing a fine on migrants subject to a deportation order, amounting to 998 dollars for each additional day in the United States, with the aim of increasing the cost of their remaining in the country.

– Removing legal review for law enforcement officers: The American administration decided in mid-July to have the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) stop investigating crimes committed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers against migrants, removing legal review of such acts following the two migrant deaths.

– Restricting residency for journalists and students: The American administration issued a decision in mid-July amending the residency period for foreign journalists, capping it at 240 days, or about eight months, with the possibility of applying for extensions for similar periods. Meanwhile, the rule for international students’ stay in the United States was amended, so that there is now a specific expiration date for the residency period instead of the previous open-ended arrangement. Under this decision, foreign nationals holding a “student visa” will not be allowed to stay in the United States for more than four years.

– Reaffirming the prevention of any flows from the southern border: U.S. Customs and Border Protection announced on July 16, 2026, that the Trump administration had gone 14 months without allowing any irregular migrant to cross the southwestern border.

– Suspending visas for diplomatic missions in Africa: The U.S. State Department issued a decision on July 15, 2026, to suspend routine visa services at 25 diplomatic missions in Africa and transfer them to regional centers starting August 1, 2026, with the aim of unifying security screening standards, reducing costs, and improving efficiency, without closing embassies or affecting valid visas.

– Reinstating the “public charge” rule for migrants: The administration is doing so by expanding the categories of cases that could become a burden on the state should they obtain permanent residency, while reducing public benefits including food stamps and the “Medicaid” program (which provides free or low-cost health insurance for people with limited income and resources). Under this rule, applicants for green cards must prove that they will not become a burden on the country, or a “public charge.”

The Calculations Behind the Hardening

Many factors help explain the Trump administration’s moves at this time, although all of them are linked to the approaching midterm congressional elections in November 2026, and the calculations of the electoral base within the Republican Party and the “MAGA” movement. The following are the most prominent reasons behind this tightened enforcement:

1- Mobilizing the Republican base electorally: Immigration represents one of the few issues that still grants Trump strong support within his own party, making hardening on this front a tool for rallying voters ahead of the midterm elections. A recent Associated Press-NORC poll, published on August 1, 2026, showed that about 80% of Republicans support his handling of the file, despite national approval declining to 39%. Pew also found that 28% of Republicans believe the administration is not doing enough on deportation, meaning escalation allows Trump to restore the cohesion of his base, particularly amid the economic challenges arising from the war against Iran. Reflecting the priority the Republican Party gives to the immigration file, Republican spending to promote the party’s positions on immigration reached about 53 million dollars between January and June 2026, compared to just 17 million dollars for the Democratic Party, whose members view it as an important issue, but not a priority.

2- Fulfilling the electoral promise and demonstrating resolve: Securing the border and carrying out broad deportation operations were among Trump’s most prominent pledges in the 2024 elections, and the administration is now seeking to prove its ability to translate that campaign rhetoric into actual policy. The Migration Policy Institute recorded the administration taking 181 immigration-related actions during its first hundred days, about six times the number taken in the corresponding period of Trump’s first term, involving the military, federal agencies, and local authorities. The pace reflects a desire to present immigration as a model of rapid implementation and a break from the Biden administration.

3- Appeasing the “MAGA” movement: Tightening immigration policy serves as a means of preserving the loyalty of the “MAGA” base within the broader Trumpist movement. The administration’s efforts to appease that base have intensified in an attempt to offset escalating criticism from a wing of the movement over Washington’s involvement in the war against Iran, and the resulting increase in military spending and rise in energy prices and living costs within the United States — developments that run counter to Trump’s pledges to prioritize domestic problems and avoid foreign wars.

4- Applying economic and social protectionism: The administration views immigration within the framework of an “America First” philosophy, arguing that foreign labor puts pressure on Americans’ wages and opportunities, while irregular migrants place additional burdens on schools, hospitals, and assistance programs. Restrictions have accordingly extended to some visa programs, benefits, and public services, not just to border crossing. However, this justification is contested: the Pew Center found that a majority of voters believe migrants mostly occupy jobs that citizens do not want.

5- Redefining citizenship and the social contract: Trump’s immigration policy does not target irregular migration alone; rather, it seeks to reformulate the terms of belonging to American society. The shift is evident in the attempt to restrict birthright citizenship for the children of irregular migrants, and even for the children of some legal but temporary residents, alongside curbing asylum and refugee resettlement and tightening scrutiny of students and visa holders. The hardening, in this sense, carries an ideological dimension aimed at making citizenship and residency a more selective privilege, and reshaping the “social contract” for migrants.

Potential Repercussions

There are potential repercussions ranging from short-term security and electoral gains, to political, economic, and institutional costs that may emerge more fully later:

1- A dual electoral effect: Hardening could contribute to mobilizing the Republican base and the MAGA movement, as about 80% of Republicans support Trump’s performance on the immigration file. It carries a corresponding risk, however, of alienating independent and Latino voters: the Pew Center found that 52% of Americans, and 65% of those of Latino origin, believe the administration is overreaching in its deportation operations. The hardening may thus benefit Republicans in conservative districts, but weaken them in swing states and diverse, urban districts.

2- Escalating institutional division: The confrontation between the administration and the courts is likely to continue, after the judiciary blocked a number of immigration policies. A judge in Rhode Island halted the freezing of immigration and asylum applications for nationals of 39 countries, and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected denying detained migrants the opportunity to seek bail release. The Fifth and Eighth Circuits, by contrast, upheld the administration’s position, paving the way for Supreme Court intervention. The Supreme Court also struck down Trump’s order restricting birthright citizenship on June 30, 2026. The obstruction may push the administration to search for legal loopholes, accelerate the passage of supporting legislation through Congress, and expand the use of executive branch officials’ discretionary powers.

3- A potentially expanded role for Congress: The administration’s ability to entrench its policies will depend on the outcome of the midterm elections. If Republicans retain their majority, they can convert more executive actions into laws that would be difficult to later repeal, and expand detention and deportation funding. If Democrats take control of one of the two chambers, oversight hearings, subpoenas, and investigations into the practices of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other law enforcement agencies are likely to escalate, alongside attempts to restrict funding and impose judicial safeguards on arrest operations. The immigration file could thereby shift from a dispute between the White House and the courts into a comprehensive conflict involving all three branches of government.

4- A conditional Democratic opportunity: The Democrats’ campaign can link the immigration hardening to a broader pattern of executive overreach beyond the law and the courts, framing the issue as one of rule of law and constitutional rights, rather than an absolute defense of open borders. They can also focus on the economic effects of deportation, labor shortages, and rising prices. Their handling will nevertheless remain cautious, since immigration represents a point of strength for Republicans, while cost-of-living issues and the war against Iran take precedence over it among some voters. The issue gives Democrats an opportunity to win back some Latino and independent voters, but does not alone guarantee electoral victory.

5- Inconsistent enforcement across states: Resistance from Democratic states and cooperation from Republican states are producing a divergent map of immigration enforcement. A group of 24 attorneys general and governors filed a lawsuit challenging the linking of emergency and homeland security grants to cooperation with federal immigration policies. In contrast, the 287(g) program, which permits the delegation of immigration authority to local law enforcement agencies, has expanded to about 2,179 agreements in 39 states and two territories by July 2026, compared to 135 agreements in January 2025. The trend foreshadows immigration becoming one of the axes of federal polarization, with rights and enforcement levels differing by state.

6- Deepening Republican division: According to The Washington Post, the gap is likely to widen between the MAGA movement, which demands mass deportation without exceptions, and the economic wing linked to the agriculture, construction, hospitality, and technology sectors that rely on foreign labor. If the administration is forced to exempt certain sectors or ease raids under business pressure, the MAGA wing may accuse it of backing away from its promises. Meanwhile, continued comprehensive enforcement could push businesspeople and Republican donors to pressure the administration, gradually turning immigration from a unifying party issue into a source of internal tension.

7- Economic and electoral repercussions: Deportation operations and fear of raids could lead to labor shortages in agriculture, construction, food, hospitality, and healthcare, raising the costs of production, housing, and services. A Brookings Institution analysis estimated that the sharp rise in Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations within cities was associated with the loss of about 668,000 jobs, including jobs held by American workers, with economic models suggesting that intensive mass deportation operations could reduce the country’s gross domestic product.

8- Declining trust and community security: Fears of arrest could push migrants, legal residents, and members of legally mixed-status families to avoid police, schools, hospitals, and government bodies. A recent study found that fear of deportation reduces migrants’ willingness to provide their information to police and public institutions. The pattern could weaken crime reporting and cooperation with security agencies, creating a paradox: measures the administration justifies as protecting security may, at the local level, lead to declining trust in law enforcement institutions.

9- Weakening universities and soft power: Tightening student visas and limiting their residency periods threatens American universities’ ability to attract students and researchers. The number of new international students declined by 17% in fall 2025, coinciding with visa difficulties and travel restrictions. Should this trend continue, it would reduce tuition revenue, research funding, and talent supply in science and technology fields, in addition to weakening the United States’ image as a global hub for education and openness.

Immigration policy over recent months reveals that the Trump administration is seeking not only to increase the numbers of those detained and deported, but to entrench a security, legal, and financial structure that makes hardening a long-term policy difficult to reverse. The approach may achieve short-term gains by reducing irregular flows, mobilizing Republicans, and restoring the cohesion of the MAGA movement. It carries, in return, accumulating costs, including escalating confrontation with the judiciary and Democratic states, disruption of the labor market, rising costs for some goods and services, and declining trust in law enforcement agencies. The electoral effect will remain dual: Republicans benefit from immigration’s centrality to their base, while Democrats gain a conditional opportunity to win back independents and Latinos, if they succeed in linking the hardening to overreach beyond the law and rising living costs, without appearing lenient on border security.

text:
https://cdn.houstonpublicmedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13155525/TPS-future-FEATURE-with-Shelby-intro.mp3?srcid=rss-feed

Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, allows immigrants facing physical threats or persecution in their home countries to live and work in the United States without a path to citizenship. Or it did until June, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can revoke the program's protections.

The high court's 6-3 ruling in Mullin v. Doe dealt with a case in which former U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem had curtailed TPS protections for immigrants from Haiti and Syria. But the decision, written by Associate Justice Samuel Alito, was worded in such a way that the White House can withdraw those protections from any nationality essentially at any time for any reason.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

The Trump administration has since done so for most TPS recipients.

"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," wrote U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) general counsel James Percival in a social media post following the decision. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."

Former President Joe Biden, a Democrat, deployed TPS widely in the cases of immigrants from countries suffering in the aftermath of wars, natural disasters and other upheavals, perhaps in the hope that doing so would pressure Congress to enact comprehensive immigration reform.

"Possibly, it was overused, but I feel it was a wedge that the administration hoped would wake up Congress to do something on a long-term basis, as opposed to just this temporary nature," said Houston immigration attorney Gordon Quan. "And eventually that’s what the court, I think, has gotten to the point of, ‘How temporary is temporary?’ "

Now, Quan said, more than 100,000 people across Texas are in a panic over what the future will bring.

"We have large communities from different countries, especially El Salvador and other places in Central America," Quan said. "We have a large Lebanese community. We have a growing Ukrainian community, and all these groups are scheduled to have their TPS expired or canceled within the next few months."

For many of those immigrants, and their allies, the best chance of reprieve might depend on a possible change in power in the Republican-led Congress this November.

RELATED: A record number of congressional lawmakers aren’t running for reelection in 2026. Here’s the list

Democrats likely would need to win significant majorities in both the House and Senate to curtail the immigration policies of Republican President Donald Trump. In order to override a presidential veto, legislation must be passed by two-thirds majorities in both chambers of Congress.

"Right now, the ask is for Congress to pass legislation, and it will be after the election," said Jose, a Salvadoran TPS recipient who asked to be identified only by his first name, for safety reasons. "The question is, how many people will be able to stay in the U.S. and not getting detained and deported before that comes up?"

"If you work hard..."

Luis, a Venezuelan TPS recipient who also asked to be identified only by his first name — fled to the United States from his homeland in 2017. He'd been in the Venezuelan military, and he says the government persecuted him for protesting against the regime of then-President Nicolas Maduro.

"First of all, I came applying for asylum," Luis said, "and after in 2021 when we were granted TPS, I applied for TPS, and then I was protected with TPS until 2025 that they took it away."

Luis had built a successful life for himself, having gone from working in a restaurant to starting his own roofing inspection company. He said he is still in the process of applying for asylum. But he's worried that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) could detain him at a future court hearing anyway.

"For sure, I'm afraid," Luis said. "I have been doing everything right, I created a company, provided jobs to some other people, but this administration doesn’t want people who were not born in the United States."

The leadership of Venezuela has changed since Luis left, with the U.S. having ousted Maduro earlier this year. But that doesn't mean he'd necessarily be any safer if he were forced to return to his home country.

RELATED: U.S. intervention in Venezuela divides Houston

"I know there are at least 500 of my colleagues still in detention," Luis said, "and that it will be a similar situation for many people if we were to go back to Venezuela."

The same concerns hold for Sara, who also asked to use only her first name. Sara traveled to the U.S. 30 years ago from Honduras. The country is rife with gang violence, and Sara herself fled poverty. She now has four children, all of whom were born in the U.S. and have U.S. citizenship.

When her TPS status was stripped away, she said, she lost her job as a Walmart manager.

"It’s just [a] hard time," Sara said. "And we're hoping this Congress [will] do something about it and help people, because we came here to work. We’re not coming here just to take the job[s] from the others. Everybody works. If you work hard, you’re going to have what you deserve."

Two strikes and you're out

While some Venezuelan immigrants like Luis have the option of applying for asylum, Honduran immigrants like Sara do not. Nor, for that matter, do Salvadoran immigrants like Jose.

Until the Supreme Court decision, however, TPS recipients could and did apply to renew their status every 18 months. Jose estimates he did so more than 10 times, at the cost of thousands of dollars.

"The good thing about TPS is that it provides you the opportunity to have a work authorization, driver’s license, and get your Social Security and live in the United States without fear of being deported," Jose said. "The bad thing is that TPS doesn’t allow you to move forward and apply for a permanent status."

Jose stressed the ability of TPS recipients to keep their status has always hinged on maintaining their best behavior.

"If you commit two misdemeanors, you lose your TPS," he said. "Don’t even think about committing a felony or something. With that, you lose your TPS and you get into a deportation procedure. So, everyone, anybody who has TPS by now is because they have been behaving and following the law."

The "ideal" immigrants

Jose works full-time for an advocacy group called the National TPS Alliance. The alliance has been fighting efforts to end TPS since the first Trump administration. Between 2017 and 2021, the group was successful at helping to keep Trump's efforts to end the program in check. But Jose said, since the Supreme Court's decision, DHS has been aggressive about closing one door after another to TPS recipients.

"We have seen an uptick of people getting detained and deported," Jose said. "And therefore, families are getting worried. People have been losing their jobs. People have been deciding what they’re going to do with their houses, what they’re going to do with the businesses, what they’re going to do with the kids."

But TPS recipients have an important ally in the business community, some of which is concerned that ending TPS protections and work permits will worsen labor shortages in fields ranging from home health care and construction to education.

"There is a narrative out there that there is this mass of Americans that want to take on these jobs," said Luis Zaldivar, business engagement director for the American Business Immigration Coalition. "The fact is that the unemployment rate has remained at about 4%. Almost all of Americans that want to work are currently working. So there’s not a lot of people taking up jobs in construction, in roofing, in the places where we need them."

The coalition has been advocating heavily, both with the Trump administration and with both parties in Congress, to get across its message that the U.S. economy will suffer if TPS recipients are deported en masse.

"We have been at it for quite some time now, basically making the argument that out of all of the people in this country that need a work permit, these folks, the TPS holders, are the best example of the type of immigration that we needed," Zaldivar said. "These are folks that are currently working here legally, pay taxes, don’t have a path to citizenship, they cannot get into welfare or any kind of government program, and they are trained to do the jobs."

text:
After nearly a month in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention, Alevtina Soboleva and her daughter emerged through the doors at San Francisco International Airport Sunday morning.

"It's been really hard for both of us. I'm glad we made it home," her daughter, Daria, said.

The 59-year-old Russian asylum-seeker from Sunnyvale arrived in the Bay Area two days after being released from a federal facility in Louisiana.

Soboleva was detained on July 20 at the Buffalo airport as she and her daughter prepared to fly home from a trip to Niagara Falls.

Daria said immigration officers stopped her mother before their flight and took her into custody, despite her asylum application still being under review.

For days, Daria did not know where her mother was. She said Soboleva was held in a cage and denied water and bathroom access.

"She was crying and my heart was breaking because she was very scared," Daria said.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said that Soboleva "is an illegal alien from Russia who was admitted to the United States lawfully in 2021 but failed to depart the country in the required time frame."

"Any allegations of poor medical care and inability to contact family are false," the Department of Homeland Security said.

Soboleva came to the U.S. on a visitor visa. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, she applied for asylum.

On Wednesday, she appeared before an immigration judge who set her bond at $10,000.

Bill Hing, professor of law and migration at the University of San Francisco, said Soboleva has a compelling case.

"The rule of law says that if you have a one-in-10 chance of being persecuted, you should be granted asylum. That's only a 10% chance and so based on that, I believe that she will be granted asylum," he said.

Soboleva's detention, he said, should serve as a warning to other immigrants who may be considering air travel, both internationally and domestically.

For Soboleva and her daughter, the immediate focus is much simpler: tea, a warm blanket, and some rest.

"I'm hopeful. I'm very grateful for all the help that we had so far. We have loads of her friends waiting for her," Daria said.

text:
A hunger strike is underway at the ICE facility in Tacoma, according to the activist group La Resistencia. The group told KIRO that around 140 detainees at the Northwest ICE Processing Center are refusing food in protest of the conditions there.

Two US congresswomen arrived at the facility for an unannounced tour Saturday to investigate the strike and the detainees’ claims. At the same time, a protest was held outside the fence in solidarity with the detainees.

“It’s just a depressing place,” Marcos Angel Hernandez told KIRO 7. “You can tell it drains everybody.”

Hernandez knows the ICE facility better than most. He wasn’t there for the protest; he was there to visit his father.

Hernandez has been to the NWIPC six times from Portland since his father was arrested outside an Oregon Home Depot earlier this month. He’d been in the US for nearly 30 years.

Hernandez recalled frantically trying to figure out what happened to him.

“We go, and his car is there. Everything that he bought is there,” he said. “But he’s not there.”

Hernandez said his father is sick.

“It’s honestly kind of scary,” he said.

According to La Resistencia, Hernandez’s father is not the only one who is sick. The activist group reports two housing blocks in the detention center are now on a hunger strike, protesting a lack of medical services and quality food.

Organizers said there have been plenty of hunger strikes before, but they are becoming more frequent.

“We have been an organization for over 12 years. We have supported, on average, a dozen hunger strikes a year,” Josefina Mora-Cheung of La Resistencia said. “This year, this is the 20th hunger strike we are supporting.”

US Representatives Emily Randall of Washington and Maxine Dexter of Oregon toured the facility.

They said 1,458 people are currently detained at NWIPC.

The representatives said they were allowed to see the kitchen, but not the area where detainees receive medical care.

They reported speaking to a detainee who is part of the hunger strike, but when the representatives asked detention center administrators about the hunger strike, they said they were only shown paperwork about areas of the center not participating in the strike.

“They misled us about who was on a hunger strike and what the status of that was,” Dexter said.

“It makes it very hard to parse what is actually happening in these facilities when we are hearing separate accounts,” Randall said.

KIRO 7 reached out to ICE and The GEO Group, the company that operates the facility, for comment on the strike and conditions but did not hear back.

text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KOIN) — A demonstration held outside the Portland Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility is highlighting what organizers describe as modern parallels to World War II-era internment camps in the U.S.

“Never again is now” was one of the many slogans on signs held by demonstrators as part of an event called Oregon Peace Pilgrimage to End Family Detention.

In the summer of 1942, Portland had its own temporary detention center where nearly 3,700 Japanese people and their families were forced to live in deplorable conditions for several months.

Peggy Nagae is the Tsuru for Solidarity Oregon hub leader and a descendant of a Japanese American WWII camp survivor.

“They spent from May to September in this infestation of manure and flies and vermin until they were then carted off to Minidoka concentration camp,” Nagae said. “So that’s why we’re saying, we’re seeing history repeat itself and we must say, ‘No more!'”

Tsuru for Solidarity, Portland Japanese American Citizens League and Free Families: The National Coalition to End Family and Child Detention were among the groups organizing the event. They make the argument that modern-day ICE facilities represent a return to the kind of internment camps Japanese Americans endured during WWII.

In particular, the organizers are demanding that the Dilley Family Detention Center in Texas be shut down and that the U.S. put a stop to family detention and separation practices associated with ICE across the nation.

The Peace Pilgrimage event began earlier Sunday with an opening ceremony at the Portland Expo Center, the very site of the formerly named Portland Assembly Center that served as a Japanese-American internment camp. From there, demonstrators also went to the Japanese American Historical Plaza on Tom McCall Waterfront Park for a kickoff rally before heading to the ICE facility. The event was concluded later in the afternoon at the Nikkei Community Picnic at Oaks Park.

text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) -- Democrats on Saturday approved dueling messages on whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished or reformed, reflecting sharp opposition to President Donald Trump's crackdown but revealing disagreement in the party ahead of the midterms.

The Democratic National Committee, gathered for a summer meeting, also signed off on a raft of policy positions, including one that calls for "concrete reforms" of ICE and another for abolishing the agency that's been at the center of several fatal encounters.

ICE has been at the heart of a progressive rallying cry since 2018 during the first Trump administration, and has been renewed among some in the party after two recent fatal shootings by the agency in July.

Saturday's vote isn't binding and doesn't set the party's platform, which will be determined at the 2028 convention, but it reflects the party's differing views on a major issue. Candidates and lawmakers will continue to determine their own positions on the issue.

Michele Johnson, a DNC member from Louisiana who proposed the measure to abolish ICE, said it's time for Democrats to take a stand and pointed to the dissolution of ICE's predecessor agency, the Immigration and Naturalization Service, as a precedent.

"I think one of the reasons why people are not trusting the party is because we sound so academic," she said. "We sound focus group tested, we sound poll tested because we're worried about saying the wrong thing or doing the wrong thing and not just like, just stand on business, like take a position."

Not every DNC member was convinced, though. Yvonne Reeves-Chong voted against the measure, saying it would only gain support from a part of the party's base, while drawing "fire" from another group of voters.

"I would strongly suggest we get to the business of winning races so we can make the policies that make a difference," she said.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin, who's from Minnesota, where Renee Good and Alex Pretti were fatally shot amid the immigration crackdown earlier this year, said in an interview that the takeaway is that Democrats find the administration's handling of immigration, including by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, unacceptable.

"Clearly, the one thing that unites Democrats, regardless of their position on reform versus abolish or whatever other ways to change what's happening, is people believe that what ICE is doing right now -- and CBP and the federal government -- should stop," he said. "There has to be a better way."

Immigration remained a stronger issue for Trump than the economy or Iran, according to a poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research released this month, even after three people were killed in encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the span of under a week in July.

Overall, the survey found that only 39% of U.S. adults approve of his performance on immigration, down from 49% at the beginning of his second term.

text: Immigration policy remains one of the most complex and heavily debated subjects in modern politics, generating strong opinions across countries, communities, and political viewpoints. Recent discussions about stricter immigration measures have once again placed issues such as national security, border enforcement, human rights, economic needs, and social integration at the centre of public attention. As expected, these debates have produced sharply different perspectives about what a fair and effective immigration system should look like. Supporters of stronger immigration controls argue that every sovereign country has both the right and responsibility to determine who may legally enter and remain within its borders. They believe secure borders, reliable identity checks, effective screening procedures, and consistent enforcement of immigration laws are necessary to protect public safety and maintain confidence in the legal immigration system. Many also argue that humanitarian responsibilities must be balanced with available resources, national interests, and governments’ obligations toward their existing populations. Critics, however, warn that immigration policies should not unfairly discriminate against people simply because of their religion, ethnicity, nationality, or cultural identity. They emphasize equality before the law and argue that immigration decisions should primarily consider factors such as legal status, individual conduct, security assessments, eligibility requirements, and established immigration rules, rather than treating entire communities as potential threats. The wider debate demonstrates the difficult challenge faced by democracies around the world: balancing national security, economic requirements, social cohesion, humanitarian obligations, individual freedoms, and the rule of law. Immigration can contribute workers, entrepreneurs, students, investment, and cultural exchange, while poorly managed migration can also create genuine pressures on housing, public services, border systems, and integration. Ultimately, there is no single policy capable of resolving every immigration challenge. Effective systems require clear laws, secure borders, transparent procedures, reliable enforcement, and respect for fundamental rights. text:
A West Hollywood man was detained by federal immigration officers during what was supposed to be a routine check-in in downtown Los Angeles. Now, his friends and attorney are fighting his removal from the United States.

Alex Pereira Alves, a Brazilian national who friends say has lived in West Hollywood since 2010, was taken into federal custody after reporting for an immigration check-in on Aug. 11.

According to friends, Alves originally came to the United States from Brazil on a visa and had an open asylum case when, in 2018, an immigration judge granted him withholding of removal, allowing him to remain in the country as long as he stayed in good standing.

Alves has since been living and working legally in Southern California, including as a security guard and personal trainer.

That suddenly changed last week.

Within minutes of arriving for what was supposed to be a routine check-in, Alves was handcuffed and detained, his friends told KTLA’s Carlos Saucedo. He was later transferred to an immigration detention facility in Adelanto.

Friends say they were told Alves could potentially be removed to Guyana, a South American nation where they say he has never lived and has no ties.

Two of Alves’ friends, Jeff Markwardt and Ellie Guthrie, visited him at the detention facility and said they were concerned about his condition and whether he was receiving due process.

“He was very overwhelmed,” Guthrie told KTLA. “He looked very tired, and he’s kind of desperate because he doesn’t know exactly where he’s going.”

The pair said they are not asking authorities to give their friend special treatment but want his immigration case to proceed through the courts.

“We just came back from the detention facility yesterday,” Guthrie said. “It was terrible to see him that way, and it was heartbreaking.”

Both friends said Alves has complied with the conditions of his immigration case since the 2018 ruling.

“Everything he’s done has been legal from 2018 onward, in the sense that the judge allowed him to stay,” Markwardt said. “He has a valid asylum case.”

An attorney representing Alves has filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus challenging his detention, according to Markwardt.

“We’ve filed a habeas corpus petition with a lawyer he had previously engaged, and we provided her all the documentation,” he said. “She’s filed it, and we’re waiting for the federal government’s response.”

A federal judge has since temporarily put Alves’ deportation on hold while the case moves forward, and his attorney is expected to receive additional information about the case by the end of the week.

In the meantime, Alves’ friends have stepped in to care for his dog, Bella, who they said otherwise would have been left alone at his West Hollywood apartment.

KTLA has reached out to federal immigration authorities for additional information about Alves’ case.

text:
On 6 August 2026, the White House announced an executive order aimed at curbing birth tourism and strengthening enforcement of immigration rules governing temporary visa categories.

Background:

The order follows the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. Barbara1 and directs the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland Security to take measures against individuals and entities facilitating birth tourism.

The White House stated that the measure forms part of broader efforts to address perceived misuse of immigration pathways. In Trump v. Barbara, 609 U.S. ___ (2026), decided on 30 06 2026, the Supreme Court held that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the country are citizens at birth under the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Administration has nevertheless stated that the executive order is aimed at preventing what it describes as abuse of temporary visa classifications through birth tourism.

Also Read: Birthright Citizenship Dispute: United States Supreme Court Strikes Down Executive Order Restricting US Citizenship at Birth

Key Highlights:

The executive order defines “birth tourism” under Section 3, as entry into the United States on a non-immigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil, as well as efforts to facilitate such entry.

Authority under U.S. immigration law has been delegated to the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland Security to implement the order.

Federal agencies have been directed to update rules, policies, operational guidance and procedures necessary to implement the order.

The order permits authorities to take action against individuals seeking entry into the United States for the purpose of engaging in birth tourism.

Measures contemplated under the order include denial of visas or travel authorisations, revocation of existing permissions, denial of entry and, in appropriate cases, permanent bars on entry for persons engaging in birth tourism.

The order also authorises action against entities, organisations or individuals involved in facilitating birth tourism schemes.

Other executive departments and agencies are required to provide records and information necessary for implementation of the order, subject to applicable law.

The Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland Security may grant exemptions on humanitarian grounds or where entry is considered to be in the national interest.

The order contains a severability clause providing that if any provision is held invalid, the remaining provisions will continue to operate.

The Administration stated that the objective of the order is to ensure that non-immigrant visa categories are used only for their intended purposes and not as a means of obtaining immigration-related benefits through temporary admission.

text:
NEEDHAM, Mass. —

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu joined WCVB's "On the Record" to discuss public safety concerns, potential Immigration and Customs Enforcement expansion plans and her state Senate endorsements.

There have been a series of violent incidents in Boston this summer, including a deadly stabbing at South Station on Aug. 12. After the stabbing, Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn suggested the city get help from the National Guard.

Mayor Wu was asked to respond to the suggestion.

"It's one thing to call attention to the need to focus on public safety," she said. "It's another thing to be then specific and productive about what's actually leading to the incidents that we're dealing with today. Not a blanket, sort of, call for militarization of our streets which would be unsafe and unproductive."

The Mayor said the city is working to build out programs and partnerships, especially to address domestic violence.

As for immigration enforcement, the Democrat shared plans to try a new tactic to watch over ICE.

Last month, ICE posted a request to lease nearly 250 parking spots in downtown Boston. It was unclear if the agency would open a new facility or just expand its current Boston office.

Now, Mayor Wu is planning to use public records requests to identify private property owners who might be considering working with ICE as the agency seeks to expand its footprint.

"We strongly oppose any expansion of their efforts here, and would encourage and will be reaching out to property owners to try to ensure that they’re not adding to a surge of unlawful and dangerous activity," she said.

The Mayor also discussed how her political battles have inspired primary endorsements.

Wu has publicly sparred with State Senators Nick Collins and William Brownsberger over property tax proposals. Now, she is backing each of their primary challengers: Latoya Gayle and Daniel Lander.

"We have two senators here who represent Boston, but have not been carrying Boston's voice and interests throughout the entire state," she said.

Sen. Collins shared a statement with NewsCenter 5, writing in part: "We simply disagree on one aspect of her proposal, which has prompted her to go on a petty politics media tour."

Sen. Brownsberger shared a similar sentiment.

He wrote: "I'm still baffled as to why the Mayor has chosen to fight with me personally about this tax issue. I believe that partners in public service should be able to disagree from time to time about policy issues."

Mayor Wu was asked if she plans to weigh in on the race for governor by endorsing incumbent Governor Maura Healey.

"I am always going to vote for the Democrat in the race and Governor Healey has been a great partner for the city of Boston," she said.

text:
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

The Trump administration is continuing to push a program that partners state and local law enforcement with ICE. The program gives local police the power to enforce federal immigration laws, but details on how it works in different parts of the country have been hard to find. NPR's Jaclyn Diaz visited one community in Florida and joins us now. Hey, Jaclyn.

JACLYN DIAZ, BYLINE: Hey.

SCHMITZ: So this program is called the 287(g) program. It was expanded under the Trump administration. Jaclyn, let's take a step back and explain a little bit more about how it works.

DIAZ: Yeah, of course. So basically, this all actually started more than 30 years ago, and both Democratic and Republican administrations have used it. But as of this week, ICE has signed more than 2,300 contracts with local agencies across the country. So this gives officers in those agencies various powers for immigration enforcement. So that can look like interrogating people suspected of being in the U.S. illegally and arresting them. The federal government is giving a lot of money to local police who join this program. And nationwide, we are talking millions of dollars.

SCHMITZ: So, Jaclyn, I understand you recently visited Walton County, Florida, to find out how this program actually plays out on the ground, right?

DIAZ: Yeah, I did. Yep. So Walton County is this fast-growing community in the Florida panhandle. It borders Alabama to the north and the Gulf of Mexico to the south. Florida as a whole, leads the nation with the most law enforcement agencies with these 287(g) agreements, and some agencies are really going all-in, like Florida Highway Patrol. They reported 9,000 immigration encounters in the last year.

SCHMITZ: OK.

DIAZ: But not every department enrolled in this program sees immigration enforcement as a major priority. Some Florida sheriffs have expressed concern about going after immigrants who aren't committing crimes and who are just trying to build a life here. So in Walton County, there's a strong immigrant population. About 10% of residents are Hispanic. Immigrants do a lot of the work in construction and tourism. Those are the big industries in the area.

Michael Adkinson is the sheriff there. His office joined this partnership with ICE last year, and he says it's not his main priority. So according to state data, Walton County had a couple hundred immigration encounters. That's compared to Florida Highway Patrol, which again, reported thousands. Adkinson explained his approach like this.

MICHAEL ADKINSON: We're not doing immigration sweeps 'cause, quite frankly, we have day jobs here. We have other things that are critically important to the local people here that they expect to be done.

DIAZ: He says they are focused on people who commit crimes or pose a danger.

SCHMITZ: OK. So you mentioned Walton County has a pretty significant immigrant population. Did you speak to anyone in that community about how they feel about law enforcement's partnership with ICE?

DIAZ: Yeah, we did. We spoke with undocumented construction workers and a housing developer there, and they all said immigrants are really scared. A lot of them don't go out much. They pretty much just go to work and back. Two workers we spoke with said they think a lot about going back home to Central America.

But the program also has its supporters. Walton County is heavily Republican, and County Commissioner Danny Glidewell told me that residents back the sheriff's role in the 287(g) program.

SCHMITZ: That is NPR's Jaclyn Diaz. The story was co-reported with NPR's Marisa Peñaloza. Thank you.

DIAZ: Thank you.

title: Congressional Investigations: What To Expect In The 120th Congress - Mondaq
authors: Andrew M.  Wright, Andrew M. Wright, David Rybicki, Robert S. Silverblatt, Tara P. Ganapathy, Vivian K. Bridges
description:
Article Insights Congressional investigations have become an increasingly attractive tool for members of Congress.
Interactions With the Trump Administration Key Democratic congressional leaders have exhibited a clear interest in exploring the private sector’s interactions with the Trump administration.
Energy Companies Congressional Democrats will likely launch significant inquiries focused on energy policy as well.
Social Media Social media companies have experienced a deluge of congressional oversight across both Republican- and Democrat-led congresses.
The increasing importance of congressional investigations means that companies should begin planning now for any potential outcome of the midterm elections.
text:
Article Insights

Congressional investigations have become an increasingly attractive tool for members of Congress. During the 119th Congress, the Republican majority conducted extensive oversight activities, leveraging their investigative authorities to prime policy proposals, probe perceived malfeasance, and platform issues salient to their political priorities. For their part, Democrats developed oversight themes related to Trump administration conduct and interactions with the private sector. Come November, control of either or both congressional chambers may flip to Democrats, who have signaled an extensive and aggressive oversight agenda. Even if neither chamber flips, a Republican-led 120th Congress would almost certainly continue its heavy oversight activity. In either case, private sector organizations of all types, including nonprofits and corporations, should be prepared for significant congressional investigative activity. Below, we describe what that might look like under either scenario.

Democratic Oversight Priorities

Despite lacking the gavel during the 119th Congress, the Democratic ranking members of key congressional committees have been active in their oversight activities, providing valuable insight into what their priorities may be if given the gavel next year. We expect the following themes to be a heavy focus of any Democrat-led congressional chamber.

Interactions With the Trump Administration

Key Democratic congressional leaders have exhibited a clear interest in exploring the private sector’s interactions with the Trump administration. In particular, congressional Democrats will be interested in investigating any settlements, deals, or other formal or informal agreements between private sector entities and the administration. Indeed, key Democratic oversight leaders have already sent dozens of letters on topics such as law firm settlements, donations to the White House ballroom project, partnerships with Trump-affiliated companies, private sector investments in Trump administration federal projects, and private sector deals to avoid the imposition or full impact of blanket policies such as tariffs. Relatedly, major companies in industries where the Trump administration has relaxed regulations are likely to have any lobbying or advocacy activities placed under a microscope.

These investigations will likely take on the framework of anticorruption, transparency, and combating alleged self-dealing. Given that the executive branch enjoys constitutional privileges and procedural levers in congressional investigations that private sector entities do not, it is highly likely that many companies with perceived dealings with the Trump administration may find themselves targeted by Democrat-led oversight committees as proxies for the Trump administration.

Ranking members of congressional oversight committees have also sent numerous letters regarding issues such as insider trading conflicts of interest, self-enrichment, and the use of government power or public resources to benefit members or allies of the administration. This theme ran through inquiries into Trump family-linked defense contracts, Freedom 250 fundraising, and other matters involving public resources. Many of these inquiries centered on individuals that retain affiliation with private sector entities, and it is possible that these types of investigations will sweep in those entities.

Artificial Intelligence

Democratic oversight leaders have also signaled interest in conducting oversight of numerous entities related to artificial intelligence (AI). This includes AI labs, AI-forward companies, and entities associated with building or financing AI-related infrastructure. While oversight of AI has been a focus of Republicans as well as Democrats, Republicans have typically focused on supply chain security and potential influence by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Under a Democrat-led House or Senate, oversight of the AI sector will likely focus on themes such as environmental effects, consumer protection issues such as surveillance pricing, labor rights associated with increased automation, interactions with the Trump administration, and financial and operational transparency. While many Democrats will likely continue investigating supply chain and CCP-related issues concerning AI, these will likely take a back seat to broader concerns about the social, environmental, and commercial impact of AI.

Energy Companies

Congressional Democrats will likely launch significant inquiries focused on energy policy as well. A confluence of factors contributes to heavy Democratic interest in energy companies. First, Democrats will be looking to scrutinize Trump administration initiatives to “unleash American energy” and correspondingly roll back incentives for green energy. These kinds of investigations will likely focus on the industry’s advocacy activities, as well as the environmental impacts of energy production. Second, controversy surrounding the Trump administration’s activities in Venezuela and Iran garnered significant congressional interest in energy companies perceived to be in a position to benefit. It is also possible that Democrats will seek to investigate the commercial reasonableness of rising gas prices, or any resulting stagflation following a ceasefire, relative to facts on the ground.

Financial Institutions

Financial institutions will likely find themselves in congressional crosshairs with respect to investigations into a variety of issues. Democrats have signaled that, consistent with midterm campaign messaging, affordability and consumer protection issues will remain a central policy platform. Meanwhile, many Democratic members have expressed ire at the dissolution or paring back of financial regulators, such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. To that end, financial institutions should expect to see inquiries into consumer-facing issues, such as overdraft policies, or issues regarding structural conduct or regulatory rollbacks, such as capital requirements.

Social Media

Social media companies have experienced a deluge of congressional oversight across both Republican- and Democrat-led congresses. While the 119th Congress saw Republican-led committees focusing on issues such as free speech and online child protection, expect Democrat-led committees to home in on issues such as content moderation, detection and disclosure surrounding deepfakes, intellectual property, and mental health. Among a small—and, in fact, bipartisan—cadre of elected officials, there has also been a push to explore revisions to Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996. Moreover, Democrats, like Republicans, are likely to continue aggressively investigating issues around children’s online safety. Finally, here as in other contexts, companies that have had dealings with the Trump administration may have those interactions scrutinized.

Consumer Protection and Labor Issues

Across all private industry sectors, we expect Democrat-led investigations to focus on general consumer protection and labor issues. This will include issues such as dynamic pricing, labor contracting practices, any mergers or acquisitions perceived to be anticompetitive, privatization of public-facing services, and alleged price gouging. Within this bucket, unregulated or newly regulated industries, such as sports betting platforms, prediction markets, and certain types of crypto and crypto-adjacent companies, may encounter oversight attention.

Republican Oversight Priorities

Should the Republican Party maintain its majority in either chamber of Congress, we can expect to see a continuation of the oversight themes apparent from the 119th Congress.

Immigration Enforcement

Immigration policy generated significant oversight activity from Republican committee chairs. Investigations focused on state-level policies or practices, nonprofits and corporate entities associated with providing services to migrants, and nonprofits engaged in immigration-related advocacy. Inquiries into state and local entities focused on cooperation with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, detainer practices, and information sharing with federal officials, while investigations into nonprofits and private sector entities focused on organized protests and services rendered to undocumented migrants. Taken together, these activities reflected a sustained Republican effort to frame local immigration policies as public-safety and federal enforcement issues, while repetition across committees suggests this was one of the clearest organized oversight priorities on the Republican side. It is likely that Republicans will continue this trend if they hold onto either chamber of Congress.

CCP Influence, Research Security, and Strategic Competition

Republican committee chairs pursued wide-ranging inquiries tied to the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and the CCP during the 119th Congress, spanning national security, trade, research, and critical infrastructure. This Republican interest in PRC-related issues cut across industry sectors and target types. Investigations have focused on issues ranging from universities regarding their research programs, to pharmaceutical companies, to alleged funding by PRC-related entities of nonprofits, to entities with operations or partnerships in the PRC. Given the Trump administration’s focus on competition with the PRC, it is likely that Republican oversight interest in this issue will not wane in a 120th Congress.

Fraud and State Administration of Federal Programs

Significant congressional resources were dedicated to investigating alleged fraud in state-administered programs during the 119th Congress. Multiple key committees, including the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, led wide-ranging investigations into issues across a number of states and types of programs. In recent months, the fraud vertical has expanded to encompass contractors associated with states’ administration of these programs. It is likely that any state contracts will experience sustained congressional scrutiny with respect to fraud controls during the 120th Congress should Republicans retain a majority in either chamber of Congress.

Foreign Funders and Tax-Exempt Entities

Republican-led committees carried out extensive oversight activities with respect to nonprofits and foreign individuals or entities that allegedly have ties to domestic nonprofits. Investigations focused primarily on funding streams, alleged ties to foreign agents and governments, protest funding, and alleged partisan activity favoring Democrats. It is likely that if either congressional chamber says within Republican control, this oversight stream will continue.

Preparing for the 120th Congress

What does this all mean for private sector entities? During this era of political volatility, it is particularly important for companies to be prepared for any political scenario that might play out. Such preparation may involve internal diligence and risk assessments with respect to potential congressional oversight, ensuring your organization is integrated into the political arena through key congressional relationships to mitigate the impact of potential activity and ensuring access to bipartisan counsel able to leverage both investigations capability and, where needed, policy advocacy to navigate both Democrat-led and Republican-led congressional committees. This type of scenario planning is crucial in priming organizational leadership for potential oversight risk. The potential for a Democrat-led House and Republican-led Senate come January 2027 only compounds this consideration.

Companies with potential exposure should also begin planning now, well ahead of the midterms, for all potential outcomes. November will precipitate a sprint within the private sector to prepare ahead of the following Congress, and it is not uncommon for ranking members who know they will ascend to committee chair to start sending oversight letters in November of a midterm year. Companies must be nimble and able to respond swiftly to any incoming letters, which means having already done internal diligence to understand vulnerabilities and craft a public-facing narrative.

The increasing importance of congressional investigations means that companies should begin planning now for any potential outcome of the midterm elections. Retaining bipartisan, seasoned counsel is crucial for any entity seeking to minimize the legal and reputational risk associated with being the target of a congressional inquiry.
